item.title: 玩家改一条规则，世界就得跟着变：WorldRuler 指出两难——规则状态要持久、规则结果还得落到画面上 ｜ WorldRuler: Interactive World Modeling under Configurable Rules
item.description:
一句话：规则决定同样的场景与动作空间能玩出什么——生成式世界模型必须服从用户定义的规则，而不只是现实物理。

要点：

  • 问题提出得很锋利：**规则决定玩家动作如何改变交互世界**，同样的场景与动作空间，换一套规则就是另一种玩法；因此可定制玩法的世界模型必须遵循**用户定义的规则**，而不只是现实世界的物理行为
  • 两个具体难点：**规则状态持久（Rule-State Persistence）**——要保留规则定义、规则之间的依赖关系以及世界演化过程；以及**规则到视觉的实现（Rule-to-Visual Realization）**
  • WorldRuler 的连接方式是：把**可执行的 3D 规则图**接到视频生成与感知反馈上，从而在多次交互之间保住物体状态与规则依赖；再用**动态对象绑定**把符号实体锚定到视觉实例，用**属性替换**把规则结果翻译成针对性的视觉变化

为什么值得看：这是「引擎守规则、模型管画面」主线上第一次把「规则」当一等公民来做：不是物理仿真，而是**用户自定义玩法规则**。做生成式玩法或 AI 关卡时，这条给了「规则图 + 绑定 + 属性替换」三段式，是可以直接照抄的结构。

中文摘要：规则决定了玩家的动作如何改变交互世界：在相似的场景与动作空间里，不同的规则会带来完全不同的玩法体验。因此面向可定制玩法的生成式世界模型，必须遵循用户定义的规则，而不只是现实世界的物理行为。作者指出实现这一点有两个难点：一是规则状态持久，需要保留规则定义、规则之间的依赖关系以及世界如何演化；二是规则到视觉的实现。WorldRuler 的解法是把可执行的 3D 规则图与视频生成、感知反馈连接起来，从而在多次交互之间维持物体状态与规则依赖；其中动态对象绑定负责把符号实体锚定到具体的视觉实例上，属性替换则把规则产生的结果翻译成针对性的视觉变化。作者还构建了在 Habitat 与 GTA-V 中采集的成对数据集 RuleVerse，用于研究规则条件下的世界演化。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-19

本期推送：2026-11-20

WorldRuler: Interactive World Modeling under Configurable Rules

Abstract

Rules govern how player actions change interactive worlds. Different rules create distinct gameplay experiences within similar scenes and action spaces. For customizable gameplay, generative world models must follow user-defined rules beyond real-world behaviors. However, realizing user-defined rules presents two challenges: Rule-State Persistence and Rule-to-Visual Realization. The former requires preserving rule definitions, dependencies, and world states across saving and loading, so that restored worlds follow the established rules. The latter requires accurately realizing rule-induced changes on designated objects and attributes, particularly when affected objects are unseen. In this paper, we propose WorldRuler, which organizes rule definitions, dependencies, and object states in an executable 3D rule graph and connects rule execution, video generation, and perceptual feedback in a closed loop. The graph supports joint saving and restoration of rules and world states, while dynamic object binding grounds rule-specified entities in visual instances and uses stored states to constrain generation from their first appearance. We further introduce object attribute state replacement and counterfactual reconstruction training, enabling accurate attribute control and compatible appearance and motion changes while limiting interference with unrelated content. We develop an automated data collection and annotation pipeline using GTA-V and Habitat to construct RuleVerse, a dataset of rule-driven interactions with detailed state and event annotations, including cases where rules take effect before affected objects become visible. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of WorldRuler in preserving rule-state consistency across saving and loading and accurately realizing rule outcomes on designated objects and attributes.

††date: November 18, 2026††footnotetext: * Work done during internship at Alaya Lab, † Corresponding author, ‡ Project lead

1 Introduction

Rules govern the consequences of player actions, creating different gameplay goals and strategies even within similar scenes and action spaces [Hunicke et al. (2004)]. For example, Cat Mario subverts conventional game rules, where seemingly safe platforms collapse and power-ups can kill players, while It Takes Two introduces unique interaction rules, such as using nails to create paths across otherwise impassable gaps. These examples motivate generative game worlds [He et al. (2025); Chen et al. (2026a)] that consistently follow user-defined rules beyond conventional real-world behaviors.

Achieving this goal requires connecting user-defined interaction logic with world-state maintenance and visual generation. Code World Model [Chen et al. (2026b)] and Programmable World Model [Huang et al. (2026)] maintain executable world states and translate them into video generation conditions. Supporting persistent interaction requires both Rule-State Persistence across saving and loading and Rule-to-Visual Realization on designated visual instances.

Rule-State Persistence requires jointly preserving rule definitions, dependencies, and world states across saving and loading. As shown in Figure 1, consider a rule chain in which a sword attack defeats a monster, the monster drops a key, and the key unlocks a door. If the player saves before collecting the key, restoration must preserve the defeated monster, dropped key, closed door, and remaining rules. A restorable world must therefore retain the states and rule dependencies that govern future interactions, including information absent from the current view.

Rule-to-Visual Realization requires grounding rule-specified objects and attributes in visual instances to realize changes at the correct time. This is particularly important when the affected object is initially unseen [Duan et al. (2026); Gu et al. (2026)]. For example, if a switch opens a gate outside the current view, the gate should already be open when the player first sees it. The stored state must constrain this first appearance and remain effective in subsequent interactions. Graph representations provide structured conditions for object relations and interactions in video generation [Shah et al. (2026); Park et al. (2026)]. Custom rules further require persistent object binding and attribute control that supports compatible appearance and motion changes without disrupting unrelated content [Li et al. (2025); Chu et al. (2025)].

In this paper, we propose WorldRuler, which connects rule execution, video generation, and perceptual feedback through an executable 3D rule graph. The graph organizes rule definitions, dependencies, object identities, and attribute states together with spatial information. Rules and world states are saved and restored jointly, allowing subsequent actions to be evaluated against the restored conditions. Dynamic object binding associates rule-specified entities with visual instances and uses stored states to constrain generation from their first appearance. Perceptual feedback verifies generated outcomes and updates object correspondences and local geometry for subsequent binding and generation, while keeping rule-prescribed states separate from visual evidence.

To enforce these rule-prescribed states, we introduce an object attribute state replacement mechanism that reads object attribute states during denoising and replaces them according to the prescribed targets, correcting deviations in the controlled attributes. We complement this mechanism with counterfactual reconstruction training to produce coherent visual outcomes. Counterfactual reconstruction learns the visual realization of each state, while paired supervision encourages compatible changes and preservation of unrelated content. Training constrains these visual adjustments to remain compatible with the prescribed states, supporting the required appearance and motion changes while limiting interference with other objects and attributes.

To support counterfactual reconstruction training and rule consistency evaluation, we develop an automated data collection and annotation pipeline using GTA-V and Habitat [Puig et al. (2024)], resulting in RuleVerse, a dataset of rule-driven interactions with detailed annotations of object states, trigger conditions, rule consequences, and event timing. RuleVerse covers diverse triggers and state changes, multi-step rule dependencies, and rules that take effect before the affected objects become visible. RuleVerse supports the evaluation of rule-state consistency across saving and loading, the accurate realization of prescribed outcomes on designated objects and attributes, and preservation of unrelated content. Experiments on the public WorldState-Bench [Ki et al. (2026)] and our RuleVerse demonstrate the effectiveness of WorldRuler. In summary, our contributions are threefold:

  • •

    We propose WorldRuler, an executable 3D rule graph framework with dynamic object binding and perceptual feedback for rule persistence and visual realization.

  • •

    We introduce object attribute state replacement with counterfactual reconstruction training to realize prescribed changes while preserving unrelated content.

  • •

    We construct RuleVerse through automated data collection and annotation in GTA-V and Habitat, supporting counterfactual training and rule consistency evaluation.

    • 2 Related Work

    2.1 Video World Models

    Video world models predict observations from visual history and actions for exploration [Kim et al. (2020); Yang et al. (2024)]. Early methods learn environment dynamics and action-conditioned generation [Bruce et al. (2024); Alonso et al. (2024); Valevski et al. (2025)]. Recent work advances real-time control and long-horizon consistency. Yume1.5 [Mao et al. (2026)] combines context compression and attention distillation for real-time generation with text-controlled events. Long interactions, however, introduce inconsistencies when revisiting scenes. WorldPlay [Sun et al. (2025)] improves geometric consistency through reconstituted context memory. Matrix-Game 3.0 [Wang et al. (2026)] combines camera-aware memory retrieval and self-correction training. AlayaWorld [Team et al. (2026)] uses a streaming 3D point cache for spatiotemporal consistency. AlayaVista [Tan et al. (2026)] uses panoramic latent states and viewport rendering for perspective generation. Alaya-EVOKE [Yin et al. (2026)] combines external spatial memory with long-horizon supervision. Despite these advances, persistent adherence to user-defined rules remains insufficiently addressed. WorldRuler maintains rule states to constrain subsequent video generation.

    2.2 Controllable Video Generation

    Controllable video generation aims to realize specified changes while preserving unrelated content. Early methods use camera poses and motion trajectories for generation control [Wang et al. (2024); He et al. (2024); Yin et al. (2023)]. H3-World [Chen et al. (2026a)] translates language instructions into aligned character and camera controls. More complex object and structural changes require explicit representations. WorldCraft [Gu et al. (2026)] uses 3D representations and world-coordinate constraints for object manipulation. CustomX [Wang et al. (2025)] customizes characters, actions, and scenes using 3D assets. SolarRenderer [Fang et al. (2026)] adapts pretrained video generators to structured scene representations. GraphVid [Shah et al. (2026)] uses interaction graphs for multi-entity control. Park et al. [Park et al. (2026)] introduce graph-aligned denoising supervision through paired video-graph modifications. However, these methods do not explicitly maintain rule-dependent states across interactions. WorldRuler binds executable rule states to persistent visual instances and uses attribute replacement to realize prescribed changes on designated objects while preserving unrelated visual content.

    2.3 State and Rules in World Models

    Persistent states maintain interaction consequences beyond current observations. Early world models learn latent dynamics [Ha and Schmidhuber (2018); Hafner et al. (2025)], and structured representations capture object identities and spatial relationships [Wu et al. (2023)]. However, unobserved states cannot always be recovered from visual history. LiveWorld [Duan et al. (2026)] models dynamic objects outside the current view. Executable logic enables explicit control over state transitions. Code World Model [Chen et al. (2026b)] uses a coding agent to maintain world states and compile them into proxy videos. Programmable World Model [Huang et al. (2026)] maintains global states through executable programs and converts them into spatial generation conditions. State World Models [Ki et al. (2026)] execute interaction rules and updates states using generated observations. Building on explicit state maintenance and rule execution, WorldRuler jointly restores rule definitions, dependencies, and execution states, ensuring their consequences are realized on designated visual instances.

    3 WorldRuler

    3.1 Problem Formulation and Overview

    Given an initial visual observation I₀, user-defined rules ℝ, and a sequence of player actions, WorldRuler generates interactive videos that follow these rules. An executable 3D rule graph Gₜ maintains rule definitions and dependencies, an execution state Xₜ records object attributes and rule progress, and bindings Bₜ associate rule entities with 3D objects and visual instances. Together, these representations determine subsequent interactions and persist when objects leave the view or a session is saved.

    As shown in Fig. 2, generation proceeds in consecutive windows. For window n, the executor evaluates actions Uₙ against the current state and produces a sequence of object states Sₙ. These states and their spatial bindings form generation conditions Cₙ

    V̂ₙ∼p_θ,φ (Vₙ|I₀,Hₙ,Uₙ,Cₙ),(1)
    Cₙ=Condition (Gₙ,Bₙ,Sₙ),

    where Hₙ denotes previously generated visual context, θ denotes the video generator parameters, and φ denotes trainable attribute replacement parameters. The state sequence follows from actions and rule execution within the current window, without future outcomes from reference videos. Object binding identifies where rule targets apply, attribute replacement corrects those regions during denoising, and perception updates correspondences and event evidence for subsequent windows. The graph and its joint checkpoint support Rule-State Persistence, while binding and replacement support Rule-to-Visual Realization.

    3.2 Executable 3D Rule Graph and Persistence

    The rule graph organizes object identities, spatial information, and interaction logic in a shared representation. Object nodes carry persistent identities, semantic descriptions, 3D support, and attribute states. Rule nodes specify triggers, state preconditions, and effect assignments. Typed edges distinguish action subjects, action targets, precondition objects, and effect targets, allowing a consequence to occur away from its trigger. Shared attributes and event conditions express dependencies between rules. For example, collecting a key changes the possession state required by an unlocking rule. Initial objects and spatial information are established from the initial observation and available scene geometry. References to objects that cannot yet be localized remain in the graph for later binding.

    Let Sₜ collect object attributes and let qₜ contain event history, rule activation records, transition progress, and pending effects. The execution state is Xₜ=(Sₜ,qₜ) and evolves according to

    Xₜ₊₁=Execute_ℝ (Xₜ,uₜ,eₜ),

    		(2)

    where uₜ is the current action and eₜ is accepted event evidence. The executor evaluates action, state, spatial, and event-order conditions before assigning effects to their designated objects. Rules requiring action completion consume confirmed completion events, so an action request alone does not satisfy them. Unknown attributes remain explicitly unknown and cannot satisfy a precondition through negation.

    For changes with a duration, the state records current values, targets, and transition progress. Generation receives the effective value at each time, while dependent predicates respect transition completion. This prevents a partially opening door from prematurely satisfying an open-door condition. Effects on invisible objects persist in the state. When an effect target is unresolved, the system retains its description, rule provenance, and event time until the target can be bound.

    A checkpoint jointly serializes the graph, execution state, and bindings

    ℂₜ=Save (Gₜ,Xₜ,Bₜ),(3)
    Load(ℂₜ)=(Gₜ,Xₜ,Bₜ).

    The checkpoint path in Fig. 2 restores rule definitions, object identities, and execution progress so that subsequent actions continue from the saved conditions. For example, a checkpoint taken after defeating a monster but before collecting its key retains the defeated monster, the key on the ground, the closed door, and the remaining collection and unlocking rules. Continuing generation additionally requires visual boundary context corresponding to the restored state. Images may vary with sampling, while identical subsequent actions and event evidence should produce consistent rule decisions.

    3.3 Dynamic Object Binding and Perceptual Feedback

    Dynamic object binding first identifies which scene instance a rule addresses and then determines where that instance can be controlled in the current view. Semantic, appearance, and spatial consistency associate candidate instances with rule entities, and Bₜ stores these correspondences. Objects of the same category retain distinct identities, while viewpoint changes, occlusion, and reappearance preserve established bindings. For localized objects, camera projection and instance segmentation [Ravi et al. (2024)] provide spatiotemporal masks Mᵢ, restricted by visibility and occlusion.

    Rules can update an object’s persistent state while it is invisible. Given an established 3D binding, the stored state is assigned to the projected region before generating the window in which the object first appears. A gate opened outside the view is therefore conditioned as open from its first appearance, without repeating the opening action. Effects on entirely unlocalized entities remain pending until reliable correspondences become available. First-appearance control thus depends on spatial grounding established before generation.

    The executed scene geometry guides layout, camera motion, and object motion, while effective states and changes form global and object-level visual descriptions. Each local condition specifies an identity, spatiotemporal support, and structured attribute targets. Surface changes use object surface support, while motion and deformation cover the current geometry and rule-executed trajectory, excluding foreground occluders and unrelated instances. Unknown attributes are omitted from local control, and completed changes persist as resulting-state conditions.

    Perception independently estimates identity, visibility, visual attributes, and action completion from generated frames, without receiving desired rule outcomes as answer cues. Evidence passing identity, confidence, and temporal validity checks updates bindings, local geometry, and ordinary observable state, and supplies events for subsequent rules that require visual confirmation. Rule-prescribed states and observed outcomes are recorded separately. If a gate appears closed despite an open-state requirement, the prescribed state is retained, and the observed discrepancy guides correction in subsequent generation windows. Feedback affects only windows generated after its acceptance, without rewriting delivered video or treating unconfirmed outcomes as successful.

    3.4 Object Attribute State Replacement

    Object binding determines the support of an edit, and attribute state replacement adjusts its visual representation to the rule target. Figure 3(a) expands the Replace module in the overview into local attribute reading, target correction, and insertion into the sampling update.

    Reading Local Attributes.

    Let z_σ denote the video latent at noise level σ>0 and let v_θ be the predicted velocity. Under the generator’s parameterization, the clean estimate is

    ẑ₀=z_σ+σv_θ(z_σ,σ,Cₙ).

    		(4)

    We omit window and latent-frame indices below. Pooling over the object mask yields local features aᵢ=Pool_Mᵢ(ẑ₀). Dynamic regions map to a fixed canonical grid within the object bounds, using only cells with valid spatial support.

    A frozen affine reader estimates current attributes from visual features as ŝᵢ=Aᵢaᵢ+bᵢ. It is fitted independently on annotated real training videos and receives no rule targets. Rule execution supplies the currently effective target sᵢ^⋆, yielding the discrepancy δᵢ=sᵢ^⋆-ŝᵢ.

    Attribute Correction and Compatible Adjustment.

    We separate direct attribute correction from compatible visual adjustments, as satisfying the attribute readout alone does not guarantee coherent appearance and motion changes. Here, Aᵢ contains only rows for currently known and controllable attributes. When these attributes are independently identifiable and Aᵢ has full row rank, define

    Bᵢ=Aᵢ^⊤(AᵢAᵢ^⊤)⁻¹, Qᵢ=I-BᵢAᵢ.

    		(5)

    The right inverse Bᵢ maps attribute discrepancies into feature space, while Qᵢ projects additional adjustments into the reader’s null space. Adding both corrections to the original features defines the local replacement operator T_φ

    aᵢ^′=T_φ(aᵢ,sᵢ^⋆)=aᵢ+Bᵢδᵢ+γ(δᵢ) Qᵢf_φ (aᵢ,hᵢ,ŝᵢ,sᵢ^⋆,σ),

    		(6)

    where hᵢ denotes local context, f_φ is a trainable writer, and γ(δ)=\min(\lVertδ\rVert_∞,c) for a fixed cap c. The term Bᵢδᵢ corrects attribute coordinates, while the branch constrained by Qᵢ learns compatible appearance and motion changes without altering the prescribed readout. Since AᵢBᵢ=I and AᵢQᵢ=0, full replacement satisfies

    Aᵢaᵢ^′+bᵢ=sᵢ^⋆.

    		(7)

    Both corrections vanish when the discrepancy is zero, preserving features that already satisfy the target. Multiple active attributes are solved jointly to avoid conflicting sequential writes. Equation (7) constrains learned attribute coordinates, while decoded visual semantics and content preservation are evaluated independently on generated videos.

    Writing Back to Denoising.

    Local corrections are inserted into the current clean estimate and used to update the sampling velocity. For disjoint object supports,

    ẑ₀^′=ẑ₀+∑ᵢScatter_Mᵢ(aᵢ^′-aᵢ),(8)
    v_θ^′=v_θ+(ẑ₀^′-ẑ₀)/(σ).

    The sampler uses v_θ^′ to advance to the next denoising step, incorporating rule corrections into the generation trajectory. Scattering is constructed as a right inverse of pooling over valid canonical cells, and compatible constraints on overlapping supports are solved jointly in their shared latent region. Writes exclude fixed history boundaries, invisible regions, and unauthorized attributes. Latents outside the support receive no direct correction.

    3.5 Counterfactual Reconstruction and Attribute Swapping

    As shown in Fig. 3(b), we train the same replacement operator using video pairs (V⁽⁰⁾,V⁽¹⁾) aligned by scene, action context, and rule events. The branches share scene, camera, and action context while differing in rule-specified attribute states. Each uses its own true states and visual outcomes, including changes caused by ordinary actions when the designated rule is disabled. Encoding yields local targets a⁽⁰⁾,a⁽¹⁾ with attributes s⁽⁰⁾,s⁽¹⁾. Unknown, invisible, and padded samples are excluded from the losses.

    We first fit a regularized affine reader on real local features and check attribute identifiability. We then freeze the reader, video generator, and visual encoder, optimizing only the writer parameters φ. Real paired videos provide training supervision, while inference conditions come from the initial observation, generated history, and rule execution.

    Counterfactual Reconstruction.

    We extract a local estimate ā_σ from a denoising trajectory and supply it to two shared replacement branches with targets s⁽⁰⁾ and s⁽¹⁾. Write ã⁽ᵏ⁾=T_φ(ā_σ,s⁽ᵏ⁾), omitting the shared context and noise level. Reconstruction and difference losses are

    L_rec=𝔼 [1/2∑_k∈{0,1}\lVertã⁽ᵏ⁾-a⁽ᵏ⁾\rVert₂²],(9)
    L_diff=𝔼 [\lVert(ã⁽¹⁾-ã⁽⁰⁾)-(a⁽¹⁾-a⁽⁰⁾)\rVert₂²].

    Shared inputs require the output difference to arise from the state condition. Reconstruction learns each state’s visual realization, while difference supervision targets the visual change associated with the attribute change.

    Bidirectional Attribute Swapping.

    Swapping starts from one real local representation, writes the other branch’s attributes, and reconstructs the corresponding target

    L_swap=𝔼 [1/2∑_k∈{0,1}\lVertT_φ(a⁽ᵏ⁾,s⁽¹⁻ᵏ⁾)-a⁽¹⁻ᵏ⁾\rVert₂²].

    		(10)

    Swapping uses clean inputs at zero noise level and changes only the supervised attribute targets. Alignment of unrelated content across the pair lets this objective supervise both attribute changes and local content preservation. The total objective is

    L=L_rec+λ_diffL_diff+λ_swapL_swap.

    		(11)

    All losses are normalized over valid object and temporal support. Counterfactual reconstruction learns to realize prescribed states, difference supervision constrains rule-induced visual changes, and attribute swapping encourages compatible adjustments while preserving unrelated content. Local insertion further limits the direct spatial extent of these changes.

    4 RuleVerse

    RuleVerse contains paired rule-driven interaction videos collected in Habitat [Puig et al. (2024)] and GTA-V, covering indoor object interactions and open game environments. Each pair shares scene configurations and action intent but differs in whether a designated rule mechanism is enabled, producing distinct state evolutions. The rule-disabled branch retains ordinary actions and other native reactions, so triggering conditions may still hold. Solo samples examine a designated rule, while Full samples cover multi-rule scripts, including explicit dependencies between earlier outcomes and later conditions in Habitat.

    4.1 Data Collection and Annotation

    Simulation-based pipelines enable automated collection of visual data with detailed ground-truth annotations [Greff et al. (2022)]. Figure 4 illustrates our data collection process. We first inspect native objects, parts, spatial relations, and initial states, together with interaction capabilities, reachable paths, and interaction and observation positions. Trigger and effect combinations are selected according to scene capabilities, prioritizing underrepresented categories during collection. For custom rules, a language model produces a rulebook containing natural-language descriptions, executable conditions, and state assignments, together with an interaction script. Code checks object bindings, syntax, initial conditions, and execution feasibility. Habitat collection additionally screens rule quality before recording. A compiler translates scripts into navigation, interaction, and camera controls bound to concrete entities.

    Both branches execute from their corresponding initial configurations. Habitat reuses the same action and camera control plan. GTA-V includes both custom rules and interventions on native mechanisms. Disabling custom rules preserves native game reactions, while native interventions suppress only the documented mechanism. GTA-V pairs share scene configurations and temporally aligned state and event annotations, while allowing minor variations in character motions due to engine dynamics.

    Recording stores videos, object identities, action events, and state trajectories, together with trigger conditions, effect timing, and task outcomes. For Habitat, an independent interpreter recomputes conditions and effects from state and event logs, followed by checks of paired controls, video integrity, and annotation correspondence, and deduplication using decoded videos. GTA-V retains native execution and observation records, with checks of pair structure and video file identity. Habitat annotations align to video frames, while GTA-V preserves the temporal mapping and synchronization uncertainty between screen recordings and engine logs. Visibility and event timing distinguish when a rule takes effect from when its target enters the view. Public inputs contain initial images, rules, and requested actions, while reference videos and subsequent state annotations remain on the answer side.

    4.2 Dataset Statistics

    The dataset contains 3,200 pairs and 6,400 videos, with 2,900 pairs for training and 300 for testing. Habitat is split by base scene, while GTA-V groups samples by source scene and spatial proximity before splitting. We characterize the dataset through rule combinations, object binding, activation timing, and dependence on action history.

    As shown in Figure 5(a), the heatmaps summarize the joint distribution of each pair’s primary trigger and effect categories. The five trigger families cover actions, spatial conditions, relations, states, and sequences. The displayed effects include changes in attributes, geometry, and object presence, together with topology changes in Habitat and behavior changes in GTA-V. Each heatmap is normalized over the sample pairs within its displayed effect categories. Habitat exhibits a more even distribution across these combinations, while GTA-V places greater emphasis on action-triggered effects.

    As shown in Figure 5(b), executed rules are categorized into single-object binding, cross-object binding, and environment effects. Cross-object rules reference multiple non-actor object or part identities across their conditions and effects, accounting for 60.2% of Habitat rules and 40.2% of GTA-V rules. Single-object rules involve one such identity, while environment effects modify scene-level properties or routes. These categories cover interactions involving individual objects, interactions involving multiple objects, and changes to the surrounding environment.

    As shown in Figure 5(c), the first activation occurs in the second half of the video for 75.4% of Habitat rules and 61.1% of GTA-V rules. In addition, 18.9% and 19.3% of rules, respectively, require action history through ordered actions or cumulative event counts. These distributions include cases in which rule conditions must remain available until later interactions and cases whose activation depends on preceding actions.

    4.3 Metrics

    We evaluate rule realization using Rule Success Rate (RSR) and Full Completion Rate (FCR). RSR comprises five components evaluated over annotated rule events in rule-enabled videos, while rule-disabled videos provide counterfactual references for evaluating rule-specific changes. Identity measures whether the relevant trigger objects and effect targets match their reference identities. Trigger assesses whether the specified trigger condition is visibly satisfied. Effect evaluates whether the prescribed change is realized on the target. Timing checks whether the effect begins after the trigger and becomes established within the specified time window. Hold measures whether the resulting state persists over the required observation interval.

    FCR evaluates complete multi-stage tasks through three components. Stages measures the proportion of tasks in which all required rule events are successfully realized, rather than the average success rate of individual stages. Order assesses whether all required stages occur in the prescribed chronological order, and Goal checks whether the final task goal is visibly achieved at the end of the video. The average FCR is the arithmetic mean of these three independently evaluated components.

    Visual judgments are obtained using a frozen vision-language evaluator with fixed-choice questions and initial identity references. Generated videos are sampled at 3 fps, including the first and last frames. The same judging protocol is applied to all compared methods. Uncertain or invalid judgments remain in the corresponding denominators and receive no success credit. All scores are reported as percentages.

    5 Experiments

    Our experiments evaluate WorldRuler along two dimensions: Rule-State Persistence and Rule-to-Visual Realization. We first compare rule realization and task-level performance on RuleVerse, followed by an external evaluation on WorldState-Bench. We then examine dynamic object binding, attribute state replacement, and the swapping objective through component ablations, and evaluate perceptual and visual consistency after saving and loading. Qualitative examples illustrate how the runtime produces different outcomes under enabled and disabled rule mechanisms.

    5.1 Implementation

    We use the MiniMax-H3 Ref2VA Turbo for video generation at a resolution of 1344×768 and 24 fps. Each generation window contains 124 frames. We use the native H3 Qwen encoder for generation conditioning, along with Qwen3.8-Max [Qwen Team (2026)], SAM2 [Ravi et al. (2024)], and DA3 [Lin et al. (2026)] for visual observations, instance segmentation, and geometry estimation.

    Attribute state replacement is applied to local clean estimates at each denoising step, with corrections written back before the next sampling update. Following Sec. 3.5, we first fit the affine attribute reader, then freeze the reader, video generator, and visual encoder while optimizing only the attribute writer. Training uses paired reconstruction, paired difference, and bidirectional attribute swapping losses, excluding unknown attributes, invisible regions, and padded frames.

    5.2 Main Results

    RuleVerse.

    As shown in Table 1, WorldRuler outperforms the compared baselines across both the Habitat and GTA-V subsets. On the Habitat subset, it achieves average RSR and FCR scores of 64.99% and 48.04%, exceeding SWM by 20.93 and 30.06 percentage points, respectively. Compared with SWM, effect accuracy increases from 20.74% to 58.47%, timing accuracy from 15.67% to 37.36%, and hold accuracy from 17.05% to 50.83%. WorldRuler also improves all three task-level components, reaching 52.61% for stages, 44.38% for order, and 47.12% for goal. These results support the effectiveness of combining explicit rule execution with state-conditioned generation for realizing rule effects and dependent interactions.

    On the GTA-V subset, WorldRuler achieves an average RSR of 67.42%, compared with 44.19% for SWM and 43.43% for MiniMax-H3. It obtains 60.00% for stages, 60.00% for order, and 80.00% for goal, yielding the highest average FCR of 66.66%. The improvements across RuleVerse indicate that the framework benefits indoor object interactions as well as open game environments.

    WorldState-Bench.

    We evaluate the complete WorldRuler framework on the 50 official WorldState-Bench [Ki et al. (2026)] pairs using the benchmark’s original judging protocol. This configuration uses a single 124-frame window, resolves the submitted action and rules before generation, and permits up to two feedback corrections before publishing the clip. The evaluation includes the trained attribute state replacement module alongside rule execution, dynamic object binding, and perceptual feedback.

    As shown in Table 2, WorldRuler matches SWM on EndFollow, TwinContrast, and Strict, while achieving higher scores on PairFollow, CntAbsent, and PairStrict. These three scores reach 94%, 99%, and 92%, compared with 92%, 98%, and 90% for SWM. WorldRuler improves PairFollow and PairStrict by two percentage points each over SWM. These results indicate competitive performance on an external rule-following benchmark, with modest gains over SWM under the reported configurations.

    5.3 Ablation Study

    We conduct ablation studies on the Habitat subset of RuleVerse to examine the contributions of dynamic object binding, attribute state replacement, and the swapping objective, as well as the information required for save/load persistence.

    Component Ablation.

    We examine dynamic object binding, attribute state replacement, and the swapping objective on the Habitat subset of RuleVerse. Alongside RSR and FCR, we evaluate First-appearance and Preservation. First-appearance measures whether targets affected by rules while off-screen exhibit the correct identities and prescribed attributes upon entering the view and during the immediately following observation interval. Preservation measures whether unrelated objects and attributes remain intact, excluding changes permitted by ordinary actions or the rules.

    As shown in Table 3, the full method achieves the highest scores across all four metrics. Replacing dynamic object binding with fixed binding reduces average RSR from 64.99% to 48.09% and First-appearance from 29.69% to 20.58%, supporting the importance of updating object correspondences when applying persistent rule states to visual instances. Removing attribute state replacement reduces average RSR and FCR by 18.56 and 9.54 percentage points, respectively, while also lowering First-appearance and Preservation. These results support local attribute replacement as a contributor to rule realization and content preservation.

    Removing the swapping objective reduces average RSR to 51.24%, First-appearance to 6.45%, and Preservation to 20.63%. Its first-appearance score is also lower than that obtained without attribute replacement, suggesting that the effectiveness of the learned replacement module depends on its training objective. The full method improves both first-appearance correctness and preservation.
item.content:encoded:
一句话：规则决定同样的场景与动作空间能玩出什么——生成式世界模型必须服从用户定义的规则，而不只是现实物理。

要点：

  • 问题提出得很锋利：**规则决定玩家动作如何改变交互世界**，同样的场景与动作空间，换一套规则就是另一种玩法；因此可定制玩法的世界模型必须遵循**用户定义的规则**，而不只是现实世界的物理行为
  • 两个具体难点：**规则状态持久（Rule-State Persistence）**——要保留规则定义、规则之间的依赖关系以及世界演化过程；以及**规则到视觉的实现（Rule-to-Visual Realization）**
  • WorldRuler 的连接方式是：把**可执行的 3D 规则图**接到视频生成与感知反馈上，从而在多次交互之间保住物体状态与规则依赖；再用**动态对象绑定**把符号实体锚定到视觉实例，用**属性替换**把规则结果翻译成针对性的视觉变化

为什么值得看：这是「引擎守规则、模型管画面」主线上第一次把「规则」当一等公民来做：不是物理仿真，而是**用户自定义玩法规则**。做生成式玩法或 AI 关卡时，这条给了「规则图 + 绑定 + 属性替换」三段式，是可以直接照抄的结构。

中文摘要：规则决定了玩家的动作如何改变交互世界：在相似的场景与动作空间里，不同的规则会带来完全不同的玩法体验。因此面向可定制玩法的生成式世界模型，必须遵循用户定义的规则，而不只是现实世界的物理行为。作者指出实现这一点有两个难点：一是规则状态持久，需要保留规则定义、规则之间的依赖关系以及世界如何演化；二是规则到视觉的实现。WorldRuler 的解法是把可执行的 3D 规则图与视频生成、感知反馈连接起来，从而在多次交互之间维持物体状态与规则依赖；其中动态对象绑定负责把符号实体锚定到具体的视觉实例上，属性替换则把规则产生的结果翻译成针对性的视觉变化。作者还构建了在 Habitat 与 GTA-V 中采集的成对数据集 RuleVerse，用于研究规则条件下的世界演化。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-19

本期推送：2026-11-20

WorldRuler: Interactive World Modeling under Configurable Rules

Abstract

Rules govern how player actions change interactive worlds. Different rules create distinct gameplay experiences within similar scenes and action spaces. For customizable gameplay, generative world models must follow user-defined rules beyond real-world behaviors. However, realizing user-defined rules presents two challenges: Rule-State Persistence and Rule-to-Visual Realization. The former requires preserving rule definitions, dependencies, and world states across saving and loading, so that restored worlds follow the established rules. The latter requires accurately realizing rule-induced changes on designated objects and attributes, particularly when affected objects are unseen. In this paper, we propose WorldRuler, which organizes rule definitions, dependencies, and object states in an executable 3D rule graph and connects rule execution, video generation, and perceptual feedback in a closed loop. The graph supports joint saving and restoration of rules and world states, while dynamic object binding grounds rule-specified entities in visual instances and uses stored states to constrain generation from their first appearance. We further introduce object attribute state replacement and counterfactual reconstruction training, enabling accurate attribute control and compatible appearance and motion changes while limiting interference with unrelated content. We develop an automated data collection and annotation pipeline using GTA-V and Habitat to construct RuleVerse, a dataset of rule-driven interactions with detailed state and event annotations, including cases where rules take effect before affected objects become visible. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of WorldRuler in preserving rule-state consistency across saving and loading and accurately realizing rule outcomes on designated objects and attributes.

††date: November 18, 2026††footnotetext: * Work done during internship at Alaya Lab, † Corresponding author, ‡ Project lead

1 Introduction

Rules govern the consequences of player actions, creating different gameplay goals and strategies even within similar scenes and action spaces [Hunicke et al. (2004)]. For example, Cat Mario subverts conventional game rules, where seemingly safe platforms collapse and power-ups can kill players, while It Takes Two introduces unique interaction rules, such as using nails to create paths across otherwise impassable gaps. These examples motivate generative game worlds [He et al. (2025); Chen et al. (2026a)] that consistently follow user-defined rules beyond conventional real-world behaviors.

Achieving this goal requires connecting user-defined interaction logic with world-state maintenance and visual generation. Code World Model [Chen et al. (2026b)] and Programmable World Model [Huang et al. (2026)] maintain executable world states and translate them into video generation conditions. Supporting persistent interaction requires both Rule-State Persistence across saving and loading and Rule-to-Visual Realization on designated visual instances.

Rule-State Persistence requires jointly preserving rule definitions, dependencies, and world states across saving and loading. As shown in Figure 1, consider a rule chain in which a sword attack defeats a monster, the monster drops a key, and the key unlocks a door. If the player saves before collecting the key, restoration must preserve the defeated monster, dropped key, closed door, and remaining rules. A restorable world must therefore retain the states and rule dependencies that govern future interactions, including information absent from the current view.

Rule-to-Visual Realization requires grounding rule-specified objects and attributes in visual instances to realize changes at the correct time. This is particularly important when the affected object is initially unseen [Duan et al. (2026); Gu et al. (2026)]. For example, if a switch opens a gate outside the current view, the gate should already be open when the player first sees it. The stored state must constrain this first appearance and remain effective in subsequent interactions. Graph representations provide structured conditions for object relations and interactions in video generation [Shah et al. (2026); Park et al. (2026)]. Custom rules further require persistent object binding and attribute control that supports compatible appearance and motion changes without disrupting unrelated content [Li et al. (2025); Chu et al. (2025)].

In this paper, we propose WorldRuler, which connects rule execution, video generation, and perceptual feedback through an executable 3D rule graph. The graph organizes rule definitions, dependencies, object identities, and attribute states together with spatial information. Rules and world states are saved and restored jointly, allowing subsequent actions to be evaluated against the restored conditions. Dynamic object binding associates rule-specified entities with visual instances and uses stored states to constrain generation from their first appearance. Perceptual feedback verifies generated outcomes and updates object correspondences and local geometry for subsequent binding and generation, while keeping rule-prescribed states separate from visual evidence.

To enforce these rule-prescribed states, we introduce an object attribute state replacement mechanism that reads object attribute states during denoising and replaces them according to the prescribed targets, correcting deviations in the controlled attributes. We complement this mechanism with counterfactual reconstruction training to produce coherent visual outcomes. Counterfactual reconstruction learns the visual realization of each state, while paired supervision encourages compatible changes and preservation of unrelated content. Training constrains these visual adjustments to remain compatible with the prescribed states, supporting the required appearance and motion changes while limiting interference with other objects and attributes.

To support counterfactual reconstruction training and rule consistency evaluation, we develop an automated data collection and annotation pipeline using GTA-V and Habitat [Puig et al. (2024)], resulting in RuleVerse, a dataset of rule-driven interactions with detailed annotations of object states, trigger conditions, rule consequences, and event timing. RuleVerse covers diverse triggers and state changes, multi-step rule dependencies, and rules that take effect before the affected objects become visible. RuleVerse supports the evaluation of rule-state consistency across saving and loading, the accurate realization of prescribed outcomes on designated objects and attributes, and preservation of unrelated content. Experiments on the public WorldState-Bench [Ki et al. (2026)] and our RuleVerse demonstrate the effectiveness of WorldRuler. In summary, our contributions are threefold:

  • •

    We propose WorldRuler, an executable 3D rule graph framework with dynamic object binding and perceptual feedback for rule persistence and visual realization.

  • •

    We introduce object attribute state replacement with counterfactual reconstruction training to realize prescribed changes while preserving unrelated content.

  • •

    We construct RuleVerse through automated data collection and annotation in GTA-V and Habitat, supporting counterfactual training and rule consistency evaluation.

    • 2 Related Work

    2.1 Video World Models

    Video world models predict observations from visual history and actions for exploration [Kim et al. (2020); Yang et al. (2024)]. Early methods learn environment dynamics and action-conditioned generation [Bruce et al. (2024); Alonso et al. (2024); Valevski et al. (2025)]. Recent work advances real-time control and long-horizon consistency. Yume1.5 [Mao et al. (2026)] combines context compression and attention distillation for real-time generation with text-controlled events. Long interactions, however, introduce inconsistencies when revisiting scenes. WorldPlay [Sun et al. (2025)] improves geometric consistency through reconstituted context memory. Matrix-Game 3.0 [Wang et al. (2026)] combines camera-aware memory retrieval and self-correction training. AlayaWorld [Team et al. (2026)] uses a streaming 3D point cache for spatiotemporal consistency. AlayaVista [Tan et al. (2026)] uses panoramic latent states and viewport rendering for perspective generation. Alaya-EVOKE [Yin et al. (2026)] combines external spatial memory with long-horizon supervision. Despite these advances, persistent adherence to user-defined rules remains insufficiently addressed. WorldRuler maintains rule states to constrain subsequent video generation.

    2.2 Controllable Video Generation

    Controllable video generation aims to realize specified changes while preserving unrelated content. Early methods use camera poses and motion trajectories for generation control [Wang et al. (2024); He et al. (2024); Yin et al. (2023)]. H3-World [Chen et al. (2026a)] translates language instructions into aligned character and camera controls. More complex object and structural changes require explicit representations. WorldCraft [Gu et al. (2026)] uses 3D representations and world-coordinate constraints for object manipulation. CustomX [Wang et al. (2025)] customizes characters, actions, and scenes using 3D assets. SolarRenderer [Fang et al. (2026)] adapts pretrained video generators to structured scene representations. GraphVid [Shah et al. (2026)] uses interaction graphs for multi-entity control. Park et al. [Park et al. (2026)] introduce graph-aligned denoising supervision through paired video-graph modifications. However, these methods do not explicitly maintain rule-dependent states across interactions. WorldRuler binds executable rule states to persistent visual instances and uses attribute replacement to realize prescribed changes on designated objects while preserving unrelated visual content.

    2.3 State and Rules in World Models

    Persistent states maintain interaction consequences beyond current observations. Early world models learn latent dynamics [Ha and Schmidhuber (2018); Hafner et al. (2025)], and structured representations capture object identities and spatial relationships [Wu et al. (2023)]. However, unobserved states cannot always be recovered from visual history. LiveWorld [Duan et al. (2026)] models dynamic objects outside the current view. Executable logic enables explicit control over state transitions. Code World Model [Chen et al. (2026b)] uses a coding agent to maintain world states and compile them into proxy videos. Programmable World Model [Huang et al. (2026)] maintains global states through executable programs and converts them into spatial generation conditions. State World Models [Ki et al. (2026)] execute interaction rules and updates states using generated observations. Building on explicit state maintenance and rule execution, WorldRuler jointly restores rule definitions, dependencies, and execution states, ensuring their consequences are realized on designated visual instances.

    3 WorldRuler

    3.1 Problem Formulation and Overview

    Given an initial visual observation I₀, user-defined rules ℝ, and a sequence of player actions, WorldRuler generates interactive videos that follow these rules. An executable 3D rule graph Gₜ maintains rule definitions and dependencies, an execution state Xₜ records object attributes and rule progress, and bindings Bₜ associate rule entities with 3D objects and visual instances. Together, these representations determine subsequent interactions and persist when objects leave the view or a session is saved.

    As shown in Fig. 2, generation proceeds in consecutive windows. For window n, the executor evaluates actions Uₙ against the current state and produces a sequence of object states Sₙ. These states and their spatial bindings form generation conditions Cₙ

    V̂ₙ∼p_θ,φ (Vₙ|I₀,Hₙ,Uₙ,Cₙ),(1)
    Cₙ=Condition (Gₙ,Bₙ,Sₙ),

    where Hₙ denotes previously generated visual context, θ denotes the video generator parameters, and φ denotes trainable attribute replacement parameters. The state sequence follows from actions and rule execution within the current window, without future outcomes from reference videos. Object binding identifies where rule targets apply, attribute replacement corrects those regions during denoising, and perception updates correspondences and event evidence for subsequent windows. The graph and its joint checkpoint support Rule-State Persistence, while binding and replacement support Rule-to-Visual Realization.

    3.2 Executable 3D Rule Graph and Persistence

    The rule graph organizes object identities, spatial information, and interaction logic in a shared representation. Object nodes carry persistent identities, semantic descriptions, 3D support, and attribute states. Rule nodes specify triggers, state preconditions, and effect assignments. Typed edges distinguish action subjects, action targets, precondition objects, and effect targets, allowing a consequence to occur away from its trigger. Shared attributes and event conditions express dependencies between rules. For example, collecting a key changes the possession state required by an unlocking rule. Initial objects and spatial information are established from the initial observation and available scene geometry. References to objects that cannot yet be localized remain in the graph for later binding.

    Let Sₜ collect object attributes and let qₜ contain event history, rule activation records, transition progress, and pending effects. The execution state is Xₜ=(Sₜ,qₜ) and evolves according to

    Xₜ₊₁=Execute_ℝ (Xₜ,uₜ,eₜ),

    		(2)

    where uₜ is the current action and eₜ is accepted event evidence. The executor evaluates action, state, spatial, and event-order conditions before assigning effects to their designated objects. Rules requiring action completion consume confirmed completion events, so an action request alone does not satisfy them. Unknown attributes remain explicitly unknown and cannot satisfy a precondition through negation.

    For changes with a duration, the state records current values, targets, and transition progress. Generation receives the effective value at each time, while dependent predicates respect transition completion. This prevents a partially opening door from prematurely satisfying an open-door condition. Effects on invisible objects persist in the state. When an effect target is unresolved, the system retains its description, rule provenance, and event time until the target can be bound.

    A checkpoint jointly serializes the graph, execution state, and bindings

    ℂₜ=Save (Gₜ,Xₜ,Bₜ),(3)
    Load(ℂₜ)=(Gₜ,Xₜ,Bₜ).

    The checkpoint path in Fig. 2 restores rule definitions, object identities, and execution progress so that subsequent actions continue from the saved conditions. For example, a checkpoint taken after defeating a monster but before collecting its key retains the defeated monster, the key on the ground, the closed door, and the remaining collection and unlocking rules. Continuing generation additionally requires visual boundary context corresponding to the restored state. Images may vary with sampling, while identical subsequent actions and event evidence should produce consistent rule decisions.

    3.3 Dynamic Object Binding and Perceptual Feedback

    Dynamic object binding first identifies which scene instance a rule addresses and then determines where that instance can be controlled in the current view. Semantic, appearance, and spatial consistency associate candidate instances with rule entities, and Bₜ stores these correspondences. Objects of the same category retain distinct identities, while viewpoint changes, occlusion, and reappearance preserve established bindings. For localized objects, camera projection and instance segmentation [Ravi et al. (2024)] provide spatiotemporal masks Mᵢ, restricted by visibility and occlusion.

    Rules can update an object’s persistent state while it is invisible. Given an established 3D binding, the stored state is assigned to the projected region before generating the window in which the object first appears. A gate opened outside the view is therefore conditioned as open from its first appearance, without repeating the opening action. Effects on entirely unlocalized entities remain pending until reliable correspondences become available. First-appearance control thus depends on spatial grounding established before generation.

    The executed scene geometry guides layout, camera motion, and object motion, while effective states and changes form global and object-level visual descriptions. Each local condition specifies an identity, spatiotemporal support, and structured attribute targets. Surface changes use object surface support, while motion and deformation cover the current geometry and rule-executed trajectory, excluding foreground occluders and unrelated instances. Unknown attributes are omitted from local control, and completed changes persist as resulting-state conditions.

    Perception independently estimates identity, visibility, visual attributes, and action completion from generated frames, without receiving desired rule outcomes as answer cues. Evidence passing identity, confidence, and temporal validity checks updates bindings, local geometry, and ordinary observable state, and supplies events for subsequent rules that require visual confirmation. Rule-prescribed states and observed outcomes are recorded separately. If a gate appears closed despite an open-state requirement, the prescribed state is retained, and the observed discrepancy guides correction in subsequent generation windows. Feedback affects only windows generated after its acceptance, without rewriting delivered video or treating unconfirmed outcomes as successful.

    3.4 Object Attribute State Replacement

    Object binding determines the support of an edit, and attribute state replacement adjusts its visual representation to the rule target. Figure 3(a) expands the Replace module in the overview into local attribute reading, target correction, and insertion into the sampling update.

    Reading Local Attributes.

    Let z_σ denote the video latent at noise level σ>0 and let v_θ be the predicted velocity. Under the generator’s parameterization, the clean estimate is

    ẑ₀=z_σ+σv_θ(z_σ,σ,Cₙ).

    		(4)

    We omit window and latent-frame indices below. Pooling over the object mask yields local features aᵢ=Pool_Mᵢ(ẑ₀). Dynamic regions map to a fixed canonical grid within the object bounds, using only cells with valid spatial support.

    A frozen affine reader estimates current attributes from visual features as ŝᵢ=Aᵢaᵢ+bᵢ. It is fitted independently on annotated real training videos and receives no rule targets. Rule execution supplies the currently effective target sᵢ^⋆, yielding the discrepancy δᵢ=sᵢ^⋆-ŝᵢ.

    Attribute Correction and Compatible Adjustment.

    We separate direct attribute correction from compatible visual adjustments, as satisfying the attribute readout alone does not guarantee coherent appearance and motion changes. Here, Aᵢ contains only rows for currently known and controllable attributes. When these attributes are independently identifiable and Aᵢ has full row rank, define

    Bᵢ=Aᵢ^⊤(AᵢAᵢ^⊤)⁻¹, Qᵢ=I-BᵢAᵢ.

    		(5)

    The right inverse Bᵢ maps attribute discrepancies into feature space, while Qᵢ projects additional adjustments into the reader’s null space. Adding both corrections to the original features defines the local replacement operator T_φ

    aᵢ^′=T_φ(aᵢ,sᵢ^⋆)=aᵢ+Bᵢδᵢ+γ(δᵢ) Qᵢf_φ (aᵢ,hᵢ,ŝᵢ,sᵢ^⋆,σ),

    		(6)

    where hᵢ denotes local context, f_φ is a trainable writer, and γ(δ)=\min(\lVertδ\rVert_∞,c) for a fixed cap c. The term Bᵢδᵢ corrects attribute coordinates, while the branch constrained by Qᵢ learns compatible appearance and motion changes without altering the prescribed readout. Since AᵢBᵢ=I and AᵢQᵢ=0, full replacement satisfies

    Aᵢaᵢ^′+bᵢ=sᵢ^⋆.

    		(7)

    Both corrections vanish when the discrepancy is zero, preserving features that already satisfy the target. Multiple active attributes are solved jointly to avoid conflicting sequential writes. Equation (7) constrains learned attribute coordinates, while decoded visual semantics and content preservation are evaluated independently on generated videos.

    Writing Back to Denoising.

    Local corrections are inserted into the current clean estimate and used to update the sampling velocity. For disjoint object supports,

    ẑ₀^′=ẑ₀+∑ᵢScatter_Mᵢ(aᵢ^′-aᵢ),(8)
    v_θ^′=v_θ+(ẑ₀^′-ẑ₀)/(σ).

    The sampler uses v_θ^′ to advance to the next denoising step, incorporating rule corrections into the generation trajectory. Scattering is constructed as a right inverse of pooling over valid canonical cells, and compatible constraints on overlapping supports are solved jointly in their shared latent region. Writes exclude fixed history boundaries, invisible regions, and unauthorized attributes. Latents outside the support receive no direct correction.

    3.5 Counterfactual Reconstruction and Attribute Swapping

    As shown in Fig. 3(b), we train the same replacement operator using video pairs (V⁽⁰⁾,V⁽¹⁾) aligned by scene, action context, and rule events. The branches share scene, camera, and action context while differing in rule-specified attribute states. Each uses its own true states and visual outcomes, including changes caused by ordinary actions when the designated rule is disabled. Encoding yields local targets a⁽⁰⁾,a⁽¹⁾ with attributes s⁽⁰⁾,s⁽¹⁾. Unknown, invisible, and padded samples are excluded from the losses.

    We first fit a regularized affine reader on real local features and check attribute identifiability. We then freeze the reader, video generator, and visual encoder, optimizing only the writer parameters φ. Real paired videos provide training supervision, while inference conditions come from the initial observation, generated history, and rule execution.

    Counterfactual Reconstruction.

    We extract a local estimate ā_σ from a denoising trajectory and supply it to two shared replacement branches with targets s⁽⁰⁾ and s⁽¹⁾. Write ã⁽ᵏ⁾=T_φ(ā_σ,s⁽ᵏ⁾), omitting the shared context and noise level. Reconstruction and difference losses are

    L_rec=𝔼 [1/2∑_k∈{0,1}\lVertã⁽ᵏ⁾-a⁽ᵏ⁾\rVert₂²],(9)
    L_diff=𝔼 [\lVert(ã⁽¹⁾-ã⁽⁰⁾)-(a⁽¹⁾-a⁽⁰⁾)\rVert₂²].

    Shared inputs require the output difference to arise from the state condition. Reconstruction learns each state’s visual realization, while difference supervision targets the visual change associated with the attribute change.

    Bidirectional Attribute Swapping.

    Swapping starts from one real local representation, writes the other branch’s attributes, and reconstructs the corresponding target

    L_swap=𝔼 [1/2∑_k∈{0,1}\lVertT_φ(a⁽ᵏ⁾,s⁽¹⁻ᵏ⁾)-a⁽¹⁻ᵏ⁾\rVert₂²].

    		(10)

    Swapping uses clean inputs at zero noise level and changes only the supervised attribute targets. Alignment of unrelated content across the pair lets this objective supervise both attribute changes and local content preservation. The total objective is

    L=L_rec+λ_diffL_diff+λ_swapL_swap.

    		(11)

    All losses are normalized over valid object and temporal support. Counterfactual reconstruction learns to realize prescribed states, difference supervision constrains rule-induced visual changes, and attribute swapping encourages compatible adjustments while preserving unrelated content. Local insertion further limits the direct spatial extent of these changes.

    4 RuleVerse

    RuleVerse contains paired rule-driven interaction videos collected in Habitat [Puig et al. (2024)] and GTA-V, covering indoor object interactions and open game environments. Each pair shares scene configurations and action intent but differs in whether a designated rule mechanism is enabled, producing distinct state evolutions. The rule-disabled branch retains ordinary actions and other native reactions, so triggering conditions may still hold. Solo samples examine a designated rule, while Full samples cover multi-rule scripts, including explicit dependencies between earlier outcomes and later conditions in Habitat.

    4.1 Data Collection and Annotation

    Simulation-based pipelines enable automated collection of visual data with detailed ground-truth annotations [Greff et al. (2022)]. Figure 4 illustrates our data collection process. We first inspect native objects, parts, spatial relations, and initial states, together with interaction capabilities, reachable paths, and interaction and observation positions. Trigger and effect combinations are selected according to scene capabilities, prioritizing underrepresented categories during collection. For custom rules, a language model produces a rulebook containing natural-language descriptions, executable conditions, and state assignments, together with an interaction script. Code checks object bindings, syntax, initial conditions, and execution feasibility. Habitat collection additionally screens rule quality before recording. A compiler translates scripts into navigation, interaction, and camera controls bound to concrete entities.

    Both branches execute from their corresponding initial configurations. Habitat reuses the same action and camera control plan. GTA-V includes both custom rules and interventions on native mechanisms. Disabling custom rules preserves native game reactions, while native interventions suppress only the documented mechanism. GTA-V pairs share scene configurations and temporally aligned state and event annotations, while allowing minor variations in character motions due to engine dynamics.

    Recording stores videos, object identities, action events, and state trajectories, together with trigger conditions, effect timing, and task outcomes. For Habitat, an independent interpreter recomputes conditions and effects from state and event logs, followed by checks of paired controls, video integrity, and annotation correspondence, and deduplication using decoded videos. GTA-V retains native execution and observation records, with checks of pair structure and video file identity. Habitat annotations align to video frames, while GTA-V preserves the temporal mapping and synchronization uncertainty between screen recordings and engine logs. Visibility and event timing distinguish when a rule takes effect from when its target enters the view. Public inputs contain initial images, rules, and requested actions, while reference videos and subsequent state annotations remain on the answer side.

    4.2 Dataset Statistics

    The dataset contains 3,200 pairs and 6,400 videos, with 2,900 pairs for training and 300 for testing. Habitat is split by base scene, while GTA-V groups samples by source scene and spatial proximity before splitting. We characterize the dataset through rule combinations, object binding, activation timing, and dependence on action history.

    As shown in Figure 5(a), the heatmaps summarize the joint distribution of each pair’s primary trigger and effect categories. The five trigger families cover actions, spatial conditions, relations, states, and sequences. The displayed effects include changes in attributes, geometry, and object presence, together with topology changes in Habitat and behavior changes in GTA-V. Each heatmap is normalized over the sample pairs within its displayed effect categories. Habitat exhibits a more even distribution across these combinations, while GTA-V places greater emphasis on action-triggered effects.

    As shown in Figure 5(b), executed rules are categorized into single-object binding, cross-object binding, and environment effects. Cross-object rules reference multiple non-actor object or part identities across their conditions and effects, accounting for 60.2% of Habitat rules and 40.2% of GTA-V rules. Single-object rules involve one such identity, while environment effects modify scene-level properties or routes. These categories cover interactions involving individual objects, interactions involving multiple objects, and changes to the surrounding environment.

    As shown in Figure 5(c), the first activation occurs in the second half of the video for 75.4% of Habitat rules and 61.1% of GTA-V rules. In addition, 18.9% and 19.3% of rules, respectively, require action history through ordered actions or cumulative event counts. These distributions include cases in which rule conditions must remain available until later interactions and cases whose activation depends on preceding actions.

    4.3 Metrics

    We evaluate rule realization using Rule Success Rate (RSR) and Full Completion Rate (FCR). RSR comprises five components evaluated over annotated rule events in rule-enabled videos, while rule-disabled videos provide counterfactual references for evaluating rule-specific changes. Identity measures whether the relevant trigger objects and effect targets match their reference identities. Trigger assesses whether the specified trigger condition is visibly satisfied. Effect evaluates whether the prescribed change is realized on the target. Timing checks whether the effect begins after the trigger and becomes established within the specified time window. Hold measures whether the resulting state persists over the required observation interval.

    FCR evaluates complete multi-stage tasks through three components. Stages measures the proportion of tasks in which all required rule events are successfully realized, rather than the average success rate of individual stages. Order assesses whether all required stages occur in the prescribed chronological order, and Goal checks whether the final task goal is visibly achieved at the end of the video. The average FCR is the arithmetic mean of these three independently evaluated components.

    Visual judgments are obtained using a frozen vision-language evaluator with fixed-choice questions and initial identity references. Generated videos are sampled at 3 fps, including the first and last frames. The same judging protocol is applied to all compared methods. Uncertain or invalid judgments remain in the corresponding denominators and receive no success credit. All scores are reported as percentages.

    5 Experiments

    Our experiments evaluate WorldRuler along two dimensions: Rule-State Persistence and Rule-to-Visual Realization. We first compare rule realization and task-level performance on RuleVerse, followed by an external evaluation on WorldState-Bench. We then examine dynamic object binding, attribute state replacement, and the swapping objective through component ablations, and evaluate perceptual and visual consistency after saving and loading. Qualitative examples illustrate how the runtime produces different outcomes under enabled and disabled rule mechanisms.

    5.1 Implementation

    We use the MiniMax-H3 Ref2VA Turbo for video generation at a resolution of 1344×768 and 24 fps. Each generation window contains 124 frames. We use the native H3 Qwen encoder for generation conditioning, along with Qwen3.8-Max [Qwen Team (2026)], SAM2 [Ravi et al. (2024)], and DA3 [Lin et al. (2026)] for visual observations, instance segmentation, and geometry estimation.

    Attribute state replacement is applied to local clean estimates at each denoising step, with corrections written back before the next sampling update. Following Sec. 3.5, we first fit the affine attribute reader, then freeze the reader, video generator, and visual encoder while optimizing only the attribute writer. Training uses paired reconstruction, paired difference, and bidirectional attribute swapping losses, excluding unknown attributes, invisible regions, and padded frames.

    5.2 Main Results

    RuleVerse.

    As shown in Table 1, WorldRuler outperforms the compared baselines across both the Habitat and GTA-V subsets. On the Habitat subset, it achieves average RSR and FCR scores of 64.99% and 48.04%, exceeding SWM by 20.93 and 30.06 percentage points, respectively. Compared with SWM, effect accuracy increases from 20.74% to 58.47%, timing accuracy from 15.67% to 37.36%, and hold accuracy from 17.05% to 50.83%. WorldRuler also improves all three task-level components, reaching 52.61% for stages, 44.38% for order, and 47.12% for goal. These results support the effectiveness of combining explicit rule execution with state-conditioned generation for realizing rule effects and dependent interactions.

    On the GTA-V subset, WorldRuler achieves an average RSR of 67.42%, compared with 44.19% for SWM and 43.43% for MiniMax-H3. It obtains 60.00% for stages, 60.00% for order, and 80.00% for goal, yielding the highest average FCR of 66.66%. The improvements across RuleVerse indicate that the framework benefits indoor object interactions as well as open game environments.

    WorldState-Bench.

    We evaluate the complete WorldRuler framework on the 50 official WorldState-Bench [Ki et al. (2026)] pairs using the benchmark’s original judging protocol. This configuration uses a single 124-frame window, resolves the submitted action and rules before generation, and permits up to two feedback corrections before publishing the clip. The evaluation includes the trained attribute state replacement module alongside rule execution, dynamic object binding, and perceptual feedback.

    As shown in Table 2, WorldRuler matches SWM on EndFollow, TwinContrast, and Strict, while achieving higher scores on PairFollow, CntAbsent, and PairStrict. These three scores reach 94%, 99%, and 92%, compared with 92%, 98%, and 90% for SWM. WorldRuler improves PairFollow and PairStrict by two percentage points each over SWM. These results indicate competitive performance on an external rule-following benchmark, with modest gains over SWM under the reported configurations.

    5.3 Ablation Study

    We conduct ablation studies on the Habitat subset of RuleVerse to examine the contributions of dynamic object binding, attribute state replacement, and the swapping objective, as well as the information required for save/load persistence.

    Component Ablation.

    We examine dynamic object binding, attribute state replacement, and the swapping objective on the Habitat subset of RuleVerse. Alongside RSR and FCR, we evaluate First-appearance and Preservation. First-appearance measures whether targets affected by rules while off-screen exhibit the correct identities and prescribed attributes upon entering the view and during the immediately following observation interval. Preservation measures whether unrelated objects and attributes remain intact, excluding changes permitted by ordinary actions or the rules.

    As shown in Table 3, the full method achieves the highest scores across all four metrics. Replacing dynamic object binding with fixed binding reduces average RSR from 64.99% to 48.09% and First-appearance from 29.69% to 20.58%, supporting the importance of updating object correspondences when applying persistent rule states to visual instances. Removing attribute state replacement reduces average RSR and FCR by 18.56 and 9.54 percentage points, respectively, while also lowering First-appearance and Preservation. These results support local attribute replacement as a contributor to rule realization and content preservation.

    Removing the swapping objective reduces average RSR to 51.24%, First-appearance to 6.45%, and Preservation to 20.63%. Its first-appearance score is also lower than that obtained without attribute replacement, suggesting that the effectiveness of the learned replacement module depends on its training objective. The full method improves both first-appearance correctness and preservation.

item.title: 世界状态别放在生成器的上下文里：WM^MLLM 把它存成「带修订历史的全景图」，让多模态大模型来写 ｜ WM^MLLM: Turning MLLMs into World Models
item.description:
一句话：世界留在生成器上下文里，于是每次回访都重新合成，早先的编辑会漂移甚至消失。

要点：

  • 病灶很明确：视频世界模型把世界**保存在生成器的上下文里**，因此每次回访都要重新合成，先前的编辑会**漂移或消失**
  • WM^MLLM 把世界状态**放在每个生成器之外**，形式是「**带修订历史的全景图**」，并让多模态大模型来写它——把每个请求翻译成对这份状态的修改
  • 于是世界状态是持久、可编辑、可回溯的，而生成器只负责从状态渲染出画面

为什么值得看：这是「状态外置」这条线到今天最干脆的实现：一个全景 + 一份修订历史 + 一个负责写它的 MLLM。引擎开发者会立刻认出这就是「场景图 + 命令流 + 渲染器」的 AI 版。与 11-12 的 Evoke（状态库）、11-19 的 PanoEvo（全景潜空间）相比，它多给了「修订历史」这一层。

中文摘要：视频世界模型把世界保存在生成器的上下文里，因此每当镜头重新访问某处，画面都要重新合成，先前的编辑可能漂移甚至彻底消失。WM^MLLM 提出把世界状态保存在**每一个生成器之外**：形式是一张带修订历史的全景图，由多模态大语言模型来书写——模型把每个交互请求翻译成对这份状态的修改，生成器再从状态渲染出画面。这样世界状态变得持久、可编辑、可回溯，而「记忆」不再依赖生成器的上下文窗口。作者称这是第一个基于 MLLM 的交互式世界模型，用于从单张图像做持久、可编辑的世界生成。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-19

本期推送：2026-11-20

WM^MLLM: Turning MLLMs into World Models

Abstract

Video world models keep the world in the context of a generator, so a revisit is synthesized again and earlier edits can drift or disappear. We present WM^MLLM, the first interactive world model built on multimodal large language models (MLLMs), for persistent, editable world generation from a single image. WM^MLLM keeps the world state outside every generator, as a panorama with a revision history, and lets the MLLMs write it: they turn each request into operations on this state, select where a local edit is written, and check every candidate before it becomes the next state. Image generators only propose views, and video only presents them. Users can walk to new places and return, edit objects through text or a box, place subjects, and change lighting, weather or season. By construction, a revisit at the same revision reproduces the earlier view exactly, a local edit leaves every panorama pixel outside its region unchanged, and each request starts from the result of the previous one. Against six world model baselines on MBench-A, WM^MLLM has the highest mean on all four environment-recovery metrics (Epipolar 91.5 versus 0.1 to 74.0) and completes the most camera round trips (85.3% versus at most 50.9%). It has the best value in all 15 CompBench columns against 15 baselines. On 112 local edits judged blind, selecting the region to write after generation raises completion from 34.8% to 83.0%. On 258 WBench and MBench-A items, all 46 revisits recover their earlier views, and all 97 local edits that pass the check leave panorama pixels outside their region unchanged.

Contents

1  Introduction

A user opens a container, relights the room and turns away. Turning back should show the open container under the new light (figure1). A world model keeps a persistent state of its environment that actions update [worldfoundry], so an interactive world model needs three properties: a revisit shows the content saved there (return), a local edit changes nothing outside its region (locality), and every request builds on the result of the previous one (persistence).

Where the world lives decides whether these properties hold. Video world models generate observations from camera moves, actions and event prompts, and streaming variants extend them to long, interactive rollouts [genie3_research2025, matrixgame3, hyworldplay, longlive]. Their world lives in the context of the generator, so a revisit synthesizes the view again and earlier edits can drift or disappear; after one camera round trip, five baselines, all video world models, end on a different scene (figure1, bottom row). 3D world models build an explicit scene, such as a mesh or a set of Gaussian surfels, that a renderer displays from new viewpoints and that supports regional edits [hunyuanworld, wonderworld, marble_official2025]. Among the systems with an explicit world state in section2.3, none documents all four of an MLLM planner, object edits, exact return and checks of an edit before it enters the state. World models for control, such as vision-language-action models [openvla, pi0] and joint-embedding predictive architectures [vjepa2], output actions or embeddings and no editable images.

Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) and image generators such as Nano Banana and GPT-Image [nanobanana, gptimage, gptimage25] understand a scene, follow detailed instructions and accept both text and image inputs. We investigate whether these models can be turned into an interactive world model that users keep editing and exploring.

WM^MLLM turns MLLMs into such a world model by keeping the world state outside every generator and letting the MLLMs write it (figure2). For each scene revision, the state stores a panorama and patches at native resolution; it also stores scene relations and facts observed in images. The MLLM GPT-6.1-sol [gpt61sol] maps each request and optional box to operations on this state, selects where a local edit is written, and checks every candidate before it becomes the next state. Rotations and revisits render the state and call no image generator; GPT-Image proposes candidate views, and the video generator Sol-H3 [solh3] presents transitions without writing the state. Return, locality and persistence therefore follow from how each turn writes the state (), whereas a video world model has to reproduce them from its context. In one session of eight requests, a room keeps its new light after the user walks away and back, and a later edit builds on it (figure3).

A local edit is written inside a region, its support, and WM^MLLM selects this support after generation. An image generator can move a subject or change its silhouette beyond a region predicted in advance, so such a region can cut off part of the change (). An MLLM therefore compares the source and the proposal and selects the old and new footprints and necessary effects.

WM^MLLM achieves state-of-the-art scene consistency and camera return and the best CompBench editing scores.
