Against six world model baselines under the same MBench evaluator, it has the highest mean on all four environment-recovery metrics, with Epipolar 91.5 versus 0.1 to 74.0. It completes 85.3% of camera round trips versus 0.4% to 50.9% (). On CompBench, it has the best value in all 15 metric columns against 15 baselines ().

Contributions.

  • •

    The first interactive world model built on MLLMs.WM^MLLM composes navigation, object editing, environmental change and subject placement in one world built from a single image. Its state lives outside every generator, and view reuse, compositing inside the support and lookup by revision give return, locality and persistence by construction (, Propositions 1–3): all 46 revisits and all 97 local edits that pass the check satisfy them exactly, and over 21 sequential requests in one world the state keeps every earlier change ().

  • •

    Local edits in the panorama state. An MLLM compares the source with the proposal to select the old and new footprints of an object and their effects. On 112 local edits, completion rises from 34.8% with support predicted before generation to 83.0% with support selected after it ().

  • •

    State-of-the-art consistency and editing.WM^MLLM leads six baselines on MBench-A and 15 baselines on CompBench ().

    • 2  Related Work

    2.1 World Representation and Memory

    Video world models maintain interaction by conditioning new frames on actions and visual context. Genie 3 supports navigation and promptable events [genie3_research2025], and LongLive updates its context cache when the prompt changes [longlive]. Camera-aware context improves spatial continuity through memory retrieval in Matrix-Game 3.0 [matrixgame3], RGB-D generation in HunyuanWorld-Voyager [voyager], and reframing of historical observations in HY-WorldPlay [hyworldplay]. WorldDirector adds planning of object and camera trajectories by a language model and preserves the appearance of dynamic objects that leave and return [worlddirector]. Genie 4 uses Gemini models to plan and verify steps on the frames it generates [genie4_official2026].

    Memory extends the visual context available to these generators. WorldMem retrieves frames by pose and time [worldmem], Context-as-Memory by field-of-view overlap [contextasmemory], and VMem through a surfel index [vmem]. Alaya-EVOKE maintains a geometry bank indexed by camera [alayaevoke], while ActWorld stores event and object tokens with visual anchors in a memory of constant capacity [actworld]. Other approaches use spatial or planar memories or compress visual context [spmem, ppmem, worldtrace, worldt3]. Persistent Computational State saves and restores the generator’s runtime state [pcs]. These memories condition a new synthesis on return.

    Explicit 3D worlds support rendering and editing through scene representations. HunyuanWorld 1.0 reconstructs a mesh from a panoramic proxy [hunyuanworld], and WonderWorld connects scenes through Gaussian surfels [wonderworld]. Marble edits and expands persistent navigable worlds by region, including weather, time of day and season [marble_official2025]. HOLODECK 2.0 and PERSIST update assets or latent 3D state [holodeck2, persist]. State updates from language also appear in WorldWeave, whose video synthesis reads an explicit 3D world [worldweave], and StateFlow, which translates intent into transitions of persistent 3D state [stateflow]. WorldAgents adds new views from a generator to a reconstruction after checks by a vision-language model (VLM) in image and reconstruction space [worldagents]. WM^MLLM uses a panorama and patches at native resolution as its editable visual state. Each physical change advances the revision, and a revisit selects a view of the current revision.

    2.2 MLLM Planning and Feedback

    Visual agents connect language planning, image generation and feedback. Yang et al.’s WorldGPT expands a request, edits a target image and animates the initial and final frames [worldgpt_yang2024]. GenArtist plans through tool trees [genartist], and EditAgent routes steps to general and task-specific editors and then judges parallel candidates [editagent2026]. Agent Banana retains the editing paths that pass its checks, rolls back image history and edits layers in isolation [agentbanana]. IMAGAgent corrects multi-turn edits through feedback from several VLM experts [imagagent2026]. Ge et al.’s WorldGPT learns multimodal state transitions [worldgpt_ge2024], and World Agent tests whether language models update an explicit world state from events in an ongoing narrative [worldagent2026].

    Agentic video systems connect this feedback to worlds that change over time. LingBot-World v2 uses a vision-language director for semantic rules, events and environmental changes, with SAM tracking objects for interaction [lingbotworldv2]. Regions that leave its context window tend to be regenerated on return. AgiWorld updates a world state from video chunks stored with geometry in spatial memory [agiworld2026]. ATAS adds clips to scene and event memories after review and state checks [atas2026]. WM^MLLM gives MLLMs control over edits and navigation in a panorama state, and its transition videos read the endpoints of each turn.

    2.3 Image Editing and Consistency

    Image editors such as Nano Banana and GPT-Image follow complex instructions [nanobanana, gptimage, gptimage25]. Spherical editors extend this capability to panoramas. SE360 and World-Shaper edit spherical imagery [se360, worldshaper], FocusDiff edits regions of indoor panoramas [focusdiff], and Mover360 moves, inserts and removes objects [mover360]. ZONE extracts the region that an edit changes as a layer and blends it into the source image [zone]. WM^MLLM selects the support from the source and the proposal to cover the old and new footprints of an object and their effects. It installs this region in a world that later operations navigate, revisit and edit again.

    CompBench measures local, multi-object and implicit-reasoning edits [compbench]. Scene-memory benchmarks measure recovery after the camera leaves and returns [mbench, mind], while WRBench tests whether events evolve outside the view [wrbench]. WorldFoundry provides infrastructure for inference and evaluation across video, 3D, 4D and interactive world systems [worldfoundry]. We evaluate both image editing and scene recovery. Section2.3 compares world representations, MLLM planning, object edits, exact return and edit checks.

HunyuanWorld 1.0 reconstructs a mesh from a panoramic proxy [hunyuanworld], and WonderWorld connects scenes through Gaussian surfels [wonderworld]. Marble edits and expands persistent navigable worlds by region, including weather, time of day and season [marble_official2025]. HOLODECK 2.0 and PERSIST update assets or latent 3D state [holodeck2, persist]. State updates from language also appear in WorldWeave, whose video synthesis reads an explicit 3D world [worldweave], and StateFlow, which translates intent into transitions of persistent 3D state [stateflow]. WorldAgents adds new views from a generator to a reconstruction after checks by a vision-language model (VLM) in image and reconstruction space [worldagents]. WM^MLLM uses a panorama and patches at native resolution as its editable visual state. Each physical change advances the revision, and a revisit selects a view of the current revision.

    2.2 MLLM Planning and Feedback

    Visual agents connect language planning, image generation and feedback. Yang et al.’s WorldGPT expands a request, edits a target image and animates the initial and final frames [worldgpt_yang2024]. GenArtist plans through tool trees [genartist], and EditAgent routes steps to general and task-specific editors and then judges parallel candidates [editagent2026]. Agent Banana retains the editing paths that pass its checks, rolls back image history and edits layers in isolation [agentbanana]. IMAGAgent corrects multi-turn edits through feedback from several VLM experts [imagagent2026]. Ge et al.’s WorldGPT learns multimodal state transitions [worldgpt_ge2024], and World Agent tests whether language models update an explicit world state from events in an ongoing narrative [worldagent2026].

    Agentic video systems connect this feedback to worlds that change over time. LingBot-World v2 uses a vision-language director for semantic rules, events and environmental changes, with SAM tracking objects for interaction [lingbotworldv2]. Regions that leave its context window tend to be regenerated on return. AgiWorld updates a world state from video chunks stored with geometry in spatial memory [agiworld2026]. ATAS adds clips to scene and event memories after review and state checks [atas2026]. WM^MLLM gives MLLMs control over edits and navigation in a panorama state, and its transition videos read the endpoints of each turn.

    2.3 Image Editing and Consistency

    Image editors such as Nano Banana and GPT-Image follow complex instructions [nanobanana, gptimage, gptimage25]. Spherical editors extend this capability to panoramas. SE360 and World-Shaper edit spherical imagery [se360, worldshaper], FocusDiff edits regions of indoor panoramas [focusdiff], and Mover360 moves, inserts and removes objects [mover360]. ZONE extracts the region that an edit changes as a layer and blends it into the source image [zone]. WM^MLLM selects the support from the source and the proposal to cover the old and new footprints of an object and their effects. It installs this region in a world that later operations navigate, revisit and edit again.

    CompBench measures local, multi-object and implicit-reasoning edits [compbench]. Scene-memory benchmarks measure recovery after the camera leaves and returns [mbench, mind], while WRBench tests whether events evolve outside the view [wrbench]. WorldFoundry provides infrastructure for inference and evaluation across video, 3D, 4D and interactive world systems [worldfoundry]. We evaluate both image editing and scene recovery. Section2.3 compares world representations, MLLM planning, object edits, exact return and edit checks.

item.title: 把场景层级里的每个单元都当成「自成一体的任务」：GTA 用一层层 agent 塔并行搭场景 ｜ GTA: Generative Tower of Agents for Scalable Holonic Scene Generation
item.description:
一句话：可扩展的世界建模要在有限时间与上下文预算下，协调场景级目标、细粒度物体与动态角色。

要点：

  • 约束条件：可扩展的世界建模必须协调**场景级目标、细粒度物体与动态角色**，而时间与上下文预算都是有限的
  • GTA 的表示选择是「holon（子整体）」：在自适应场景层级的每一层，每个单元既是**一个自成一体的构建任务**，也是**一个可组合的场景单元**——这同时解决了分解与复用
  • 执行上是并行 agent：自顶向下递归地规划层级、生成资产，再组装与精修；论文强调这正是为「有限上下文」设计的结构

为什么值得看：上下文窗口装不下一个开放世界，而 holon 式层级正是引擎里场景图/预制体（prefab）的思想。把 agent 编排成塔、按层级并行，是把「大量内容」塞进「有限预算」的现实解法。

中文摘要：可扩展的世界建模需要在有限的时间与上下文预算下，协调场景级目标、细粒度物体与动态角色。GTA（Generative Tower of Agents）的表示选择是「子整体（holon）」：在自适应场景层级的每一层，每个单元既是一个自成一体的构建任务，也是一个可组合的场景单元。执行时，并行的 agent 自顶向下递归地规划这一层级结构、生成资产，再进行组装与精修。这种分层与并行的组织方式，本质上与游戏引擎里的场景图与预制体思路一致——都是为了在有限预算下把大量内容组织起来。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-19

本期推送：2026-11-20

GTA: Generative Tower of Agents for Scalable Holonic Scene Generation

Abstract

Scalable world modeling requires coordinating scene-wide goals with fine-grained objects and dynamic characters under limited time and context budgets. We introduce GTA (Generative Tower of Agents), which represents every unit at every level of an adaptive scene hierarchy as a holon, both a self-contained construction task and a composable scene unit. Parallel agents recursively plan the hierarchy top-down, generate assets, and assemble and refine them bottom-up. Uniform interfaces carry scene-wide requirements down the hierarchy, guiding local construction so that each holon fits into the larger one. GTA accelerates scalable world modeling through high-throughput parallel execution while preserving well-structured layouts and fine-grained asset details. GTA then populates the assembled environments with dynamic human characters whose appearance and motion are guided by the scene, yielding realized 4D worlds. Project page:https://zt-zeng-tao.github.io/GTA/

1 Introduction

“Parts and wholes in an absolute sense do not exist in the domains of life.”

— Arthur Koestler, 1969 [17]

Recent advances in agentic scene generation have enabled agents to construct complex 4D worlds through semantic reasoning, planning, and tool use [41, 39, 28, 10]. Rather than relying on rigid generation pipelines, agents can interpret open-ended instructions, orchestrate heterogeneous tools, and iteratively refine scene geometry and spatial relationships. This flexibility offers a promising path toward open-world scene generation.

However, agentic capabilities alone do not guarantee scalability across arbitrary scene types. As scenes grow more complex, scene generation must reconcile scene-wide semantic goals with spatial constraints while preserving fine-grained object detail. It must also place objects precisely to avoid interpenetration and ensure stable support for simulation within limited time and context budgets. Consider the construction of the Tower of Babel in Fig. GTA: Generative Tower of Agents for Scalable Holonic Scene Generation: agents must coordinate the layout of a production district, place workbenches within workshops, and model details as small as the teeth of a handsaw. Existing approaches often encode this process in predefined hierarchies or specialized sequential workflows, limiting their flexibility in open-world settings [6, 18, 9], making it difficult to scale to larger scenes, preserve fine-grained object detail, and adapt to open-world settings. This raises a fundamental question: How can agents autonomously organize and construct scenes across diverse types and scales through a unified paradigm?

We introduce GTA, a Generative Tower of Agents for scalable scene construction built upon a unified parallel recursive framework. GTA is guided by three core agentic insights. (1) Adaptivity, enabling agents to determine scene organization and decomposition based on open-ended inputs. (2) Uniformity, allowing agents to reuse the same reasoning and tool-use procedures across scene units. (3) Interoperability, enabling agents to pass constraints down and construction results up through uniform interfaces.

At the core of GTA is the Holon. Arthur Koestler introduced the concept of the holon in The Ghost in the Machine[16]. In GTA, a holon is a construction unit that is both a whole in itself and a part of a larger scene. Each Holon forms a self-contained construction task while remaining a composable component of a larger Holon. A world is a Holon, just as a city is a Holon, a park is a Holon, a flowerbed is a Holon, and a plant is a Holon. What changes across scales is the content of the Holon, not the paradigm by which it is constructed. This unified abstraction, named Holarchy, allows agents to recursively organize diverse scenes without predefined hierarchies.

Building on Holarchy, GTA establishes a unified recursive agentic scene generation paradigm consisting of Top-down Planning, Asset Generation, and Bottom-up Placement. Top-down Planning decomposes the scene specification into a hierarchy of holons, Asset Generation produces the corresponding assets, and Bottom-up Placement assembles these assets within their holon groups and recursively integrates the groups into a complete scene. The recursive structure of the holarchy and its uniform interfaces allow independent branches to be processed in parallel at each stage, preserving fine-grained asset detail while respecting scene-level semantic constraints. A post-generation stage then enriches the resulting 4D world with high-quality dynamic human characters whose appearance and motion suit the scene’s spatiotemporal semantics.

We evaluate GTA across diverse scene types, spatial scales, and levels of semantic complexity, examining scene quality, generation efficiency, and the scalability of recursive and parallel construction.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    We introduce a unified scene unit representation that enables agents to adaptively organize heterogeneous scenes without scene-specific templates, supporting a consistent agentic workflow across types and scales.

  • •

    We develop a recursive framework integrating top-down planning, asset generation, and bottom-up placement. By combining reusable skills with parallel execution of independent Holons, our approach enables scalable and accelerated scene construction.

  • •

    We evaluate GTA across a range of scene types and scales, showing that high-throughput parallel execution speeds up scalable world modeling while maintaining coherent layouts and detailed assets, as well as 4D worlds populated with scene-guided animated characters.

    • 2 Related Work

    2.1 3D Scene Generation

    Early learning-based methods [44, 36] such as ATISS [26] synthesize indoor layouts autoregressively from room types and floor plans. Recent approaches [8, 19, 7, 5] offer greater control over scene structure. HOG-Layout [13] uses a hierarchical representation and vision-language reasoning to generate, optimize, and edit indoor layouts. WorldGen [37] combines procedural layout planning with holistic image-to-3D reconstruction, then decomposes the result into individual meshes for object-level refinement. GTA recursively decomposes each scene into a hierarchy of holons, adapting its depth and branching to the scene structure. The hierarchy specifies which components to construct and how they are nested within the scene.

    2.2 Agentic Scene Generation

    Language-guided systems use foundation models to infer scene content and coordinate specialized tools [12, 6, 41, 9, 18, 20]. Holodeck [42] retrieves assets from Objaverse and optimizes their placement under spatial constraints proposed by an LLM. SAGE [39] generates simulation environments for embodied tasks and iteratively refines them using visual and physical feedback. SceneSmith [28] uses designer, critic, and orchestrator agents across specialized indoor construction stages and parallelizes work across rooms. From visual captures, SceneAgent [10] uses simulator-based inspection and repair to turn reconstructed scenes into interactive environments. GTA treats holon groups at every level as uniform units of agentic execution. Through common interfaces, agents reuse the same operations across levels and process groups in parallel as their dependencies are resolved, accelerating scene construction.

    2.3 Compositional and Multi-Agent Systems

    Agent systems coordinate subtasks [38, 11] and schedule execution by dependency [15, 43]. ADaPT [31] decomposes subtasks on demand, while ROMA [1] combines recursive decomposition, parallel execution, and bottom-up aggregation. GTA ties each construction task to a spatial component, passing constraints down the hierarchy and placing completed child holons within their parents.

    3 Method

    3.1 Overview

    Given scene text prompts, GTA outputs a detailed 3D scene constructed through a unified holon representation and parallel recursive execution, together with scene-guided 4D humans. We represent the scene as holons as shown in Fig. 2 and organize agentic operations around holon groups, with shared interfaces propagating constraints across levels (Sec. 3.2). Construction proceeds in three stages: top-down planning recursively decomposes the scene; asset generation in parallel creates assets for leaf holons; and bottom-up placement and refinement assembles highly detailed components (Sec. 3.3). Finally, a scene-guided human generation pipeline creates and integrates dynamic characters with appropriate activities and appearance (Sec. 3.4).

    3.2 Holon Representation for Agents

    In GTA, a holon is the fundamental unit of scene processing. A leaf holon represents an indivisible object, while an internal holon represents a composition of child holons. As shown in Fig. 3, the entire scene forms the root holon. These parent–child relationships define the holarchy as a rooted tree T=(H,E), where H is the set of holons and (h,c)∈E means that c is an immediate child of h. The children of h are siblings and can themselves be leaf or internal holons. Agents operate on holon groups. For each internal holon h, its group contains h and its immediate children Ch(h):

    G(h)={h}∪Ch(h).

    		(1)

    Groups communicate through parent-facing and child-facing interfaces. This recursive structure supports a common workflow across scene types and scales. Groups without interdependencies run in parallel across agentic slots, accelerating generation.

    Unification. At every level of the scene hierarchy, agents operate on holon groups using the same reasoning and tool-use procedures. Uniform interfaces pass constraints downward and construction results upward. Given the global context, each agent only needs to reason about relationships within its group and the interfaces that connect it to other groups. This local scope allows the same workflow to scale to larger scenes.

    Parallelism. At each stage, the system maintains a queue of holons awaiting execution and a set of agentic slots, as shown in Fig. 4. Once a holon group is ready for processing, it enters the queue. The scheduler continuously dispatches queued groups to available slots. GTA reduces the bottleneck of sequential construction and allows throughput to scale with system capacity, thus accelerating generation.

    3.3 Parallel Recursive Agentic Execution

    Building on the holon representation, our pipeline consists of three stages, each supporting parallel agent execution over the recursive scene structure. As the scene grows, the potential for concurrent processing also increases.

    Top-down Planning. Stage 1 recursively plans the scene from the root holon, processing independent groups in parallel. For each internal holon, an agent only deals with the global and group-level local context to determine its child holons. Once the group has been planned, all internal child holons are added to the processing queue. Available agentic slots then process these holons concurrently. Planning is complete when the queue is empty and no planning tasks remain active.

    Asset Generation. Stage 2 generates assets for all leaf holons. Each leaf holon represents an indivisible object with specified attributes, allowing its asset to be generated independently. Image guidance enriches visual detail, and text guidance is well suited to modeling assets according to explicit specifications. In Stage 2, GTA uses GPT-6 Astra [24] and Blender for text-guided modeling, matching the specifications and dimensions set in Stage 1 to facilitate subsequent placement. In Stage 3, GTA uses image models [23] to guide appearance refinement during asset placement.

    Bottom-up Placement and Refinement. Stage 3 assembles the scene from the bottom up. The system maintains a queue of groups that are ready for placement. Each group has one of three states: not-ready, ready, or finished, while leaf holons are treated as finished. A group becomes ready and enters the queue once all its children have finished. Consequently, placement begins with groups whose children are all leaf holons and progressively moves upward through the hierarchy. Agents process ready groups concurrently in the available slots. Alongside placement, refinement agents improve the visual quality of the assets. They first use image editing to enhance renderings of the initial assets produced in the second stage, then use the edited images as visual guidance to refine the assets’ details.

    3.4 Human Generation

    After generating the 3D scene, we populate it with human characters through a scene-guided post-generation pipeline. We first determine their number, roles, activities, and appearance based on the scene’s function, regional context, and available space, and then generate reference images to guide character creation. The pipeline comprises two generation branches: the static branch employs NLF [34] and SMPL-X [27] to recover body shapes and poses from reference images, while the dynamic branch uses Kimodo [32] to generate motion sequences conditioned on textual descriptions and trajectories. DressAgent [14] generates garments and textures, DiffLocks [33] produces hair, and Meshy 7.1 [22] and TRELLIS.2 [40] generate footwear. Reference-based facial texture mapping and skin-tone harmonization further enrich character-specific appearance details. These components are assembled around a common body representation, with garment simulation performed once the body geometry and pose are established. Finally, the characters are integrated into the scene, with adjustments to ensure proper ground contact, object interactions, and collision avoidance, as illustrated in Fig. 2.

    4 Experiments

    4.1 Experimental Setup

    GTA uses GPT-6 Astra [24] with medium reasoning effort both to process holons through agents running in the Codex CLI and to make direct API calls. We use GPT Image 1.5 [23] for image generation. For the main experiments, we configure GTA with 32 parallel agentic slots. Each baseline runs a single model agent, and each GTA slot runs one model agent. We evaluate on a set of 20 indoor scenes and 20 additional outdoor or semi-outdoor scenes spanning a range of scales and types. Target counts range from 10 to 1,000 objects. All rendering throughout scene generation and evaluation uses Blender 4.5.0 with the Cycles engine and OptiX backend on the same set of NVIDIA H100 GPUs, with fixed parameters across methods within each evaluation group. We use Claude Opus 5.5 [2] and GPT-6.1 Sol [25] for visual evaluation.

    4.2 Comparison with other methods

    We compare GTA with SAGE [39] and SceneSmith [28] on indoor scenes, using GPT-6 Astra (medium reasoning effort) for language model calls and GPT Image 1.5 for image generation. On a broader set of scenes, we compare GTA with Claude Fable 5.2 [3] and GPT-6 Astra, both at medium reasoning effort. We evaluate the Original (Astra-O) and Staged (Astra-S) baselines, with Astra-S following the same three-stage workflow as GTA.

    Qualitative Comparison. Fig. 6 compares GTA with several baselines across different scene types. The scene overviews and object close-ups highlight differences in layout, object detail, and physical plausibility. (1) Richer, function-aware layouts. In Fig. 6 C, Fable and Astra-O reuse similar spatial units, stall structures, and display arrangements. GTA lays out and furnishes each stall according to its function. The bakery stall displays different baked goods in a glass case, and the flower stall groups flowers of different shapes and colors in textured buckets. These variations make individual stalls easier to distinguish within a coherent street layout. (2) Finer per-object detail. Fig. 6 A and B show recognizable functional details, including the sewing machine’s needle and presser foot, the grooves in the developing tray, and the markings on an equipment dial. In D, Fable and Astra-O create scene-level variety largely through color and simplified geometry. GTA maintains clear paths and distinct exhibition areas while modeling details such as the strings and frame of the harp-shaped installation and the individual components of the hanging sculpture. (3) More plausible physical relationships. The close-ups reveal visible interpenetration in some baseline assets, including a vase in Fable’s result (Fig. 6 C). GTA’s corresponding examples show clearer object boundaries and more plausible contacts, consistent with the lower penetration rates reported in Table 1.

    Quantitative Comparison. We evaluate quantity compliance, physical plausibility, and visual quality. As shown in Table 1, GTA achieves the lowest errors in both total instance count and distinct type count across indoor and general scenes. GTA also reduces the fraction of objects with penetration depths exceeding 1 mm (P₁), corresponding to relative reductions of 52.7% and 44.1% over the best baseline in each setting. GTA ranks second in mean penetration depth (MPD) in both groups, achieves the highest NAV score in both groups, and the highest opening-clearance score on general scenes. GTA receives the highest visual-quality score in six of the eight comparisons, suggesting that GTA can preserve geometric and material detail in individual objects while constructing complete scenes. With the GPT-6 Astra backbone held fixed, GTA outperforms Astra-O and Astra-S on different metrics.

    Speed and Throughput. Fig. 5 shows that GTA achieves the lowest wall-clock time per object across all the compared methods. GTA achieves a 3.36× speedup over Astra-S in wall-clock time per object. Compared with Astra-O, GTA reduces time per object from 19.26 to 18.80 seconds and achieves 15.4× the system-level token throughput. Stage 3 refinement accounts for 73.3% of GTA’s token usage, indicating that most of this capacity is devoted to refining individual objects. These results show that GTA’s parallel execution accommodates more per-object refinement within a shorter generation time.

    4.3 Ablation Studies

    We evaluate the effect of the number of agentic slots on generation speed using three scenes containing 80, 250, and 800 objects. For each scene, we hold the input and experimental conditions fixed and measure the runtime of each stage with 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, and 32 slots. We run each configuration three times and report the mean runtime. We compute speedups relative to the single-slot runtime. As shown in Fig. 9, increasing the number of slots accelerates generation for all scenes. Larger scenes achieve higher end-to-end speedups. The 80-object scene reaches a plateau early, the 250-object scene attains a higher speedup, and the 800-object scene achieves the largest speedup at 32 slots. These results indicate that larger scenes can make better use of additional parallel resources. Stage 2 scales closest to the ideal linear speedup. As scene scale and slot count increase, Stage 3 becomes the dominant contributor to end-to-end runtime. At 32 slots, it accounts for more than half of the total runtime in each scene, making it the primary bottleneck for further speedup.

    Fig. 10 compares GTA with and without object-level refinement in Stage 3. Even without refinement, GTA produces more structurally complete objects than Astra. For example, GTA models a detailed gatehouse and side doorway, yielding a more complete structure than Astra’s simple frame. Refinement largely preserves the gate’s structure while making the masonry texture, roof tile edges, and timber framing more distinct. It also highlights the cart wheel’s wood texture and spoke joints. This comparison shows that GTA establishes the main structure of each object before refinement, and that Stage 3 further improves details.

    5 Application

    GTA for game production. Clear routes and distinct functional areas help players navigate and explore, while detailed modeling of interactable objects makes the scene more convincing up close. Fig. 7 shows additional GTA results across diverse regional settings with scene-guided NPCs. GTA for robotic training. GTA can support task-driven robot training by generating functional scenes, as shown in Fig. 11. GTA creates visually diverse environments for diverse robot-training scenarios with context-appropriate human characters. Holarchy for other agentic tasks. While scenes are naturally hierarchical, holarchy can also scale other agentic tasks with a dependency graph by executing ready subtasks in parallel and combining outputs through unified interfaces.

    6 Conclusion

    We introduce GTA, a framework for scalable scene generation in which each holon serves as a scale-agnostic scene unit. This shared representation allows agents to process independent branches concurrently during planning, asset generation, and assembly. GTA generates scenes faster and at higher throughput across diverse types and scales, producing coherent layouts, detailed assets, and fewer object interpenetrations. Scaling studies show that larger scenes benefit more from additional agentic slots. Limitations. GTA tends to generate layouts with distinct spatial groups, making transitions between neighboring regions less gradual, and there is room to improve token usage efficiency.

    （参考文献见原文。）
