一句话：现有基准的参考本身是从被测视频里拟合出来的——这种循环验证无法暴露错误。

要点：

  • 交互式视频世界模型要把用户命令变成对生成场景的探索，因此有两个硬要求：**镜头移动时场景要守住 3D 结构**，**每个动作要有一致的、稳定的效果**
  • 现有基准的参考大多**从被测视频自身拟合**（用它自己的帧重建的场景，或一条对齐到命令路径、尺度自由相机轨迹），因此这类循环验证会掩盖错误
  • StrideWorld 因此改用外部基准来评「场景刚性」与「动作一致性」

为什么值得看：评测的循环验证是这个领域最隐蔽的问题：参考来自被测对象，错了也测不出来。与 11-16 WMEval（Unity 当 oracle）、11-18 FlipTest（反事实）一起，这三条构成了「怎么才算真的在模拟」的三种独立答案。

中文摘要：交互式视频世界模型要把用户命令转化为对生成场景的探索，这对场景提出了两项硬性要求：镜头移动时场景必须保持 3D 结构，且每个动作要产生一致而稳定的效果。作者指出，现有基准大多把参考对象**从被测视频自身拟合出来**——或是用它自己的帧重建出的场景，或是一条对齐到命令路径、尺度自由的相机轨迹；这种循环式的验证会掩盖错误。StrideWorld 因此引入外部基准来评估「场景刚性」与「动作一致性」，使评测不再依赖被测模型自己的输出。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-19

本期推送：2026-11-20

StrideWorld: Benchmarking Scene Rigidity and Action Consistency
in Interactive Video World Models

Abstract

Interactive video world models turn user commands into the exploration of a generated scene, which requires the scene to keep its 3D structure as the camera moves and each action to keep a stable effect. Existing benchmarks mostly evaluate these properties against references fitted to the video under test, either a scene reconstructed from its own frames or a camera trajectory aligned to the command path with a free scale. Such references can absorb gradual scene deformation and changes in pace and route length, so these errors can pass undetected. We therefore introduce StrideWorld, a benchmark whose references are fixed before the motion they judge. It evaluates scene rigidity against the ground-truth geometry of the start view, and action consistency against the stride of each action, the camera motion of one command. The stride is measured on the model’s first steps and then used to test the steps that follow, so each model is judged only against its own steps. Its measurements are validated on rendered videos with known camera motion, and its scores agree with human judgments. Across 54,600 videos generated by fifteen open models from 140 start views, all models but one deform their scenes as the camera moves, with offsets up to 7.3 times those of a rigid rendering along the same camera path. Most models keep a steady pace when a single action is held. Along composed routes, several models often stall, and most completed routes end away from the positions predicted by each model’s own strides. Only the two models that scale commands by the estimated scene depth bring most routes close to these positions. Fine-tuning two models on a few rendered clips removes most of their mid-route stalls. Code, data, and a leaderboard are publicly available at https://github.com/chuangwang123/strideworld.

††footnotetext: ∗Equal contribution. †Corresponding authors.

1 Introduction

Interactive video world models shift video generation from producing clips for passive viewing to synthesizing environments that respond to user commands [45, 64, 18, 28, 54, 39, 38, 13, 41]. Systems such as Genie 3 [33, 34, 6, 45] build controllable generative worlds on demand, aiming to offer a new form of interactive entertainment. For the generated content to constitute a world rather than a sequence of individually plausible frames, it must first preserve its 3D structure, without deformation, as the viewpoint changes. At the same time, usable interaction requires the model to give stable feedback to user commands. Basic operations such as moving and turning the camera should have a consistent and predictable effect throughout the interaction.

Evaluating whether an interactive world model meets these requirements takes more than measuring the perceptual quality targeted by conventional video benchmarks [21, 22, 31]. Recent benchmarks have therefore begun to assess such models along two axes, spatial consistency and action control. To assess 3D structure, metrics such as those of WBench and MEt3R [61, 2, 58, 56] reconstruct the scene from the generated frames with 3D foundation models such as VGGT [47] and Depth Anything 3 [30]. They then check whether the frames are consistent with this reconstruction. This geometric reference, however, is fitted to the video under test. Since such foundation models can fit seemingly coherent geometry even to inconsistent images [35], gradual scene deformation can be absorbed into the reference and go undetected by these benchmarks.

For action control, the reference raises the same issue. Benchmarks such as WorldScore and WBench [9, 61, 58] compare the recovered camera trajectory with the commanded one after aligning their scales, which accommodates models with different control interfaces. This scale is likewise estimated from the trajectory under test, so it averages out changes in the distance per command. A model whose steps lengthen or shorten midway can therefore still match the commanded path. Loop-closure tests [29, 25, 56, 55, 59, 51, 14] avoid rescaling but typically assume that opposite commands cancel, an assumption that many current models violate, as shown in App. H.3. They also test whether a loop returns to its start rather than whether each command keeps a stable effect along an open route. How to test scene geometry and action control against references independent of the video under test therefore remains open.

To this end, we introduce StrideWorld, a benchmark for scene rigidity and action consistency. Each of its references is fixed before the motion it judges, as shown in Fig. 1. The Rigidity test places 3D anchors at the ground-truth depth of each start view and checks whether the visible surfaces stay in place as the camera moves. For actions, we measure the stride of each action from the model’s own first four steps, so models with different interfaces need no shared unit of motion. The stride is the camera motion of one command, and it predicts the camera pose at every later step. The Pace test checks whether the camera keeps this stride when a single action is held, and the Composition test checks whether the strides add up along multi-action routes. These routes come in pairs designed to reach the same end, for example the same translations in a different order. Each route is compared with its own prediction and with its partner. The camera is recovered at every step, which locates where a route stalls or drifts from its prediction.

We evaluate fifteen open models on 54,600 videos generated from 140 start views across 30 scenes, as shown in Fig. 2. All models but one deform their scenes as the camera moves. How well a model preserves the scene does not predict how well it composes actions. When a single action is held, most models move in the commanded direction and keep a steady pace. When actions are combined into routes, however, several models often stall partway. Even completed routes mostly end away from the positions predicted by the model’s own strides. Part of this error arises at action switches, where models carry the previous action over or start the new one slowly. Only the two models that scale commands by the estimated scene depth bring most routes close to their predictions. Existing metrics largely miss these failures, as a reconstruction-based reprojection error detects scene deformation in only three of the fifteen models. When the pace of a rendered video grows by half, a scale-fitted trajectory error flags 43% of such videos, whereas the Pace test flags 94% at the same false-alarm rate. Finally, fine-tuning two models on 112 rendered clips with exact camera paths removes most of their mid-route stalls and more than doubles their Composition scores.

In summary, our contributions are as follows:

  • 1.

    We propose StrideWorld, which measures scene rigidity against the ground-truth geometry of the start view and action consistency against each model’s own action strides. We validate its measurements on rendered videos with known camera motion and its scores against the judgments of ten human raters.

  • 2.

    We benchmark fifteen open interactive video world models and find that most deform their scenes as the camera moves. They keep a steady pace under a single action but often fail when actions are combined into routes.

  • 3.

    We show that fine-tuning two models on 112 rendered clips with exact camera paths removes most of their mid-route stalls and brings route endpoints closer to their predictions without lowering image-quality scores.

    • 2 Related Work

    Interactive video world models.

    World models were first studied in reinforcement learning as learned simulators of an agent’s environment [15, 16]. Building on video generation models trained at scale [5, 46, 57, 1], camera-controlled video models condition an entire clip on a prescribed camera trajectory [17, 65], whereas 3D world generators lift generated content into explicit 3D scenes [42, 38, 44]. Interactive video world models instead generate each new segment in response to user commands [6, 33, 45, 28, 64], given as discrete keys [18, 49, 66, 41, 39], camera poses [36, 44, 38, 13, 60, 62, 20, 40], or text prompts [7]. To keep the scene stable over long interactions, recent models maintain a memory of past frames, patches, or implicit 3D features [54, 49, 36, 62, 39], condition on an explicit 3D cache [38], encode camera geometry in their positional embeddings [53], or use reinforcement learning to reduce long-horizon drift [50, 14]. Their control interfaces express motion in different units, from key presses of unspecified length to camera displacements normalized by scene depth. The same command therefore moves the camera by different amounts across models.

    Evaluating action control.

    Early video benchmarks assessed perceptual quality, physical plausibility, and instruction following [21, 22, 31, 3, 4, 27]. Interactive benchmarks add action control and use different motion references, as listed in Tab. 1. Direction metrics check the commanded motion axis [56, 63], and WorldMark also measures held-command speed decay in optical flow. Trajectory metrics compare the recovered camera path with a reference after scale alignment or normalization [9, 11, 61, 58, 59, 8], so their sensitivity to pace depends on the reference and the temporal alignment. WorldRoamBench [55] builds an adaptive reference from each predicted segment’s displacement and compares paths at matched arc length. Revisit tests avoid rescaling by comparing return views, matched portions of retraced paths, or reconstructed scene segments after a loop [29, 25, 56, 11, 61, 58, 55, 59]. Similarly, group-action tests [51] check identity, inverse, and composition relations, and WorldCycle [14] evaluates endpoint closure, mirrored forward–reverse frames, and phase-aligned repeated cycles. StrideWorld instead uses separately calibrated strides to measure each step on open routes, without fitting the route’s scale or requiring opposite actions to cancel, since each action has its own stride.

    Evaluating geometric consistency.

    Evaluating 3D consistency hinges on what serves as the geometric reference, which Tab. 1 also lists. Most benchmarks derive this reference from the generated video itself. Like MEt3R [2] for generated images, they reconstruct the scene and camera from the generated frames with SLAM or 3D foundation models and measure how well the views agree with this reconstruction [9, 61, 58, 52, 56, 48, 32]. This approach needs no external 3D reference, but the reference is fitted to the generated frames. Because 3D foundation models can fit seemingly consistent geometry even to inconsistent images [35], gradual deformation can be absorbed into the reference. Other benchmarks compare generated views with ground truth rendered by a game engine or simulator [59, 55, 19] or with registered RGB-D captures [32]. Such references constrain the available viewpoints, and control errors can enter the comparison when the generated and reference viewpoints differ. Orbia also evaluates self-consistency at recovered cameras and renders held-out generated views from a reconstructed Gaussian scene [32]. StrideWorld instead takes ground-truth depth only from the start view and evaluates rigidity at the recovered camera, using disjoint anchors for pose fitting and testing.

    3 The StrideWorld Benchmark

    Start views.

    To provide a 3D reference that is independent of the generated video, every start view comes with ground-truth depth and camera parameters. The benchmark comprises 140 start views across 30 scenes that span indoor and outdoor, natural and built environments, as shown in Fig. 2a. Twenty-four scenes are built in Unreal Engine 5 [10] and provide 104 start views with exact depth, and six are real ETH3D scenes [37] that provide 36 start views with depth from laser scans. Preprocessing is described in App. A and results by domain in App. F.1.

    Action programs.

    Every model is driven by six basic actions, forward (W), backward (S), left and right translation (A, D), and left and right yaw turns (YL, YR), with pitch evaluated separately in App. A.6. One step is a single command interval of the model’s native interface. From every start view, each action is held for 16 steps under three random seeds. The first four steps calibrate the action’s stride, and the later steps test whether the model keeps a steady pace. Each start view is also assigned eight multi-action routes of 8 to 14 steps, run with one seed, in which a switch occurs whenever two consecutive steps take different actions. The routes form four pairs, and the two routes of each pair are designed to end at the same place under ideal actions. In the cancel pair, the two routes insert back-and-forth detours of equal length along different axes into a shared base path, schematically W→A→D→W versus W→W→S→W. The three swap pairs execute the same translations in different orders, either directly (W→W→D vs. D→W→W), after a turn (YR→W→D vs. YR→D→W), or across turns. All sequences are kept short enough for the surfaces of the start view to remain visible, so that the camera can be recovered from ground-truth geometry throughout. Long-horizon exploration and revisits are therefore outside the scope of StrideWorld. In total, each model generates 3,640 videos (2,520 single-action and 1,120 route videos), for 54,600 videos across all models.

    Models and interfaces.

    We evaluate fifteen open models covering three control interfaces. Five are driven by discrete keys or tokens (Matrix-Game 2.0 and 3.0 [18, 49], SANA-WM [66], DreamX-World [41], and HY-World 1.5 [39]), nine by camera poses (Matrix-Game 3.5 [36], HY-World 2.0 [44], LingBot-World v2 [13], AlayaWorld [40], Lyra 2.0 [38], EVOKE [60], WorldCrafter [62], SolarWM [20], and HY-WorldPlay [39]), and one by text prompts (H3-World [7]). Each model runs its released inference configuration, and a thin adapter maps the six actions to its native interface. As shown in Fig. 2b, a single step moves the camera by widely different amounts across models, and the interfaces share no unit of motion. Because our tests measure motion in each model’s own strides, command magnitudes need not match across models. We therefore use a model’s default per-step command when its motion is clearly measurable and keeps the start-view surfaces visible over 16 held steps, and otherwise set a fixed magnitude that does. All command magnitudes are released with the benchmark, as detailed in App. A and H.6.

    4 Evaluation Protocol

    StrideWorld tests scene rigidity, single-action pace, and multi-action composition. The headline metrics of the three tests in Tab. 2 are the Rigidity offset relative to the rigid counterpart, the pace ratio, and the Composition score, and the remaining columns locate failures.

    4.1 Scene rigidity

    If a generated scene is rigid, the 3D points of the start view stay in place in every later frame. Using the ground-truth depth z and intrinsics K of the start view, we lift feature pixels pᵢ to 3D anchors Xᵢ=z(pᵢ) K⁻¹pᵢʰ and split them alternately into disjoint pose anchors ℙ and held-out anchors ℚ, as illustrated in Fig. 1. In generated frame t, CoTracker3 [23] tracks anchor i to the position x̃_i,t, and for a camera T∈SE(3) we measure the angle between the tracked viewing ray and the ray toward the rigid position of the anchor in the camera frame,

    φ_i,t(T)=∠(K⁻¹x̃_i,tʰ, T⁻¹Xᵢ).

    		(1)

    The camera of frame t is fitted to the pose anchors alone, and the Rigidity offset (∘)eₜ of the frame is the mean residual of the held-out anchors under this camera,

    T̂ₜ=\arg\min_T∈SE(3)∑_i∈ℙₜφ_i,t(T)²,(2)
    eₜ=(1)/(|ℚₜ|)∑_i∈ℚₜφ_i,t(T̂ₜ),

    where ℙₜ⊆ℙ holds the RANSAC inliers of an EPnP initialization [26, 12] and ℚₜ⊆ℚ the held-out anchors tracked in frame t. Because T̂ₜ is estimated from the generated frames, errors in following the command do not enter eₜ. In Tab. 2, Offset is the median eₜ over route-video frames at matched image motion, since the offset grows with how far the anchors move in the image. vs. rigid divides the offset of twenty routes by that of their rigid counterpart, a rendering of the true scene along the same camera paths and in the same video format, so that a ratio of one means no excess over tracking noise (App. B.2 and G.3).

    4.2 Single-action pace

    Holding a command should move the camera by the same amount at every step. Models share no unit of motion, so we measure each action in units of the motion it produces in its first steps. Let H_a,k∈SE(2) denote the planar pose of the recovered camera relative to the start view, its horizontal position and heading, after k steps of a single action a. The strideUₐ∈SE(2) of the action averages the per-step motion of the first four steps in the Lie algebra se(2),

    Uₐ=Exp(1/4∑ₖ₌₁⁴(LogH_a,k)/(k)),

    		(3)

    and the predicted pose after k held steps is Ĥ_a,k=Uₐᵏ. A stride is calibrated separately for each model, start view, and seed, and strides are never compared across start views, since a model’s scale of motion may differ between scenes. Tab. 2 reports three metrics for single actions. Resp. (%) is the share of videos that move the camera in the commanded direction. The pace ratio divides the observed displacement or turn along the commanded axis at step 16 by the predicted one, so values above and below 1 indicate acceleration and slowdown. The Pace score takes the endpoint error at steps 12 and 16 relative to the predicted motion, r, and maps it to s(r)=100/(1+r), which is 100 for an exact prediction and 50 when the error equals the predicted motion. Videos that do not respond or whose camera can no longer be recovered score zero (App. C).

    4.3 Multi-action composition

    Along a multi-action route q=(a₁,…,aₙ), each step should move the camera by the stride of its action, expressed in the camera frame at the start of that step. The predicted endpoint therefore chains the strides calibrated under the same start view and seed, Ĥ_q=U_a₁⋯U_aₙ, and no parameter is fitted to the route itself. We evaluate endpoints at two levels, each route against its own prediction, E_q=Ĥ_q⁻¹H_q, and the two routes of a pair (q,q^′) against each other,

    E_qq^′=(Ĥ_q⁻¹Ĥ_q^′)⁻¹(H_q⁻¹H_q^′),

    		(4)

    which compares where the two routes end relative to each other with where their strides place them. Position and heading errors are divided by the median translation stride bₜ and the median turn stride bᵣ of the start view and seed, so all errors are expressed in strides.

    A step is stalled if it moves or turns less than 10% of its stride along the commanded axis, and a route is completed if its first frame matches the start view, its camera is recovered at every step boundary, and none of its steps stalls. Tab. 2 reports five composition metrics, of which the first three compare each route with its own prediction. Stall (%) is the share of routes with at least one stalled step. End err. (str.) is the median position error of completed routes, and Near (%) is the share of all routes that are completed and end within one stride of their prediction in both position and heading. The fourth compares the two routes of a swap pair with each other. Swap gap (str.) is the median distance between the ends of the two routes of a completed swap pair, which reflects the order of actions because both routes contain the same actions. The Composition score covers both levels and averages s(r) of the position and heading errors over all routes and route pairs, with incomplete ones scoring zero, so it combines completion and endpoint accuracy in a single number (App. C).

    5 Results

    We evaluate the fifteen open models on all 54,600 videos. Tab. 2 reports every metric for each model, and Fig. 3 places the headline metric of each test side by side. Fourteen models are ranked, since the first steps of AlayaWorld are too small for a reliable stride. The first three subsections take the tests in turn, and Sec. 5.4 checks the measurements against known camera motion and human judgments.

    5.1 Generated scenes deform as the camera moves

    Most models deform the generated scene to some degree as the camera moves. The measured offset also contains tracking noise, which depends on a model’s resolution, frame rate, and compression. To separate the two, we re-render the true scene along the camera paths of twenty routes of each model in the same video format, which gives a rigid counterpart of these videos, and divide the offset of each model by that of its counterpart on the same frames. Every model deviates 1.6 to 7.3 times more than its rigid counterpart, as shown in Fig. 3a, so tracking noise alone does not account for the excess.

    This excess has two possible sources, a scene that deforms over time and a scene that stays rigid at a wrong depth. Refitting the depth of each held-out anchor and the camera freely removes the second. The ratio of Lyra 2.0 then falls to one, whereas the other fourteen models stay at 1.2× or above, so the excess of Lyra 2.0 comes mostly from a fixed depth error. It conditions each new view on an explicit 3D cache built from estimated depth [38], so the surfaces it has already shown keep the same geometry, which suggests that a 3D representation mitigates deformation.

    Preserving the scene does not make a model follow commands. The Rigidity ranking of the models shows no relation to their Composition score ranking, with Spearman correlations of -0.01 for the offset and -0.07 for the counterpart ratio (App. G.3 and D.1).

    5.2 Held actions keep a steady pace

    When a single action is held for 16 steps, most models move in the commanded direction and keep the pace set by their first four steps. Twelve of the fourteen ranked models have a median pace ratio within the steady band of 0.8 to 1.25, as shown in Fig. 3b, and the text-driven H3-World is only slightly faster. The same pattern holds with equally weighted strides (App. E.2).

    Among the ranked models, only DreamX-World changes pace strongly. It accelerates over the first steps of a hold, so its first four steps no longer predict where a held command leads. AlayaWorld moves slowly during its first steps, which makes its stride hard to measure, and its stride-based metrics are therefore shown in grey, left unranked, and marked by † in Tab. 2 (App. E).

    5.3 Composed routes stall and drift

    Once actions are combined into routes, the strides of most models no longer predict where their routes end, as shown in Fig. 3c. Only HY-World 2.0 and Lyra 2.0 bring more than three quarters of their routes within one stride of the predicted endpoint, whereas most other models do so for fewer than a quarter. Both take camera poses as input and scale translations by the estimated depth of the start view, so the same command moves the camera by a consistent fraction of the scene. Tying commands to scene depth thus appears to help strides add up along a route. The interface alone does not explain this gap, as Near ranges from 3.1% to 84.3% across the ranked camera-pose models and the key-driven Matrix-Game 3.0 outperforms all of them except HY-World 2.0 and Lyra 2.0.

    The routes of the other models fail in two main ways, illustrated in Fig. 4. The first is mid-route stalls, where the camera stops for a step partway through a route, most often when a new action starts. Stalls affect more than a third of the routes in four ranked models, as listed in Tab. 2, and account for most incomplete routes.

    The second is endpoint drift, where even completed routes end well away from their prediction. The median error is above one stride in eleven of the fourteen ranked models. In four ranked models, the same actions in a different order end about two to three times farther apart than repeated generation predicts. Regenerating the routes with two further seeds shows that this drift is systematic, as a route’s end error is a median 1.8 to 3.7 times the spread of its ends across seeds. Part of the error arises at action switches, where some models carry the previous action over and others start the new action with only about half a stride, whereas the leading models keep the same step before and after the switch (App. F).

    Existing control metrics miss much of this, as direction checks miss both failure modes and direction accuracy shows no clear relation to a model’s Composition score. A trajectory error with a fitted scale also misses many failed routes, even when it is given the stride-predicted path as its reference. After fitting one scale, about a fifth of the stalled routes still have an error below 10% of the path, and so do about a quarter of the routes that end more than two strides from their prediction. The error also does not show where along a route the failure occurs (App. F.7).

    5.4 Measurements are accurate and robust

    On videos rendered in UE5 along known camera paths, the recovered cameras deviate from the true ones by a median of 1.5% in translation and 0.3% in rotation. Adding blur, compression, flicker, or moderate wobble keeps these median errors within 4.0% and 2.1%. On the generated videos, other calibration lengths, stall thresholds, and camera-recovery anchors leave all findings unchanged, and the route findings hold when the commands of three models are halved or doubled (App. G, H, and A.4).

    We then change one property of a rendered video by a known amount to test whether each metric responds to the failure it targets, as shown in Fig. 5. Deformation injected into the rigid counterparts raises the Rigidity offset linearly, while texture drift, flicker, and occluders leave it near its level on the rigid counterparts. The reprojection error of a feed-forward reconstruction, by contrast, responds to texture drift and to blur with compression at least as strongly as to deformation. On the generated videos, it separates only three of the fifteen models from their rigid counterparts, whereas the Rigidity offset separates all fifteen.

    On the action side, Fig. 5a applies every test at its default threshold. When each test is instead set to flag 5% of the ideal held videos, the Pace test flags 94% of the held videos whose pace grows to 1.5 times. A scale-fitted trajectory error flags only 43% of them, because its scale absorbs part of the change. Scene deformation also shifts the recovered camera, which at the level seen in generated videos changes the Near decision of 8% to 20% of routes but leaves the model ranking unchanged (App. G.4).

    The scores also agree with the judgments of ten non-author raters blind to the models and metrics. They rated 160 randomly sampled videos for whether the camera follows the commands, with a Fleiss’ κ of 0.87, and the score of each video separates those judged good with an AUC of 0.88. On 140 completed swap pairs, the pair score separates those judged to end at the same place with an AUC of 0.83, against at most 0.74 for scores with a fitted scale. For two videos of the same route whose Rigidity offsets differ at least twofold, the majority of raters chose the one with the smaller offset as more stable in all 39 untied pairs (App. I).

    6 Fine-Tuning on Rendered Camera Paths

    Along composed routes, several models often stall and most completed routes end away from their predictions, as shown in Sec. 5.3. Since every command step in a rendered clip moves the camera by an exact displacement or turn, we test whether fine-tuning on a few such clips reduces these failures. We render 112 training clips in procedural Blender scenes that share no assets or routes with StrideWorld, and fine-tune LoRA adapters on the non-distilled base models of HY-World 1.5 and SANA-WM.

    On the full benchmark of 3,640 videos, both fine-tuned models improve over their base models on every consistency metric without lowering image-quality scores. Stalled routes fall from 72.0% to 11.2% for HY-World 1.5 and from 57.9% to 23.1% for SANA-WM. The Composition score of both models more than doubles and exceeds that of the released models in Tab. 2, and the Rigidity offset also falls, by about two fifths for SANA-WM. For HY-World 1.5, we further examine what these gains depend on. They hold on the real ETH3D views although all training clips are rendered. We then randomly perturb the step lengths of the training clips, so that every command step still moves the camera but by a varying amount. Fine-tuning on these clips retains about four fifths of the stall reduction, and exact step lengths add the rest. Tab. J.1 and App. J give the full results.

    7 Conclusion

    StrideWorld tests interactive video world models against references that are fixed before the motion they judge. It compares the scene with the ground-truth geometry of the start view, and each action with the stride set by the model’s own first steps. Across fifteen open models, nearly all deform their scenes as the camera moves. Most keep a steady pace under a single held action, but their composed routes often stall partway or end away from the positions predicted by their own strides. Two design choices stand out among the stronger models. The one that conditions on an explicit 3D cache preserves the scene best, and the two that scale commands by the estimated scene depth compose routes best. Fine-tuning two models on a few rendered clips with exact camera paths also removes most of their mid-route stalls. Extending StrideWorld to dynamic scenes and full 6-DoF trajectories is a natural next step (App. M).

    （参考文献见原文。）

    StrideWorld: Benchmarking Scene Rigidity and Action Consistency
    in Interactive Video World Models
    Supplementary Material

    Contents

    This supplement follows the structure of the main paper; each appendix lists the section it supports.

    AppendixSupports
    ABenchmark details
    start views, route pairs, adapters, command magnitude, Genie 3, GameCraft, pitch    		Sec. 3
    BPose recovery and geometric scoring
    anchors, measurable field of view, Rigidity offset, Scene stability    		Sec. 4
    CStrides, Pace, and Composition scoring
    stride calibration, Response, Pace, Composition    		Sec. 4

    matched image speed, alternative statistics    		Sec. 5.1
    EFurther results on Pace
    per-step pace, equal-weight strides, response profiles    		Sec. 5.2
    FFurther results on Composition
    step-by-step routes, regeneration error, repeated generations, scale fitting, existing metrics    		Sec. 5.3
    GValidation on known motion and rigid renderings
    pose accuracy, degradations, rigid floor, rigid counterparts, controlled changes, VGGT    		Sec. 5.4
    HSensitivity and robustness
    anchor splits, evaluation parameters, opposite actions, stride references, intervals, step duration, matched motion, stride variation    		Sec. 5.4
    IHuman study
    ten blinded raters, control and rigidity    		Sec. 5.4
    JFine-tuning details
    training routes, checkpoints, command-scaled and perturbed-path controls    		Sec. 6
    KReproducibility and supplementary video
    released artifacts, video contents    		–

    per-benchmark evidence for the comparison    		Sec. 2
    MLimitations
    measurement range, scene and motion scope, fine-tuning    		Sec. 7

    Appendix A Benchmark Details

    A.1 Start views

    Camera coordinates follow the right-handed OpenCV convention with x pointing right, y down, and z forward. Ground-truth depth is stored as camera-axis depth z, obtained for UE5 views by scaling the EXR depth channel with the conversion factor recorded for each view and for ETH3D views by aligning the laser-scan depth to the same convention, and 3D anchors are placed only at pixels with valid depth. All control metrics divide displacements by the model’s own stride or by the median depth of the start view, so the internal length unit cancels out. When an adapter crops or resizes the start view with a 2D affine pixel transform A, the intrinsics become K^′=AK and the anchor pixels are transformed in the same way. As shown in Fig. A.1, the rendered views have dense depth and the real views have sparse laser-scan depth.

    A.2 Route construction and assignment

    As shown in Tab. A.1, the four route families vary the translation axes, the lengths of action blocks, the turning directions, and the insertion positions. G1 tests back-and-forth cancellation (cancel), and G2–G4 test reordering without a turn, after a turn, and across turns (swap). The route library contains 96 pairs per family, for 384 pairs and 768 distinct action sequences in total. Each of the 30 scenes is assigned one pair from each family, so all start views and models in a scene execute the same eight routes and the benchmark contains 120 distinct route pairs. G2 routes have eight steps, G3 routes have eleven, and G1 and G4 routes have fourteen. Every step is one of the six basic actions, the two routes of a pair have the same number of steps, and no action sequence is repeated.

    A.3 Control settings

    As shown in Tab. A.2, each model keeps its native control interface and output format, and its single-action and route videos use the same adapter settings. Discrete-key models receive their actions in the encoding of their released inference code, and camera-pose models receive per-step translations and yaw turns in their native input units. Matrix-Game 3.5, EVOKE, WorldCrafter, and SolarWM run their released distilled samplers with 3, 3, 6, and 4 denoising steps, and SolarWM uses its public stage-2 EMA checkpoint. HY-World 1.5 and HY-WorldPlay come from the same model family [39], the first as a step-distilled checkpoint conditioned on discrete control tokens and the second as an RL-trained autoregressive checkpoint conditioned on continuous pose tokens.

    A.4 Command magnitude

    Discrete-key models and the camera-pose models EVOKE and HY-WorldPlay use their release default per-step command, whereas the remaining camera-pose interfaces accept arbitrary step magnitudes, as listed in Tab. A.2. Matrix-Game 2.0 and 3.0 keep their default keyboard translation with the mouse yaw sensitivity lowered from 0.1 to 0.035 and 0.04, so that 16 held turn steps rotate the camera by roughly 17^∘–18^∘ instead of about 54^∘, which is close to the roughly 60^∘ beyond which the camera is rarely recovered from the start-view anchors (App. B.3). SolarWM runs at half its default translation and a third of its default yaw, as 16 steps of its default turn would rotate the camera by 120^∘. For AlayaWorld, the default per-step translation moves the camera by about the tracking noise, so we scale up its translation within the official interface. At the default command, its translation stride stays near the noise floor, its 16-step pace still accelerates, and its Pace score changes by only 2.0 points.

    We also scale the per-step translation and yaw of EVOKE, WorldCrafter, and Lyra 2.0 by 0.5×, 1×, and 2× on 30 start views, the first view of each scene with seed 0, across all six actions and eight routes (420 videos per setting). The composition findings hold at every magnitude, as EVOKE brings at most 3.3% of its routes within one stride, WorldCrafter misses the endpoints of its completed routes by 2.1 to 3.7 strides, and Lyra 2.0 brings 61.7% to 85.0% of its routes within one stride. For EVOKE, these runs scale a smaller base command (0.03125 units and 0.5^∘ per action unit, about 1/5 of the release default translation and 1/10 of the default yaw in Tab. 2). Only the held pace of EVOKE varies with the command magnitude, as its median pace ratio grows from 0.51, 0.64, and 0.81 at 0.5×, 1×, and 2× of this command to 1.11 at the release default on the same views.

    A.5 Directional tests for Genie 3 and GameCraft

    Genie 3.

    We collect 672 videos from the closed-source Genie 3 [33] through its web interface, comprising 288 single-action and 384 route videos from 48 start views in ten UE5 scenes. Because the web stream does not provide frame-accurate input timestamps, step boundaries and strides cannot be recovered, so we test the direction of the net camera motion between the first and the last frame on videos whose endpoint pose reaches an inlier ratio and coverage of at least 0.3. All 115 translation videos with a recoverable endpoint move in the commanded direction, and the cosine between their net horizontal displacement and the commanded axis has a median between 98.9% and 100.0% across the four translations. Sustained turns mostly leave the field of view of the start view, so only 2 of 48 YL and 3 of 48 YR videos keep a recoverable endpoint.

    GameCraft.

    We test Hunyuan-GameCraft [28] on 180 videos in five UE5 scenes, 90 single-action videos of two native control intervals and 90 route videos, of which 172 have valid poses at all step boundaries. It moves in the commanded direction in 100.0% of forward and 93.3% of backward videos, but shows a strong directional bias for lateral translations (26.7% for A and 58.3% for D) and turns (20.0% for YL and 80.0% for YR), as both turn commands mostly rotate the camera in the same direction.

    A.6 Pitch control

    We test upward and downward pitch commands (PU and PD) for ten models on 19 start views with three seeds, for 114 videos of 16 steps per model. Because sustained pitch in 16:9 videos quickly moves the surfaces of the start view out of frame, we evaluate all models over the first eight steps. Direction is the share of videos whose recovered pitch ϑ₈ at step 8 has the commanded sign, and the extra rotation Cᵣₒₜ(8)=100√ψ₈²+φ₈²/|ϑ₈| measures the yaw ψ₈ and roll φ₈ that accompany the pitch. As shown in Tab. A.3, eight of the ten models pitch in the commanded direction in 99.1% to 100.0% of videos with less than 7% extra rotation, whereas AlayaWorld and the text-driven H3-World control vertical camera motion poorly.

    Appendix B Pose Recovery and Geometric Scoring Details

    B.1 Coordinates, anchors, and solver

    An anchor pixel p=[u,v,1]^⊤ of the start view with valid camera-axis depth z(p) gives the 3D point P_cam=z(p)K⁻¹p in the initial camera frame. With Tᶜ²ʷ₀ the initial camera-to-world transform and T̂ʷ²ᶜₜ the recovered world-to-camera transform at frame t, the camera pose of frame t relative to the initial camera is

    Gₜ=(Tᶜ²ʷ₀)⁻¹(T̂ʷ²ᶜₜ)⁻¹.

    		(B.1)

    Rigidity uses the full SE(3) pose, and Pace and Composition use its planar part (App. C.1).

    Anchors are selected once per start view as SIFT keypoints whose neighbouring depths lie within 5% of their own, or as Shi–Tomasi corners on ETH3D views whose laser depth is sparse. The image is divided into an 8×6 grid whose cells keep at most 12 anchors each, and the anchors, sorted by a hash of their identifiers, are assigned alternately to the pose anchors ℙ and the held-out anchors ℚ. A start view thus has a median of 446 anchors (33 to 576) spread over 42 of the 48 cells, with 223 pose and 223 held-out anchors, and every model is evaluated with the same anchors. CoTracker3 [23] tracks both sets through the generated video, and a track at frame t is kept if its coordinates are finite and in frame, its visibility is at least 0.9, and its confidence is at least 0.5. The camera of each frame is initialized from ℙ by EPnP with RANSAC [26, 12] at an angular threshold of 1^∘ (√fₓf_y\tan(1^∘) in pixels) and refined by Levenberg–Marquardt and nonlinear least squares on the viewing rays. Initialization requires at least 12 valid pose anchors, and the refined solution must keep at least six inliers within 1^∘. With vᵢₜ∈{0,1} indicating a valid track of pose anchor i at frame t and φᵢₜ^Pose its angular residual, the tracking coverage cₜ and inlier ratio ρₜ are

    cₜ=(∑_i∈ℙvᵢₜ)/(|ℙ|), ρₜ=(#{i∈ℙ:vᵢₜ=1, φᵢₜ^Pose≤1^∘})/(|ℙ|).

    		(B.2)

    A frame has a valid pose if the solver returns a finite rigid transform with cₜ≥0.1 and ρₜ≥0.1.

    B.2 Rigidity offset and Scene stability

    For a held-out anchor Xᵢ∈ℚ with tracked position x̃_i,t and recovered camera-to-world transform T̂ₜ=(T̂ʷ²ᶜₜ)⁻¹, its rigid projection, angular ray residual, and the mean offset of video v are

    x̂_i,t=π_K (T̂ₜ⁻¹Xᵢʰ),(B.3)
    e_i,tʳᵃʸ=∠ (K⁻¹x̃_i,tʰ,K⁻¹x̂_i,tʰ),
    ē_ray(v)=(1)/(|𝔼ᵥ|)∑_(i,t)∈𝔼ᵥe_i,tʳᵃʸ,

    where π_K is perspective projection, superscript h denotes homogeneous coordinates, and 𝔼ᵥ collects the valid held-out tracks in frames t>0 of video v. A frame enters the Rigidity evaluation if it has a valid pose and at least 12 valid held-out anchors in front of the camera. Its offset eₜ averages eʳᵃʸ_i,t over these anchors, and its image motion is the median angle between the viewing ray of each held-out anchor in the start view and its rigidly projected ray in frame t. Tab. 2 reports the median eₜ over route-video frames whose image motion lies between 2^∘ and 8^∘, and App. G.3 establishes its floor on rigid scenes.

    Scene stability (Scene stability).

    The supplementary video-level score Scene stability maps ē_ray(v), in degrees, to s(ē_ray(v)/1^∘) with s of Eq. (C.5), assigns zero to a video without valid observations, and averages over the eight route videos of each start view and then over the 140 start views. Because it pools all frames regardless of how far the camera moves, it favors models that move the camera little (App. H.5).

    B.3 Measurable range of the start-view anchors

    The camera can be recovered from the start-view anchors as long as enough of the initial surfaces remain in view. As shown in Tab. B.1, pose recovery succeeds on at least 99.6% of steps while the cumulative translation stays within 25% of the start view’s median depth and the cumulative yaw within 30^∘. It remains at 93%–96% up to 150% of the depth and 45^∘–60^∘ of yaw, and drops to 76.9% beyond 60^∘, where rotation moves most of the initial scene out of view. The per-step yaw commands rotate the camera by roughly 15^∘–35^∘ over 16 held steps, keeping 99% of single-action turn videos within the high-recovery range through step 16 (App. A.4).

    Appendix C Strides, Pace, and Composition Scoring Details

    C.1 Planar transforms and strides

    Let c₀ be the start frame of an action sequence and cₖ the frame at the end of step k. The relative pose G_c₀⁻¹G_cₖ has rotation R_a,k and translation (t_x,a,k,t_y,a,k,t_z,a,k)^⊤, and the projection Π keeps its horizontal position and heading,

    H_a,k=Π (G_c₀⁻¹G_cₖ)=\beginbmatrix\cosθ_a,k&\sinθ_a,k&t_x,a,k -\sinθ_a,k&\cosθ_a,k&t_z,a,k 0&0&1\endbmatrix,(C.1)
    θ_a,k=atan2 ((R_a,k)₀₂,(R_a,k)₀₀),

    where matrix indices are zero-based, transforms act on column vectors, H_a,0=I, and positive yaw rotates the camera toward +x. For H∈SE(2), t(H) is its 2D translation and θ(H)=atan2(H₀₁,H₀₀) its yaw. For a twist ξ=(ρₓ,ρ_z,θ)^⊤∈se(2), the hat operator and the exponential and logarithmic maps of Eq. (3) are

    ξ^∧=\beginbmatrix0&θ&ρₓ -θ&0&ρ_z 0&0&0\endbmatrix, Exp(ξ)=\exp(ξ^∧), (Log(H))^∧=\logH.

    		(C.2)

    Calibration requires valid poses at the start and at each of the first four step boundaries, with cumulative yaw below 170^∘. With ξ̄ₐ=(ρ_x,a,ρ_z,a,ωₐ)^⊤ the mean twist of Eq. (3), the signed axial stride component uₐ is positive in the commanded direction,

    uₐ=\begincasesρ_z,a,&a=W, -ρ_z,a,&a=S, -ρ_x,a,&a=A, ρ_x,a,&a=D, -ωₐ,&a=YL, ωₐ,&a=YR.\endcases

    		(C.3)

    It enters the stall check of the composition score and the stride variation statistics (App. H.8).

    Pace score (Pace score).

    Let Aₜ={W,S,A,D} denote the translations and Aᵣ={YL,YR} the turns. At the checkpoints k∈{12,16}, the relative error of the predicted pose Ĥ_a,k=Uₐᵏ is

    r_a,k=\begincases(∥t(H_a,k)-t(Ĥ_a,k)∥₂)/(k∥t(Uₐ)∥₂),&a∈Aₜ, [10.0pt] (|wrap (θ(H_a,k)-θ(Ĥ_a,k))|)/(k|θ(Uₐ)|),&a∈Aᵣ,\endcases k∈{12,16},

    		(C.4)

    where wrap(·) returns the shortest signed angular difference. Each relative error is mapped to [0,100] by

    s(r)=100/1+r,

    		(C.5)

    and the Pace score of a video averages the scores at steps 12 and 16. A checkpoint without a recovered pose and every checkpoint of a video that fails the response check below score zero.

    Response (Response).

    For a single-action video, let uₖ be the signed cumulative displacement along the commanded axis after k steps and k^∗≤16 the last step with a recovered pose. The video responds if u_k^∗≥0.02 dᵥ for a translation, with dᵥ the median valid depth of the start view, or u_k^∗≥2^∘ for a turn, and a video without any recovered pose does not respond. As shown in Tab. C.1, halving or doubling both thresholds changes Response and Pace score by at most 1.5 points for thirteen models and by up to 12.2 points for AlayaWorld and Matrix-Game 3.5, the two models with the smallest single-step motion.

    C.2 Composition scoring

    The route prediction Ĥ_q=U_a₁⋯U_aₙ and the errors E_q=Ĥ_q⁻¹H_q and E_qq^′ (Eq. (4)) use the strides calibrated under the same model, start view, and seed. For either error E, position and heading are measured in units of the model’s own translation stride bₜ and turn stride bᵣ,

    bₜ=median_a∈Aₜ∥t(Uₐ)∥₂,rₜ=(∥t(E)∥₂)/(bₜ),(C.6)
    bᵣ=median_a∈Aᵣ|θ(Uₐ)|,r_ψ=(|wrap(θ(E))|)/(bᵣ),

    so that s(rₜ)=50 when the position error equals one stride and s(r_ψ)=50 when the heading error equals one turn stride. The score of a route q or a pair p averages the two components, s_q=1/2(s(rₜ)+s(r_ψ)) and sₚ=1/2(s(rₜ)+s(r_ψ)).

    A route is completed and enters the set V_q if (i) all six strides of its start view and seed are calibrated with bₜ,bᵣ>0, (ii) its start frame and every step boundary have valid poses, (iii) no step stalls, meaning that every step moves or turns the camera along the commanded axis by at least 0.1|uₐ|, and (iv) the generated first frame matches the adapter-processed start view with a mean RGB L₁ difference of at most 32 on the 0–255 scale. A pair is completed and enters Vₚ when both of its routes are completed. Over the N_q=1,120 routes and Nₚ=560 pairs of a model, incomplete routes and pairs score zero,

    Route=(1)/(N_q)∑_q∈V_qs_q, Pair=1/Nₚ∑_p∈Vₚsₚ,

    		(C.7)

    Composition score is 1/2(Route+Pair), and the completion rate is 100 |V_q|/N_q. End err. in Tab. 2 is the median of rₜ over V_q, and Near is the share of all N_q routes that are completed with both rₜ≤1 and r_ψ≤1, so a completed route whose position lies within one stride of the prediction but whose heading deviates by more than one turn stride is not counted as Near. This heading condition matters mainly for Matrix-Game 3.0, whose Near would be 65.6% instead of 42.5% with the position condition alone, while it changes Near by at most 4.3 points for every other model.

    Aggregation.

    Relative errors are mapped to scores before averaging. Response and Pace score average over the three seeds of a view, then over the views of a scene and across the 30 scenes, weighting the six actions equally. Route, Pair, and Composition score average over all routes and pairs of a model (Eq. (C.7)). Repeat variation and Cross-view variation average relative standard deviations within each scene and then across scenes. Confidence intervals use 2,000 bootstrap resamples of the 30 scenes, and scores restricted to completed routes and split by domain are reported in App. F.1.

    Appendix D Further Results on Rigidity

    D.1 Rigidity offset at matched speed and under other statistics

    Tab. D.1 splits the frames whose image motion is 2^∘–8^∘ by the speed of that motion, the change of image motion from the previous frame. Below 0.4^∘ per frame, where 58% to 100% of each model’s frames lie, the offsets of twelve models are 2.1 to 6.7 times Lyra 2.0’s in every speed range, and rigid renderings give a floor of 0.11^∘ to 0.15^∘ in every range including the fastest. HY-World 2.0 and Lyra 2.0 share resolution, frame rate, and resize and differ only in frames per step, yet HY-World 2.0’s offset is 3.2 times Lyra’s (95% interval [3.0,3.4] over videos). With equal weight on each 1^∘ bin of image motion or with per-frame medians, every model except SolarWM still stays at least 2.4 times Lyra’s offset, and SolarWM stays at 1.6 to 1.7 times it (App. G.3). Across the fourteen ranked models, neither the offset nor its ratio to the rigid counterpart is related to the Composition score, with Spearman’s ρ of -0.01 and -0.07.

item.title: NVIDIA 把 CAD 转 USD 做成了「Agent Skill」：一个仓库只放给 agent 看的说明书与工作流契约 ｜ NVIDIA-Omniverse/usd-convert-cad
item.description:
一句话：转换器本身走 Python wheel 单独发布，仓库里装的是「agent 怎么安装、验证、运行它」。

要点：

  • 职责切分很清楚：**转换能力**由单独的 `usd-convert-cad` Python wheel 提供，仓库里放的是**给 AI agent 用的 skill**——包括安装、验证与运行该 wheel 的指令、文档与工作流契约
  • 面向多个 agent 同时适配：仓库里同时有 `.claude/`、`.codex/`、`.cursor/` 与 `.agent/` 目录，即同一份 skill 按各家 agent 的约定各放一份
  • 仓库自称是「Skillhub 风格」的仓库，说明这类「把工具封装成 agent skill」正在成为 NVIDIA 在 Omniverse 侧的分发方式；文档注明在 Python 3.12 + `usd-convert-cad==0.4.0` 上测过

为什么值得看：这条的价值不在 CAD 转换，而在**分发形态**：工具本体走包管理器，agent 侧只放「说明书 + 契约」。对内部维护 DCC/引擎工具链的团队，这是把老工具接进 AI 工作流最低成本的方式——不用改工具，只加一份 skill。

中文摘要：NVIDIA 的 usd-convert-cad 仓库体现了「工具 + agent skill」的分工方式：真正的转换能力由单独发布的 usd-convert-cad Python wheel 提供，而仓库里存放的是给 AI agent 使用的 skill——包括安装、验证与运行该 wheel 的指令、文档以及工作流契约。仓库同时包含 .claude、.codex、.cursor 与 .agent 等目录，即同一份 skill 按各家 agent 的约定各放一份，并自称「Skillhub 风格」的仓库。文档说明其内容在 Python 3.12 与 usd-convert-cad==0.4.0 上测试过，并提醒新版本可能改变选项、应以 --help 与已安装版本为准。对维护引擎与 DCC 工具链的团队，这是一种低成本接入 AI 工作流的形态：工具本体不动，只补一份 skill。

Repository files navigation README Contributing License Security usd-convert-cad

The Omniverse CAD Converter, distributed using the usd-convert-cad package and command-line identifier, converts supported CAD files to OpenUSD.

This repository contains the NVIDIA Agent Skill and documentation for the Omniverse CAD Converter. The converter is distributed separately through the usd-convert-cad Python wheel.

The documentation and agent skill in this repository were tested with usd-convert-cad==0.4.0 on Python 3.12. Newer wheel versions may add or change options; check usd-convert-cad --help and the installed package version before relying on behavior not documented here.

This is a Skillhub-style repository for agent-assisted CAD conversion workflows. It contains the instructions, documentation, and workflow contract that AI agents use to install, verify, and run the usd-convert-cad wheel from a Python environment.

The repository does not require agents to install Omniverse Kit, pull an extension from an extension registry, or run a Kit app. Conversion is performed through the pip-installable usd-convert-cad package, which provides the usd-convert-cad command-line entry point and bundles the OpenUSD (pxr) and CAD conversion runtime needed by the tool.

Key repository areas:

skills/omniverse-cad-to-usd - canonical NVIDIA Agent Skill for CAD-to-USD conversion. docs - CAD-to-OpenUSD concept mapping and related documentation. LIMITATIONS.md - known package and converter limitations. CONTRIBUTING.md - contribution policy and supported-format update policy. Getting Started

Create an isolated Python 3.12 environment, install the package, and verify the command is available.

Windows:

python -m venv .venv .\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1 python -m pip install --upgrade pip python -m pip install usd-convert-cad usd-convert-cad --help

Linux:

python -m venv .venv source .venv/bin/activate python -m pip install --upgrade pip python -m pip install usd-convert-cad usd-convert-cad --help

If the package is hosted on an NVIDIA package index rather than public PyPI, add the appropriate index URL:

python -m pip install usd-convert-cad --extra-index-url https://pypi.nvidia.com

The canonical skill lives at skills/omniverse-cad-to-usd/SKILL.md. The installed wheel also includes the skill so agents can discover the same workflow guidance from the package.

Requirements Runtime: Python 3.12. Package: usd-convert-cad installed from a Python package index. Network: package-index access during install only. OS/Arch: Windows x86_64, Linux x86_64, or Linux aarch64. Licensing: proprietary CAD formats can require CAD converter licensing.

Use a dedicated virtual environment. The wheel bundles its own OpenUSD (pxr) runtime, so isolation avoids conflicts with other OpenUSD distributions in the same interpreter.

The wheel is self-contained at runtime and does not depend on Omniverse Kit, usd-core, or a separately installed pxr package.

Usage

After installing the wheel, convert an input CAD asset from the command line. usd-convert-cad is the installed console script; python -m usd_convert_cad runs the same CLI through the Python module.

usd-convert-cad -i path/to/input.step -o path/to/output.usdc

See skills/omniverse-cad-to-usd/SKILL.md for the full option table.

License And Contributions

This project is governed by the NVIDIA agreements in LICENSE.md. The agent skill under skills/omniverse-cad-to-usd carries its Apache-2.0 and CC-BY-4.0 license text in skills/omniverse-cad-to-usd/LICENSE.md. See THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md for third-party notices.

This project is not currently accepting external contributions or pull requests. See CONTRIBUTING.md for the contribution policy and issue-reporting guidance.

Repository Layout usd-convert-cad/ ├── skills/ │ └── omniverse-cad-to-usd/ │ └── SKILL.md # canonical skill source ├── .agent -> skills # symlink ├── .cursor -> skills # symlink ├── .claude -> skills # symlink ├── .codex -> skills # symlink ├── docs/ │ └── concept_mapping.md ├── CHANGELOG.md ├── CONTRIBUTING.md ├── LICENSE.md ├── README.md ├── SECURITY.md └── THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md

The output path determines the USD file format. Supported output extensions are .usd, .usda, .usdc, and .usdz. USDZ export converts to a temporary {stem}.usdc layer in an isolated staging directory, then packages it with OpenUSD. USDZ requires monolithic conversion (--composition-style none, the default). Packaging writes to a temporary archive and replaces the final .usdz only on success. If --material-type preview-surface-omnipbr is set, USDZ export switches to preview-surface because OmniPBR materials are not packageable.

The command returns exit code 0 on success and prints Successfully converted: . On failure, it returns a non-zero exit code and prints the converter error message to stderr. Agent workflows should branch on the exit code and confirm the expected output file exists before continuing.

Common conversion options include --tess-lod, --revit-lod, --accurate-tessellation, --convert-curves, --convert-metadata, --no-dedup, --no-normals, --no-materials, --material-type, --up-axis, --instancing-style, --composition-style, --filter-style, --load-hidden, --progress, --convert-physics-data, --read-constraints, and --view-layer-name.

Use --material-type preview-surface-materialx to author OpenPBR MaterialX with a USD Preview Surface fallback.

Source UVs and supported material textures are preserved by default. Images are written to Textures/ beside the USD; keep that directory with the output. Use --no-texture-coordinates to omit source UVs and texture images. --up-axis changes stage metadata only; it does not rotate geometry or transforms.

Use --prototype-all-parts to prototype unique parts as well as repeated parts; it has no effect with --instancing-style none.

With --read-constraints, named constraint sets become Scope prims and supported Contact constraints produce rigid bodies and convex-hull mesh collisions. Joint paths can change, and Contact export can disable instancing. Convex hulls can fill openings and concavities; inspect collisions before simulation.

See Limitations for texture and constraint restrictions.

Common examples:

Choose output format by extension: .usd, .usda, .usdc, or .usdz.

usd-convert-cad -i assembly.step -o assembly.usdc usd-convert-cad -i assembly.step -o assembly.usdz

Export geometry without materials.

usd-convert-cad -i assembly.step -o assembly.usda --no-materials

Convert metadata and keep hidden CAD elements as hidden USD prims.

usd-convert-cad -i plant.ifc -o plant.usdc --convert-metadata --filter-style hide

Convert model-space geometry from supported DWG/DXF files—including 2D linework and 3D curves—to USD BasisCurves.

usd-convert-cad -i drawing.dwg -o drawing.usdc --convert-curves

Increase tessellation level of detail.

usd-convert-cad -i part.jt -o part.usdc --tess-lod 4

Export CATIA V5/NX/SolidWorks Fix, CATIA V5 Fix Together, NX Bond,

or SolidWorks Lock mate constraints as USD Physics fixed joints.

usd-convert-cad -i assembly.sldasm -o assembly.usdc --read-constraints

Convert a CAD view layer or simplified representation by name.

usd-convert-cad -i assembly.asm -o assembly.usdc --view-layer-name "Manufacturing"

Run usd-convert-cad --help for the authoritative option list for the installed wheel version.

Supported Input Formats

The package supports the CAD, AEC, and interchange formats documented by the installed wheel, including:

JT: .jt DGN: .dgn CATIA V5 / V6: .catpart, .catproduct, .cgr, .3dxml IFC: .ifc, .ifczip NX / Creo / Solid Edge: .prt, .asm, .par, .pwd, .psm Parasolid: .xmt, .x_t, .x_b, .xmt_txt SolidWorks: .sldprt, .sldasm Autodesk Inventor: .ipt, .iam AutoCAD 3D: .dwg, .dxf Revit: .rvt, .rfa STEP / IGES: .stp, .step, .igs, .iges Rhino: .3dm Common 3D interchange formats: .stl, .dae, .fbx, .obj, .3ds, .3mf, .gltf, .glb ACIS: .sat, .sab

AutoCAD (.dwg, .dxf) and Revit (.rvt, .rfa) inputs are not supported on Linux aarch64.

Known limitations are documented in LIMITATIONS.md.

item.content:encoded:
一句话：转换器本身走 Python wheel 单独发布，仓库里装的是「agent 怎么安装、验证、运行它」。

要点：

  • 职责切分很清楚：**转换能力**由单独的 `usd-convert-cad` Python wheel 提供，仓库里放的是**给 AI agent 用的 skill**——包括安装、验证与运行该 wheel 的指令、文档与工作流契约
  • 面向多个 agent 同时适配：仓库里同时有 `.claude/`、`.codex/`、`.cursor/` 与 `.agent/` 目录，即同一份 skill 按各家 agent 的约定各放一份
  • 仓库自称是「Skillhub 风格」的仓库，说明这类「把工具封装成 agent skill」正在成为 NVIDIA 在 Omniverse 侧的分发方式；文档注明在 Python 3.12 + `usd-convert-cad==0.4.0` 上测过

为什么值得看：这条的价值不在 CAD 转换，而在**分发形态**：工具本体走包管理器，agent 侧只放「说明书 + 契约」。对内部维护 DCC/引擎工具链的团队，这是把老工具接进 AI 工作流最低成本的方式——不用改工具，只加一份 skill。

中文摘要：NVIDIA 的 usd-convert-cad 仓库体现了「工具 + agent skill」的分工方式：真正的转换能力由单独发布的 usd-convert-cad Python wheel 提供，而仓库里存放的是给 AI agent 使用的 skill——包括安装、验证与运行该 wheel 的指令、文档以及工作流契约。仓库同时包含 .claude、.codex、.cursor 与 .agent 等目录，即同一份 skill 按各家 agent 的约定各放一份，并自称「Skillhub 风格」的仓库。文档说明其内容在 Python 3.12 与 usd-convert-cad==0.4.0 上测试过，并提醒新版本可能改变选项、应以 --help 与已安装版本为准。对维护引擎与 DCC 工具链的团队，这是一种低成本接入 AI 工作流的形态：工具本体不动，只补一份 skill。

item.title: 单图生成 PBR 贴图，金属度与粗糙度总是猜错：UltraTex 走级联多视图，先把「外观」剥到「物理属性」 ｜ UltraTex: Aligning Physical Knowledge for High-Fidelity PBR Texture Generation
item.description:
一句话：观察到的外观把材质身份、表面反射率与光照纠缠在一起，所以这本质上是个病态问题。

要点：

  • 病态性说清了：从单张参考图给 3D 网格生成 PBR 贴图高度**歧义**——观测到的外观把**材质身份、表面反射率与光照**纠缠在一起
  • 现有生成方法能产出很真实的反照率图，但在**金属度与粗糙度**上仍不准，而这两项恰恰决定重打光时的表现
  • UltraTex 是一个**级联多视图**框架，目标是「超越外观」，把物理属性对齐出来，而不是只拟合可见像素

为什么值得看：PBR 贴图是资产进引擎前的最后一道关：反照率好看但金属度/粗糙度错了，换光照立刻穿帮。用级联多视图去解耦物理属性，比单视图端到端更符合这个问题的病态本质。

中文摘要：从单张参考图为 3D 网格生成基于物理的渲染（PBR）贴图本质上高度病态：所观测到的外观把材质身份、表面反射率与光照纠缠在一起。现有生成方法能够产出逼真的反照率贴图，但在推断准确的金属度与粗糙度属性上仍然吃力——而这恰恰是重打光效果的决定因素。UltraTex 因此提出一个级联多视图框架，目标不只是拟合外观，而是对齐物理属性。它把任务从「复现看到的像素」推进到「恢复能让重打光正确的材质参数」，这也正是 PBR 资产能不能直接进引擎的分界线。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-19

本期推送：2026-11-20

UltraTex: Aligning Physical Knowledge for High-Fidelity PBR Texture Generation

© none

Abstract.

Generating physically based rendering (PBR) texture maps for a 3D mesh from a single reference image is highly ambiguous, as the observed appearance entangles material identity, surface reflectance, and illumination. While current generative methods produce realistic albedo maps, they still struggle to infer accurate metallic and roughness attributes for relighting. We present UltraTex, a cascaded multi-view framework that moves beyond appearance matching by integrating physical knowledge into multi-view diffusion-based PBR generation. UltraTex first jointly predicts albedo and world-space shading normals to generate more detailed albedo maps, and then predicts metallic-roughness (MR) maps conditioned on the generated albedo, reference image, and material semantic priors. To inject material semantics, a lightweight adapter transforms hidden-layer features of a vision-language model (VLM) into intrinsic material representation tokens, providing part-level knowledge anchors for MR estimation. To model material-light interaction, photometric representation alignment guides intermediate diffusion features toward ground-truth material renderings under controlled lighting. This makes metallic and roughness variations observable through highlight intensity, specular sharpness, and local reflectance contrast, providing stronger guidance for fine-grained material prediction without explicit lighting supervision. Extensive experiments show that UltraTex generates high-quality textures and outperforms existing open-source and commercial methods in visual fidelity, material accuracy, and physical plausibility.

Keywords:

Texture generation, Material appearance, Generative models, Physically based rendering

1. Introduction

Physically based rendering (PBR) is the industry standard for material representation of 3D assets in games, films, and AR/VR [(Burley, 2012; Pharr et al., 2016)]. PBR texture maps separate visible appearance from intrinsic material attributes, enabling assets to respond plausibly under different lighting conditions. While albedo defines the base color of a surface, realistic relighting depends critically on properties such as metallic and roughness. These attributes describe physical reflectance behavior rather than directly observable image signals, making high-quality PBR texture authoring a labor-intensive process that still relies heavily on expert-driven workflows [(Adobe Systems Inc., 2024)].

Generating PBR texture maps for a 3D mesh from a single reference image is therefore highly ambiguous. The observed appearance entangles material identity, surface reflectance, geometry, and illumination. For example, a bright region in the input may arise from polished metal, glossy dielectric coating, baked illumination, or a local color pattern. This ambiguity is especially severe for metallic–roughness (MR) estimation, where the desired outputs are abstract intrinsic maps rather than natural RGB images.

Early inverse-rendering methods reduce this ambiguity by using controlled capture setups, such as co-located flash lighting, to expose physical cues like specular highlights [(Guo et al., 2021; Ma et al., 2021; Bao et al., 2025)]. Although effective in constrained environments, these methods do not generalize well to arbitrary in-the-wild images. Recent generative approaches instead leverage powerful image-domain priors from diffusion models [(Rombach et al., 2022; Esser et al., 2024; BlackForestLabs, 2024)] and multi-view generation techniques [(Shi et al., 2023; Huang et al., 2024a; Team, 2025a; Seed3D, 2026)] to synthesize multi-view texture or PBR images, which are then reprojected onto the mesh surface to construct texture maps. While this paradigm has substantially improved albedo generation, it remains unreliable for intrinsic MR prediction. Existing methods often assign metallic values to incorrect regions or produce overly conservative roughness maps with limited fine-scale variation. These failures indicate that strong appearance priors alone are insufficient: the model must also understand what each object part is made of and how its material should respond to light.

Professional PBR creation follows this reasoning naturally: artists infer material maps by considering asset style, part-wise material composition, surface structure, and illumination behavior, rather than matching pixels alone. We argue that high-fidelity PBR generation requires aligning such physical knowledge with the generative process. This alignment can be achieved in two complementary ways. First, physical knowledge can be injected as conditioning priors for material semantics. Vision-language models are well suited for this role, as their hidden representations encode rich world knowledge and semantic reasoning from large-scale image-text pretraining; however, an adapter is needed to translate them into diffusion-compatible material tokens. Second, physical knowledge can guide learning through training objectives. Since metallic and roughness maps are abstract intrinsic parameters whose effects become visible only after interacting with albedo, geometry, and illumination, MR generation should be supervised in a photometric representation space where controlled-light renderings reveal material-light responses.

To this end, we introduce UltraTex, a cascaded multi-view framework for high-quality PBR texture generation from a single reference image and an input mesh. UltraTex first jointly predicts albedo and world-space shading normals to obtain detailed albedo maps, and then predicts MR maps conditioned on the generated albedo, reference-image features, and material semantic priors. For material-semantic conditioning, we introduce a VLM-guided intrinsic material adapter that transforms hidden-layer vision-language features into intrinsic material tokens, providing part-level knowledge anchors for MR estimation. For photometric guidance, we propose photometric representation alignment, which guides intermediate MR diffusion features toward visual representations of ground-truth materials rendered under controlled lighting. This rendered RGB space reveals fine-grained MR variations through highlight intensity, specular sharpness, and local reflectance contrast, providing stronger guidance without explicit lighting supervision.

Extensive experiments demonstrate that UltraTex generates high-quality PBR textures and substantially outperforms state-of-the-art open-source and commercial methods in visual fidelity, material accuracy, and physical plausibility.

In summary, we make the following contributions:

  • •

    To the best of our knowledge, we present the first diffusion-based PBR texture generation framework that explicitly aligns physical knowledge through material-semantic conditioning and photometric representation guidance.

  • •

    We introduce a VLM-guided intrinsic material adapter that translates hidden-layer vision-language features into material-aware tokens, injecting part-wise semantic priors into MR generation.

  • •

    We propose photometric representation alignment, which guides intermediate MR diffusion features with controlled-light material renderings to capture fine-grained material-light interactions.

  • •

    Extensive experiments demonstrate that UltraTex substantially outperforms existing open-source and commercial methods in visual fidelity, material accuracy, and physical plausibility.

    • 2. Related Work

    2.1. Texture Generation

    Foundation models have opened new directions for automating texture generation in 3D content creation. Early methods adopt optimization-based paradigms, using Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) [(Poole et al., 2023)] to distill priors from pretrained 2D diffusion models into 3D assets [(Poole et al., 2022; Lin et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023; Po and Wetzstein, 2024; Metzer et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2023b; Khalid et al., 2022; Michel et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2022)]. However, iterative optimization over renderings is costly and often produces over-saturated textures or artifacts that limit practical use.

    Feed-forward approaches explored progressive inpainting across pre-defined views conditioned on explicit 3D attributes [(Yu et al., 2023; Bensadoun et al., 2024; Cao et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2024b)]. However, the geometric fidelity is frequently compromised by the cross-view latent synchronization. Alternatively, to bypass such occlusion and alignment issues, other methods directly target the UV space [(Yu et al., 2023; Zeng et al., 2024; Bensadoun et al., 2024; Yu et al., 2024)]. Yet, the topological fragmentation inherent to UV parameterizations severely degrades the generative capacity of 2D diffusion models, hindering high-fidelity synthesis.

    Recent methods  [(Huang et al., 2024a; Zhao et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025; Yeo et al., 2026; He et al., 2026)] incorporate multi-view attention mechanisms [(Li et al., 2024; Kant et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2024c; Shi et al., 2023; Wang and Shi, 2023; Feng et al., 2025)] to generate globally consistent textures while respecting 3D geometry. However, they mainly target appearance texturing, producing either albedo maps or illumination-baked textures without intrinsic material attributes required for physically based relighting.

    Another line of work performs texture generation directly in native 3D space [(Lai et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026; Zeng et al., 2025; Xiang et al., 2025)]. These methods directly generate complete surface textures in 3D space, providing inherent geometric consistency while avoiding view-projection artifacts such as edge bleeding. However, the scarcity of high-quality 3D data with high-resolution textures limits fine-detail modeling.

    2.2. PBR Texture Generation

    Building upon texture synthesis, recent methods extend pretrained diffusion models to PBR material generation. Early works incorporate BRDF formulations into SDS optimization to infer material properties [(Chen et al., 2023a; Zhang et al., 2024a; Liu et al., 2024a; Youwang et al., 2024a; Wu et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2023; Yeh et al., 2024)], but often struggle to decompose lighting and surface reflectance, leading to unrealistic or flat results.

    To enhance spatial alignment and material accuracy, subsequent approaches either employ iterative latent synchronization [(Huang et al., 2024b; Zhang et al., 2024c)] or leverage LLMs for retrieval-augmented generation [(Zhang et al., 2024b; Dang et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024; Fang et al., 2024; Wei et al., 2025)]. Despite this, these methods primarily transfer generative priors to the PBR task without end-to-end training on large-scale PBR datasets, which fundamentally constrains their generalization ability.

    A recent line of work fine-tunes image or video models to predict multi-channel PBR maps [(He et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2024; Vainer et al., 2024; Vecchio et al., 2024; Hasselgren et al., 2026; Ma et al., 2025; Munkberg et al., 2025; Yuan et al., 2025)]. These methods mainly transfer appearance-generation priors to intrinsic material prediction through pixel-level reconstruction losses. While scalable, this transfer does not directly resolve the ambiguity of MR estimation, where metallic and roughness are latent material properties rather than observable appearance. As a result, these models remain biased toward appearance matching, leading to frequent ambiguity in intrinsic material decomposition. In contrast, our method introduces explicit material reasoning from VLM world knowledge and representation-level photometric regularization to provide semantic and physical supervision for MR generation.

    3. Method

    Given a single reference image and an input mesh, UltraTex generates cross-view consistent PBR texture maps through a cascaded two-stage multi-view diffusion pipeline (Fig. 2). Stage 1 jointly predicts orthographic-view albedo maps and world-space shading normals from the reference image and multi-view geometry normals (Sec. 3.1). Conditioned on the generated albedo, Stage 2 predicts metallic-roughness (MR) maps with a VLM-guided intrinsic material adapter (Sec. 3.2.1) and photometric representation alignment (Sec. 3.2.2). Both stages are built upon an image diffusion backbone and are trained separately; following [(Team, 2025a)], MR maps are represented as two channels of a single RGB image.

    3.1. Multi-view Albedo and Shading Normal Generation

    The first stage generates multi-view albedo maps and world-space shading normals from the reference image and rendered geometry normals. We adopt a two-step architecture: a Multi-Modal Transformer (MM-T) fuses conditioning tokens and noisy view latents per view, then a Multi-View Transformer (MV-T) models cross-view interactions for global consistency.

    3.1.1. Multi-Modal DiT

    For each view, MM-T integrates the reference-image and geometry-normal conditions into a unified latent representation. Specifically, for the i-th view, we extract geometry-normal tokens T_geoⁱ by encoding the rendered geometry normal Gᵢ with a fixed VAE encoder 𝔼_VAE, and derive reference-image tokens T_img from both VAE latents and DINOv2 embeddings. These conditional tokens, together with the noisy view latent zᵢ, are processed by l₁ transformer blocks with intra-view self-attention:

    (1)T_geoⁱ=Linear_geo[𝔼_VAE(Gᵢ)],
    (2)T_img=Linear_img[𝔼_VAE(I);DINOv2(I)],
    (3)zᵢ^l₁=MM-T^l₁(zᵢ,T_img,T_geoⁱ).

    3.1.2. Multi-View DiT

    After per-view multi-modal fusion, we perform global reasoning across views. To focus this stage strictly on cross-view interaction, we discard all conditional tokens (T_img, T_geo) and retain only the view-wise latents zᵢ from all N views. Formally, the intermediate features from all views are aggregated into a unified sequence and processed through a series of l₂ Transformer blocks. In this joint representation {ẑᵢ}∈ℝ^NL×C, self-attention is performed globally to capture cross-view correlations and ensure 3D coherence.

    (4)

    {ẑᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^N=MV-T^l₂(z₁^l₁,z₂^l₁,…,z_N^l₁)∈ℝ^NL×C.

    The stage is trained with a flow matching objective, where z₀ denotes the noise-free latent of the ground-truth albedo map and c={T_img,T_geo} denotes the conditioning tokens:

    (5)

    L_alb(θ)=𝔼_t,z₀,ε[∥v_θ(zₜ;t,c)-(ε-z₀)∥²].

    3.1.3. Joint Estimation of Shading Normal

    We introduce a computationally efficient scheme to jointly predict world-space shading normals (S) alongside albedo maps. This auxiliary prediction provides geometry-aware supervision for albedo generation, encouraging richer surface structure and high-frequency details.

    Why world-space shading normals? Unlike tangent-space normal or bump maps, which depend on local UV coordinates, world-space shading normals are expressed in a global coordinate frame and remain independent of UV parameterization. This avoids the inconsistent tangent frames introduced by rotated or flipped UV islands, making normal prediction less prone to seams (Fig. 4(a)).

    We denote the VAE latent of S as Tₛₙ. Our key insight is that the geometry normal tokens T_geo, which serve as input conditioning during albedo training, naturally reside in the same modality as world-space shading normals. Leveraging this geometric alignment, we reuse the existing pathway to predict a joint velocity field. Specifically, the model is optimized by a multi-task objective consisting of an albedo flow matching loss L_alb and a shading-normal refinement loss Lₙₒᵣₘₐₗ. While the albedo component follows the standard flow from Gaussian noise ε to the ground-truth albedo latent T_alb, the shading-normal component treats T_geo as the starting point to learn the residual micro-geometry:

    (6)L_alb(θ)=𝔼_t,T_alb,ε[∥v_θ,alb(zₜ;t,c)-(ε-T_alb)∥²],
    (7)Lₙₒᵣₘₐₗ(θ)=𝔼_t,Tₛₙ,T_geo[∥v_θ,sn(zₜ;t,c)-(T_geo-Tₛₙ)∥²],
    (8)Lⱼₒᵢₙₜ=L_alb+λₙₒᵣₘₐₗLₙₒᵣₘₐₗ,

    where λₙₒᵣₘₐₗ is a balancing weight, and v_θ,alb,v_θ,sn represent the respective velocity components predicted by the model.

    3.2. Multi-view MR Generation

    Our multi-view MR generator follows the same MM-T/MV-T architecture as the albedo model in Sec. 3.1, but replaces the geometry-normal condition with the Stage-1 albedo maps. It further introduces two physical knowledge alignment modules for intrinsic material estimation: a VLM-guided intrinsic material adapter and photometric representation alignment.

    3.2.1. VLM-Guided Intrinsic Material Adapter

    Before training the multi-view MR generator, we train a VLM-guided intrinsic material adapter in a separate stage, as illustrated in Fig. 3. The goal is to translate material-aware visual knowledge from a frozen vision-language model (VLM) into diffusion-compatible intrinsic material tokens. During this adapter training stage, both the VLM and the image diffusion model are kept frozen, and only the adapter is optimized.

    Previous studies [(Neo et al., 2024; Kaduri et al., 2025)] indicate that VLM hidden representations evolve progressively across layers: early layers capture raw visual features, whereas intermediate layers encode more abstract semantic and reasoning cues. Since MR generation requires reasoning about intrinsic material properties rather than direct appearance transfer, we exploit intermediate VLM tokens extracted from the encoded reference image I as a source of material-aware context. Specifically, let Vₘ(I)∈ℝ^P×dᵥₗₘ denote the visual-token subsequence of the VLM hidden state at layer m, where P is the number of image patch tokens. We select a set of intermediate layers M and concatenate their visual tokens along the channel dimension:

    (9)

    Hᵛˡᵐ_M=concat_m∈M[Vₘ(I)]∈ℝ^P×|M|dᵥₗₘ.

    The VLM token space is not directly compatible with the conditioning space of the image diffusion model. We therefore introduce an Intrinsic Material Token AdapterA, which projects Hᵛˡᵐ_M into 1D intrinsic material tokens:

    (10)

    Tₘₐₜ=A(Hᵛˡᵐ_M).

    These tokens are injected into the frozen image diffusion model through token-wise concatenation in the denoising blocks, where they interact with noisy latents to reconstruct ground-truth metallic and roughness maps. We optimize the adapter with the standard flow-matching objective on rendered reference images paired with their ground-truth MR maps. After training, the learned tokens encode part-aware material semantic priors and are used as conditional inputs for Stage-2 MR generation.

    3.2.2. Photometric Representation Alignment

    Inspired by representation alignment methods such as REPA [(Yu et al., 2025)], we introduce photometric representation alignment to provide stronger guidance for MR generation. Directly aligning raw MR maps with pretrained visual encoders is ill-posed, since encoders such as DINOv2 [(Oquab et al., 2023)] and MAE [(He et al., 2022)] are trained on natural images, while metallic and roughness maps are abstract intrinsic parameters.

    To bridge this domain gap, we construct alignment targets in a photometrically meaningful RGB space. For each training view, we render the ground-truth materials x into an auxiliary photometric response xₚₘ under a controlled point-light setup, where the light source is collocated with the camera. The rendered response exposes material-light interactions, such as highlight intensity, specular sharpness, and local reflectance contrast, while remaining compatible with pretrained visual encoders. We use a frozen DINOv2 encoder f to extract the target representation y=f(xₚₘ).

    During MR generation, the intermediate transformer features hₜ at timestep t are projected by a MLP layer h_φ and aligned with y:

    (11)
