    L_REPA(θ,φ)=-𝔼_(x,xₚₘ),t[1/Nₚ∑ₙ₌₁^Nₚsim(yₙ,h_φ(hₜ^[n]))],

    where Nₚ denotes the number of patches and sim(·,·) is the patch-wise cosine similarity. This representation-level alignment guides MR diffusion features toward the visual response of physically valid materials, providing stronger cues for fine-grained metallic and roughness prediction without explicit lighting supervision.

    3.2.3. Network

    The MR network follows the same MM-T and MV-T design as the albedo stage. For the i-th view, we replace the geometry-normal condition with the generated albedo map Aᵢ from Stage 1:

    (12)

    T_albⁱ=Linear_alb[𝔼_VAE(Aᵢ)].

    Together with the reference-image tokens T_img and the VLM-derived material tokens Tₘₐₜ, the noisy MR latent is fused by MM-T:

    (13)

    zᵢ^l₁=MM-T^l₁(zᵢ,T_img,T_albⁱ,Tₘₐₜ).

    The fused view latents are then processed by the same MV-T formulation in Sec. 3.1.2.

    We optimize the MR generation model with a flow-matching loss L_flow^MR and the photometric representation alignment loss:

    (14)

    Lₜₒₜₐₗ^MR=L_flow^MR+λ_RL_REPA,

    where λ_R balances the representation alignment term.

    4. Experiments

    We compare UltraTex against open-source and commercial state-of-the-art PBR generation methods through qualitative comparisons, quantitative metrics, and a user study in Sec. 4.2, comprehensively examining both intrinsic PBR accuracy and human visual preference. We also ablate main factors of our architecture in Sec. 4.3.

    4.1. Implementation Details

    4.1.1. Dataset.

    We curate a dataset of 130K objects from Objaverse-XL [(Deitke et al., 2023b; Deitke et al., 2023a)] and TexVerse [(Zhang et al., 2025)]. For diversity, each object is rendered into 32 reference images under random cameras and environment maps. For supervision, we extract ground-truth PBR maps (albedo, metallic, roughness), normals (geometry, shading), and render photometric images across six 1024² orthogonal views. We provide more details in the supplementary.

    4.1.2. Training.

    We use the intrinsic material token adapter to integrate the Qwen3.5-4B VLM [(Qwen Team, 2026)] with our diffusion framework. The adapter is a two-layer MLP with channel dimensions {12288,4096,3072} and an intermediate SiLU activation. Hierarchical visual features are extracted from intermediate VLM layers M={8,16,24}. Both the albedo and MR models initialize their DiT backbones from a pretrained text-to-image diffusion model. The multi-view models are trained at a per-view resolution of 768². Each model is trained on 32 NVIDIA A100 GPUs for about 2 days.

    4.1.3. Inference.

    At inference time, we first generate six-view albedo maps, which then condition the MR network to estimate corresponding metallic and roughness maps. All maps per view are upscaled to 1536² by a super-resolution module and mapped onto 4K UV textures. To ensure complete surface coverage, unobserved regions not captured by the orthogonal projections are inpainted using the novel view synthesis model from LumiTex [(Bao et al., 2026)] (see original paper for details).

    4.2. Comparison with Existing Methods

    4.2.1. Baselines.

    We compare UltraTex with representative open-source PBR texture synthesis methods, including Paint-it [(Youwang et al., 2024b)], DreamMat [(Zhang et al., 2024a)], Hunyuan3D v2.1 [(Team, 2025a; Huang et al., 2025)], LumiTex [(Bao et al., 2026)], and TRELLIS.2 [(Xiang et al., 2025)]. We also compare against commercial methods, including Hunyuan3D v3.1, Hyper3D [(Hyper3D, 2026)], Meshy 6 [(Meshy, 2026)], and TripoAI v3.1 [(TripoAI, 2026)] and Seed3D 2.0 [(Seed3D, 2026)].

    4.2.2. Evaluation Metrics

    To evaluate texture fidelity, we follow the protocol of Hunyuan3D [(Team, 2025a; Team, 2025b; Zhao et al., 2025)] by employing FID [(Heusel et al., 2017)], CLIP-FID, and LPIPS [(Zhang et al., 2018)]. For a more fine-grained assessment, we use CLIP Maximum-Mean Discrepancy (CMMD) [(Jayasumana et al., 2024)] to measure detail diversity and CLIP-I [(Radford et al., 2021)] for prompt alignment. Notably, all aforementioned perceptual and semantic metrics are computed exclusively on the albedo maps. For MR estimation, accuracy is validated via the MSE (×10⁻³). We also conduct a user study to benchmark texture quality based on human preferences.

    4.2.3. Quantitative Results

    We quantitatively compare UltraTex with baselines on 152 held-out Objaverse-XL objects, using Blender-rendered GT assets as reference inputs and rendering outputs at 1024² resolution. Except for MSE on MR attributes, all perceptual and semantic metrics are computed on rendered albedo/MR images, covering visual fidelity, semantic alignment, and PBR accuracy.

    As shown in Tab. 1, our method consistently outperforms existing baselines across all metrics. It achieves better FID and LPIPS for perceptual quality, lower CMMD for texture diversity, higher CLIP-I/CLIP-FID for semantic alignment, and the lowest MSE across PBR attributes, validating its superior physical accuracy. Additionally, Table 3 further shows that our method outperforms both the state-of-the-art multi-view baseline (LumiTex) and the 3D-native baseline (TRELLIS.2) under environment relighting.

    To evaluate perceptual quality, we conduct a blind user study where 31 professional 3D modelers rate results from 1 to 5 based on overall rendering, albedo, roughness, and metallic fidelity. UltraTex achieves the highest scores across all dimensions (Tab. 2) and substantially outperforms competitors in pairwise win rates (Fig. 5), demonstrating strong expert preference.

    4.2.4. Qualitative Results

    We qualitatively compare UltraTex with recent open-source and commercial baselines for PBR texture generation. For test data, we generate reference images via Seedream 4.5 [(Seedream et al., 2025)], followed by mesh generation with Hunyuan3D v3.1, then apply each method for texture generation.

    As shown in Fig. 7 and 7, existing methods like Hunyuan3D and Hyper3D often suffer from illumination leakage, producing albedo maps with baked-in lighting artifacts. Furthermore, most baselines have difficulty resolving intrinsic material ambiguity, frequently misclassifying metallic regions or producing over-smoothed roughness maps. In contrast, by leveraging material knowledge and illumination cues, UltraTex consistently produces more accurate metallic estimates and fine-grained roughness details, while also delivering albedo maps with superior physical fidelity and structural richness.

    This advantage is especially evident in challenging cases (Fig. 8), including micro-scale roughness variations, oxidized or coated metals, and part-wise material changes, where baselines often fail. Furthermore, the diverse gallery in Fig. 18 demonstrates our model’s ability to produce physically plausible textures across a wide array of geometric complexities and material compositions.

    We further evaluate the generated PBR textures through relighting under diverse novel illumination conditions. As shown in Fig. 9, the recovered material properties respond naturally to changes in lighting, producing consistent highlights, reflections, and surface appearance across different environments.

    To further evaluate the accuracy of intrinsic material decomposition, we compare against baselines on objects with ground-truth PBR maps. Given the same clay mesh and reference image, UltraTex more faithfully recovers the target material properties than the multi-view baseline LumiTex and the 3D-native baseline TRELLIS.2, particularly in base color, metallic separation, and spatially varying roughness (Fig. 11).

    4.2.5. Results on Real-World Inputs

    We further evaluate UltraTex on casually captured real-world inputs and scanned meshes, including three examples collected from Sketchfab and two from the DTC dataset [(Dong et al., 2025)]. These inputs exhibit uncontrolled illumination, appearance ambiguity, and imperfect scanned geometry. As shown in Fig. 10, UltraTex remains robust under these conditions, producing coherent PBR materials and physically plausible relighting. The results demonstrate that our method generalizes beyond clean rendered inputs to practical real-world asset creation.

    4.3. Ablation Study

    VLM-derived Intrinsic Material Token

    To validate the impact of VLM priors, we train a variant of MR estimation network without intrinsic material token guidance. As shown in Fig. 12 and Tab. 4, removing the VLM-derived tokens leads to clear material misclassification and increases both metallic and roughness errors. The ablated model relies heavily on low-level visual cues, such as color and specular highlights, and therefore mistakes strong reflections for metallic materials. This confirms that VLM guidance provides essential semantic and part-level material priors, enabling more physically grounded MR estimation that is robust to misleading appearance-based heuristics. In addition, removing the visual conditions also degrades MR quality, demonstrating their complementary role in providing dense spatial guidance for material generation.

    Decoding Probe of VLM Encoder

    To quantify the intrinsic material information encoded by the 1D material tokens, we conduct a decoding probe by replacing the VLM encoder with VAE and DINOv2 encoders under the same setting and directly decoding MR maps from the resulting tokens. As shown in Tab. 5, VLM features consistently outperform VAE and DINOv2 features, demonstrating that the resulting tokens carry richer material semantics and better disentangle intrinsic MR properties from observed appearance. This is because intrinsic material properties require semantic reasoning beyond observable appearance, which is better captured by the world knowledge encoded in VLM representations.

    VLM-token Attention Map Visualization

    To better understand the part-level spatial localization of the 1D material tokens, we visualize the attention from VLM tokens to noisy image tokens at the 4th layer of the Multi-Modal DiT. As shown in Fig. 13, the responses are strongly localized to material-relevant object parts, such as metallic ornaments, buckles, and other hardware regions. Notably, the VLM tokens themselves carry no explicit spatial coordinates; their spatial correspondence emerges through interaction with the image tokens inside the DiT. This indicates that the material tokens are not merely used as global semantic conditions, but establish part-level correspondence with regions exhibiting the associated material properties.
item.content:encoded:
一句话：观察到的外观把材质身份、表面反射率与光照纠缠在一起，所以这本质上是个病态问题。

要点：

  • 病态性说清了：从单张参考图给 3D 网格生成 PBR 贴图高度**歧义**——观测到的外观把**材质身份、表面反射率与光照**纠缠在一起
  • 现有生成方法能产出很真实的反照率图，但在**金属度与粗糙度**上仍不准，而这两项恰恰决定重打光时的表现
  • UltraTex 是一个**级联多视图**框架，目标是「超越外观」，把物理属性对齐出来，而不是只拟合可见像素

为什么值得看：PBR 贴图是资产进引擎前的最后一道关：反照率好看但金属度/粗糙度错了，换光照立刻穿帮。用级联多视图去解耦物理属性，比单视图端到端更符合这个问题的病态本质。

中文摘要：从单张参考图为 3D 网格生成基于物理的渲染（PBR）贴图本质上高度病态：所观测到的外观把材质身份、表面反射率与光照纠缠在一起。现有生成方法能够产出逼真的反照率贴图，但在推断准确的金属度与粗糙度属性上仍然吃力——而这恰恰是重打光效果的决定因素。UltraTex 因此提出一个级联多视图框架，目标不只是拟合外观，而是对齐物理属性。它把任务从「复现看到的像素」推进到「恢复能让重打光正确的材质参数」，这也正是 PBR 资产能不能直接进引擎的分界线。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-19

本期推送：2026-11-20

UltraTex: Aligning Physical Knowledge for High-Fidelity PBR Texture Generation

© none

Abstract.

Generating physically based rendering (PBR) texture maps for a 3D mesh from a single reference image is highly ambiguous, as the observed appearance entangles material identity, surface reflectance, and illumination. While current generative methods produce realistic albedo maps, they still struggle to infer accurate metallic and roughness attributes for relighting. We present UltraTex, a cascaded multi-view framework that moves beyond appearance matching by integrating physical knowledge into multi-view diffusion-based PBR generation. UltraTex first jointly predicts albedo and world-space shading normals to generate more detailed albedo maps, and then predicts metallic-roughness (MR) maps conditioned on the generated albedo, reference image, and material semantic priors. To inject material semantics, a lightweight adapter transforms hidden-layer features of a vision-language model (VLM) into intrinsic material representation tokens, providing part-level knowledge anchors for MR estimation. To model material-light interaction, photometric representation alignment guides intermediate diffusion features toward ground-truth material renderings under controlled lighting. This makes metallic and roughness variations observable through highlight intensity, specular sharpness, and local reflectance contrast, providing stronger guidance for fine-grained material prediction without explicit lighting supervision. Extensive experiments show that UltraTex generates high-quality textures and outperforms existing open-source and commercial methods in visual fidelity, material accuracy, and physical plausibility.

Keywords:

Texture generation, Material appearance, Generative models, Physically based rendering

1. Introduction

Physically based rendering (PBR) is the industry standard for material representation of 3D assets in games, films, and AR/VR [(Burley, 2012; Pharr et al., 2016)]. PBR texture maps separate visible appearance from intrinsic material attributes, enabling assets to respond plausibly under different lighting conditions. While albedo defines the base color of a surface, realistic relighting depends critically on properties such as metallic and roughness. These attributes describe physical reflectance behavior rather than directly observable image signals, making high-quality PBR texture authoring a labor-intensive process that still relies heavily on expert-driven workflows [(Adobe Systems Inc., 2024)].

Generating PBR texture maps for a 3D mesh from a single reference image is therefore highly ambiguous. The observed appearance entangles material identity, surface reflectance, geometry, and illumination. For example, a bright region in the input may arise from polished metal, glossy dielectric coating, baked illumination, or a local color pattern. This ambiguity is especially severe for metallic–roughness (MR) estimation, where the desired outputs are abstract intrinsic maps rather than natural RGB images.

Early inverse-rendering methods reduce this ambiguity by using controlled capture setups, such as co-located flash lighting, to expose physical cues like specular highlights [(Guo et al., 2021; Ma et al., 2021; Bao et al., 2025)]. Although effective in constrained environments, these methods do not generalize well to arbitrary in-the-wild images. Recent generative approaches instead leverage powerful image-domain priors from diffusion models [(Rombach et al., 2022; Esser et al., 2024; BlackForestLabs, 2024)] and multi-view generation techniques [(Shi et al., 2023; Huang et al., 2024a; Team, 2025a; Seed3D, 2026)] to synthesize multi-view texture or PBR images, which are then reprojected onto the mesh surface to construct texture maps. While this paradigm has substantially improved albedo generation, it remains unreliable for intrinsic MR prediction. Existing methods often assign metallic values to incorrect regions or produce overly conservative roughness maps with limited fine-scale variation. These failures indicate that strong appearance priors alone are insufficient: the model must also understand what each object part is made of and how its material should respond to light.

Professional PBR creation follows this reasoning naturally: artists infer material maps by considering asset style, part-wise material composition, surface structure, and illumination behavior, rather than matching pixels alone. We argue that high-fidelity PBR generation requires aligning such physical knowledge with the generative process. This alignment can be achieved in two complementary ways. First, physical knowledge can be injected as conditioning priors for material semantics. Vision-language models are well suited for this role, as their hidden representations encode rich world knowledge and semantic reasoning from large-scale image-text pretraining; however, an adapter is needed to translate them into diffusion-compatible material tokens. Second, physical knowledge can guide learning through training objectives. Since metallic and roughness maps are abstract intrinsic parameters whose effects become visible only after interacting with albedo, geometry, and illumination, MR generation should be supervised in a photometric representation space where controlled-light renderings reveal material-light responses.

To this end, we introduce UltraTex, a cascaded multi-view framework for high-quality PBR texture generation from a single reference image and an input mesh. UltraTex first jointly predicts albedo and world-space shading normals to obtain detailed albedo maps, and then predicts MR maps conditioned on the generated albedo, reference-image features, and material semantic priors. For material-semantic conditioning, we introduce a VLM-guided intrinsic material adapter that transforms hidden-layer vision-language features into intrinsic material tokens, providing part-level knowledge anchors for MR estimation. For photometric guidance, we propose photometric representation alignment, which guides intermediate MR diffusion features toward visual representations of ground-truth materials rendered under controlled lighting. This rendered RGB space reveals fine-grained MR variations through highlight intensity, specular sharpness, and local reflectance contrast, providing stronger guidance without explicit lighting supervision.

Extensive experiments demonstrate that UltraTex generates high-quality PBR textures and substantially outperforms state-of-the-art open-source and commercial methods in visual fidelity, material accuracy, and physical plausibility.

In summary, we make the following contributions:

  • •

    To the best of our knowledge, we present the first diffusion-based PBR texture generation framework that explicitly aligns physical knowledge through material-semantic conditioning and photometric representation guidance.

  • •

    We introduce a VLM-guided intrinsic material adapter that translates hidden-layer vision-language features into material-aware tokens, injecting part-wise semantic priors into MR generation.

  • •

    We propose photometric representation alignment, which guides intermediate MR diffusion features with controlled-light material renderings to capture fine-grained material-light interactions.

  • •

    Extensive experiments demonstrate that UltraTex substantially outperforms existing open-source and commercial methods in visual fidelity, material accuracy, and physical plausibility.

    • 2. Related Work

    2.1. Texture Generation

    Foundation models have opened new directions for automating texture generation in 3D content creation. Early methods adopt optimization-based paradigms, using Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) [(Poole et al., 2023)] to distill priors from pretrained 2D diffusion models into 3D assets [(Poole et al., 2022; Lin et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023; Po and Wetzstein, 2024; Metzer et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2023b; Khalid et al., 2022; Michel et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2022)]. However, iterative optimization over renderings is costly and often produces over-saturated textures or artifacts that limit practical use.

    Feed-forward approaches explored progressive inpainting across pre-defined views conditioned on explicit 3D attributes [(Yu et al., 2023; Bensadoun et al., 2024; Cao et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2024b)]. However, the geometric fidelity is frequently compromised by the cross-view latent synchronization. Alternatively, to bypass such occlusion and alignment issues, other methods directly target the UV space [(Yu et al., 2023; Zeng et al., 2024; Bensadoun et al., 2024; Yu et al., 2024)]. Yet, the topological fragmentation inherent to UV parameterizations severely degrades the generative capacity of 2D diffusion models, hindering high-fidelity synthesis.

    Recent methods  [(Huang et al., 2024a; Zhao et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025; Yeo et al., 2026; He et al., 2026)] incorporate multi-view attention mechanisms [(Li et al., 2024; Kant et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2024c; Shi et al., 2023; Wang and Shi, 2023; Feng et al., 2025)] to generate globally consistent textures while respecting 3D geometry. However, they mainly target appearance texturing, producing either albedo maps or illumination-baked textures without intrinsic material attributes required for physically based relighting.

    Another line of work performs texture generation directly in native 3D space [(Lai et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026; Zeng et al., 2025; Xiang et al., 2025)]. These methods directly generate complete surface textures in 3D space, providing inherent geometric consistency while avoiding view-projection artifacts such as edge bleeding. However, the scarcity of high-quality 3D data with high-resolution textures limits fine-detail modeling.

    2.2. PBR Texture Generation

    Building upon texture synthesis, recent methods extend pretrained diffusion models to PBR material generation. Early works incorporate BRDF formulations into SDS optimization to infer material properties [(Chen et al., 2023a; Zhang et al., 2024a; Liu et al., 2024a; Youwang et al., 2024a; Wu et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2023; Yeh et al., 2024)], but often struggle to decompose lighting and surface reflectance, leading to unrealistic or flat results.

    To enhance spatial alignment and material accuracy, subsequent approaches either employ iterative latent synchronization [(Huang et al., 2024b; Zhang et al., 2024c)] or leverage LLMs for retrieval-augmented generation [(Zhang et al., 2024b; Dang et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024; Fang et al., 2024; Wei et al., 2025)]. Despite this, these methods primarily transfer generative priors to the PBR task without end-to-end training on large-scale PBR datasets, which fundamentally constrains their generalization ability.

    A recent line of work fine-tunes image or video models to predict multi-channel PBR maps [(He et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2024; Vainer et al., 2024; Vecchio et al., 2024; Hasselgren et al., 2026; Ma et al., 2025; Munkberg et al., 2025; Yuan et al., 2025)]. These methods mainly transfer appearance-generation priors to intrinsic material prediction through pixel-level reconstruction losses. While scalable, this transfer does not directly resolve the ambiguity of MR estimation, where metallic and roughness are latent material properties rather than observable appearance. As a result, these models remain biased toward appearance matching, leading to frequent ambiguity in intrinsic material decomposition. In contrast, our method introduces explicit material reasoning from VLM world knowledge and representation-level photometric regularization to provide semantic and physical supervision for MR generation.

    3. Method

    Given a single reference image and an input mesh, UltraTex generates cross-view consistent PBR texture maps through a cascaded two-stage multi-view diffusion pipeline (Fig. 2). Stage 1 jointly predicts orthographic-view albedo maps and world-space shading normals from the reference image and multi-view geometry normals (Sec. 3.1). Conditioned on the generated albedo, Stage 2 predicts metallic-roughness (MR) maps with a VLM-guided intrinsic material adapter (Sec. 3.2.1) and photometric representation alignment (Sec. 3.2.2). Both stages are built upon an image diffusion backbone and are trained separately; following [(Team, 2025a)], MR maps are represented as two channels of a single RGB image.

    3.1. Multi-view Albedo and Shading Normal Generation

    The first stage generates multi-view albedo maps and world-space shading normals from the reference image and rendered geometry normals. We adopt a two-step architecture: a Multi-Modal Transformer (MM-T) fuses conditioning tokens and noisy view latents per view, then a Multi-View Transformer (MV-T) models cross-view interactions for global consistency.

    3.1.1. Multi-Modal DiT

    For each view, MM-T integrates the reference-image and geometry-normal conditions into a unified latent representation. Specifically, for the i-th view, we extract geometry-normal tokens T_geoⁱ by encoding the rendered geometry normal Gᵢ with a fixed VAE encoder 𝔼_VAE, and derive reference-image tokens T_img from both VAE latents and DINOv2 embeddings. These conditional tokens, together with the noisy view latent zᵢ, are processed by l₁ transformer blocks with intra-view self-attention:

    (1)T_geoⁱ=Linear_geo[𝔼_VAE(Gᵢ)],
    (2)T_img=Linear_img[𝔼_VAE(I);DINOv2(I)],
    (3)zᵢ^l₁=MM-T^l₁(zᵢ,T_img,T_geoⁱ).

    3.1.2. Multi-View DiT

    After per-view multi-modal fusion, we perform global reasoning across views. To focus this stage strictly on cross-view interaction, we discard all conditional tokens (T_img, T_geo) and retain only the view-wise latents zᵢ from all N views. Formally, the intermediate features from all views are aggregated into a unified sequence and processed through a series of l₂ Transformer blocks. In this joint representation {ẑᵢ}∈ℝ^NL×C, self-attention is performed globally to capture cross-view correlations and ensure 3D coherence.

    (4)

    {ẑᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^N=MV-T^l₂(z₁^l₁,z₂^l₁,…,z_N^l₁)∈ℝ^NL×C.

    The stage is trained with a flow matching objective, where z₀ denotes the noise-free latent of the ground-truth albedo map and c={T_img,T_geo} denotes the conditioning tokens:

    (5)

    L_alb(θ)=𝔼_t,z₀,ε[∥v_θ(zₜ;t,c)-(ε-z₀)∥²].

    3.1.3. Joint Estimation of Shading Normal

    We introduce a computationally efficient scheme to jointly predict world-space shading normals (S) alongside albedo maps. This auxiliary prediction provides geometry-aware supervision for albedo generation, encouraging richer surface structure and high-frequency details.

    Why world-space shading normals? Unlike tangent-space normal or bump maps, which depend on local UV coordinates, world-space shading normals are expressed in a global coordinate frame and remain independent of UV parameterization. This avoids the inconsistent tangent frames introduced by rotated or flipped UV islands, making normal prediction less prone to seams (Fig. 4(a)).

    We denote the VAE latent of S as Tₛₙ. Our key insight is that the geometry normal tokens T_geo, which serve as input conditioning during albedo training, naturally reside in the same modality as world-space shading normals. Leveraging this geometric alignment, we reuse the existing pathway to predict a joint velocity field. Specifically, the model is optimized by a multi-task objective consisting of an albedo flow matching loss L_alb and a shading-normal refinement loss Lₙₒᵣₘₐₗ. While the albedo component follows the standard flow from Gaussian noise ε to the ground-truth albedo latent T_alb, the shading-normal component treats T_geo as the starting point to learn the residual micro-geometry:

    (6)L_alb(θ)=𝔼_t,T_alb,ε[∥v_θ,alb(zₜ;t,c)-(ε-T_alb)∥²],
    (7)Lₙₒᵣₘₐₗ(θ)=𝔼_t,Tₛₙ,T_geo[∥v_θ,sn(zₜ;t,c)-(T_geo-Tₛₙ)∥²],
    (8)Lⱼₒᵢₙₜ=L_alb+λₙₒᵣₘₐₗLₙₒᵣₘₐₗ,

    where λₙₒᵣₘₐₗ is a balancing weight, and v_θ,alb,v_θ,sn represent the respective velocity components predicted by the model.

    3.2. Multi-view MR Generation

    Our multi-view MR generator follows the same MM-T/MV-T architecture as the albedo model in Sec. 3.1, but replaces the geometry-normal condition with the Stage-1 albedo maps. It further introduces two physical knowledge alignment modules for intrinsic material estimation: a VLM-guided intrinsic material adapter and photometric representation alignment.

    3.2.1. VLM-Guided Intrinsic Material Adapter

    Before training the multi-view MR generator, we train a VLM-guided intrinsic material adapter in a separate stage, as illustrated in Fig. 3. The goal is to translate material-aware visual knowledge from a frozen vision-language model (VLM) into diffusion-compatible intrinsic material tokens. During this adapter training stage, both the VLM and the image diffusion model are kept frozen, and only the adapter is optimized.

    Previous studies [(Neo et al., 2024; Kaduri et al., 2025)] indicate that VLM hidden representations evolve progressively across layers: early layers capture raw visual features, whereas intermediate layers encode more abstract semantic and reasoning cues. Since MR generation requires reasoning about intrinsic material properties rather than direct appearance transfer, we exploit intermediate VLM tokens extracted from the encoded reference image I as a source of material-aware context. Specifically, let Vₘ(I)∈ℝ^P×dᵥₗₘ denote the visual-token subsequence of the VLM hidden state at layer m, where P is the number of image patch tokens. We select a set of intermediate layers M and concatenate their visual tokens along the channel dimension:

    (9)

    Hᵛˡᵐ_M=concat_m∈M[Vₘ(I)]∈ℝ^P×|M|dᵥₗₘ.

    The VLM token space is not directly compatible with the conditioning space of the image diffusion model. We therefore introduce an Intrinsic Material Token AdapterA, which projects Hᵛˡᵐ_M into 1D intrinsic material tokens:

    (10)

    Tₘₐₜ=A(Hᵛˡᵐ_M).

    These tokens are injected into the frozen image diffusion model through token-wise concatenation in the denoising blocks, where they interact with noisy latents to reconstruct ground-truth metallic and roughness maps. We optimize the adapter with the standard flow-matching objective on rendered reference images paired with their ground-truth MR maps. After training, the learned tokens encode part-aware material semantic priors and are used as conditional inputs for Stage-2 MR generation.

    3.2.2. Photometric Representation Alignment

    Inspired by representation alignment methods such as REPA [(Yu et al., 2025)], we introduce photometric representation alignment to provide stronger guidance for MR generation. Directly aligning raw MR maps with pretrained visual encoders is ill-posed, since encoders such as DINOv2 [(Oquab et al., 2023)] and MAE [(He et al., 2022)] are trained on natural images, while metallic and roughness maps are abstract intrinsic parameters.

    To bridge this domain gap, we construct alignment targets in a photometrically meaningful RGB space. For each training view, we render the ground-truth materials x into an auxiliary photometric response xₚₘ under a controlled point-light setup, where the light source is collocated with the camera. The rendered response exposes material-light interactions, such as highlight intensity, specular sharpness, and local reflectance contrast, while remaining compatible with pretrained visual encoders. We use a frozen DINOv2 encoder f to extract the target representation y=f(xₚₘ).

    During MR generation, the intermediate transformer features hₜ at timestep t are projected by a MLP layer h_φ and aligned with y:

    (11)

    L_REPA(θ,φ)=-𝔼_(x,xₚₘ),t[1/Nₚ∑ₙ₌₁^Nₚsim(yₙ,h_φ(hₜ^[n]))],

    where Nₚ denotes the number of patches and sim(·,·) is the patch-wise cosine similarity. This representation-level alignment guides MR diffusion features toward the visual response of physically valid materials, providing stronger cues for fine-grained metallic and roughness prediction without explicit lighting supervision.

    3.2.3. Network

    The MR network follows the same MM-T and MV-T design as the albedo stage. For the i-th view, we replace the geometry-normal condition with the generated albedo map Aᵢ from Stage 1:

    (12)

    T_albⁱ=Linear_alb[𝔼_VAE(Aᵢ)].

    Together with the reference-image tokens T_img and the VLM-derived material tokens Tₘₐₜ, the noisy MR latent is fused by MM-T:

    (13)

    zᵢ^l₁=MM-T^l₁(zᵢ,T_img,T_albⁱ,Tₘₐₜ).

    The fused view latents are then processed by the same MV-T formulation in Sec. 3.1.2.

    We optimize the MR generation model with a flow-matching loss L_flow^MR and the photometric representation alignment loss:

    (14)

    Lₜₒₜₐₗ^MR=L_flow^MR+λ_RL_REPA,

    where λ_R balances the representation alignment term.

    4. Experiments

    We compare UltraTex against open-source and commercial state-of-the-art PBR generation methods through qualitative comparisons, quantitative metrics, and a user study in Sec. 4.2, comprehensively examining both intrinsic PBR accuracy and human visual preference. We also ablate main factors of our architecture in Sec. 4.3.

    4.1. Implementation Details

    4.1.1. Dataset.

    We curate a dataset of 130K objects from Objaverse-XL [(Deitke et al., 2023b; Deitke et al., 2023a)] and TexVerse [(Zhang et al., 2025)]. For diversity, each object is rendered into 32 reference images under random cameras and environment maps. For supervision, we extract ground-truth PBR maps (albedo, metallic, roughness), normals (geometry, shading), and render photometric images across six 1024² orthogonal views. We provide more details in the supplementary.

    4.1.2. Training.

    We use the intrinsic material token adapter to integrate the Qwen3.5-4B VLM [(Qwen Team, 2026)] with our diffusion framework. The adapter is a two-layer MLP with channel dimensions {12288,4096,3072} and an intermediate SiLU activation. Hierarchical visual features are extracted from intermediate VLM layers M={8,16,24}. Both the albedo and MR models initialize their DiT backbones from a pretrained text-to-image diffusion model. The multi-view models are trained at a per-view resolution of 768². Each model is trained on 32 NVIDIA A100 GPUs for about 2 days.

    4.1.3. Inference.

    At inference time, we first generate six-view albedo maps, which then condition the MR network to estimate corresponding metallic and roughness maps. All maps per view are upscaled to 1536² by a super-resolution module and mapped onto 4K UV textures. To ensure complete surface coverage, unobserved regions not captured by the orthogonal projections are inpainted using the novel view synthesis model from LumiTex [(Bao et al., 2026)] (see original paper for details).

    4.2. Comparison with Existing Methods

    4.2.1. Baselines.

    We compare UltraTex with representative open-source PBR texture synthesis methods, including Paint-it [(Youwang et al., 2024b)], DreamMat [(Zhang et al., 2024a)], Hunyuan3D v2.1 [(Team, 2025a; Huang et al., 2025)], LumiTex [(Bao et al., 2026)], and TRELLIS.2 [(Xiang et al., 2025)]. We also compare against commercial methods, including Hunyuan3D v3.1, Hyper3D [(Hyper3D, 2026)], Meshy 6 [(Meshy, 2026)], and TripoAI v3.1 [(TripoAI, 2026)] and Seed3D 2.0 [(Seed3D, 2026)].

    4.2.2. Evaluation Metrics

    To evaluate texture fidelity, we follow the protocol of Hunyuan3D [(Team, 2025a; Team, 2025b; Zhao et al., 2025)] by employing FID [(Heusel et al., 2017)], CLIP-FID, and LPIPS [(Zhang et al., 2018)]. For a more fine-grained assessment, we use CLIP Maximum-Mean Discrepancy (CMMD) [(Jayasumana et al., 2024)] to measure detail diversity and CLIP-I [(Radford et al., 2021)] for prompt alignment. Notably, all aforementioned perceptual and semantic metrics are computed exclusively on the albedo maps. For MR estimation, accuracy is validated via the MSE (×10⁻³). We also conduct a user study to benchmark texture quality based on human preferences.

    4.2.3. Quantitative Results

    We quantitatively compare UltraTex with baselines on 152 held-out Objaverse-XL objects, using Blender-rendered GT assets as reference inputs and rendering outputs at 1024² resolution. Except for MSE on MR attributes, all perceptual and semantic metrics are computed on rendered albedo/MR images, covering visual fidelity, semantic alignment, and PBR accuracy.

    As shown in Tab. 1, our method consistently outperforms existing baselines across all metrics. It achieves better FID and LPIPS for perceptual quality, lower CMMD for texture diversity, higher CLIP-I/CLIP-FID for semantic alignment, and the lowest MSE across PBR attributes, validating its superior physical accuracy. Additionally, Table 3 further shows that our method outperforms both the state-of-the-art multi-view baseline (LumiTex) and the 3D-native baseline (TRELLIS.2) under environment relighting.

    To evaluate perceptual quality, we conduct a blind user study where 31 professional 3D modelers rate results from 1 to 5 based on overall rendering, albedo, roughness, and metallic fidelity. UltraTex achieves the highest scores across all dimensions (Tab. 2) and substantially outperforms competitors in pairwise win rates (Fig. 5), demonstrating strong expert preference.

    4.2.4. Qualitative Results

    We qualitatively compare UltraTex with recent open-source and commercial baselines for PBR texture generation. For test data, we generate reference images via Seedream 4.5 [(Seedream et al., 2025)], followed by mesh generation with Hunyuan3D v3.1, then apply each method for texture generation.

    As shown in Fig. 7 and 7, existing methods like Hunyuan3D and Hyper3D often suffer from illumination leakage, producing albedo maps with baked-in lighting artifacts. Furthermore, most baselines have difficulty resolving intrinsic material ambiguity, frequently misclassifying metallic regions or producing over-smoothed roughness maps. In contrast, by leveraging material knowledge and illumination cues, UltraTex consistently produces more accurate metallic estimates and fine-grained roughness details, while also delivering albedo maps with superior physical fidelity and structural richness.

    This advantage is especially evident in challenging cases (Fig. 8), including micro-scale roughness variations, oxidized or coated metals, and part-wise material changes, where baselines often fail. Furthermore, the diverse gallery in Fig. 18 demonstrates our model’s ability to produce physically plausible textures across a wide array of geometric complexities and material compositions.

    We further evaluate the generated PBR textures through relighting under diverse novel illumination conditions. As shown in Fig. 9, the recovered material properties respond naturally to changes in lighting, producing consistent highlights, reflections, and surface appearance across different environments.

    To further evaluate the accuracy of intrinsic material decomposition, we compare against baselines on objects with ground-truth PBR maps. Given the same clay mesh and reference image, UltraTex more faithfully recovers the target material properties than the multi-view baseline LumiTex and the 3D-native baseline TRELLIS.2, particularly in base color, metallic separation, and spatially varying roughness (Fig. 11).

    4.2.5. Results on Real-World Inputs

    We further evaluate UltraTex on casually captured real-world inputs and scanned meshes, including three examples collected from Sketchfab and two from the DTC dataset [(Dong et al., 2025)]. These inputs exhibit uncontrolled illumination, appearance ambiguity, and imperfect scanned geometry. As shown in Fig. 10, UltraTex remains robust under these conditions, producing coherent PBR materials and physically plausible relighting. The results demonstrate that our method generalizes beyond clean rendered inputs to practical real-world asset creation.

    4.3. Ablation Study

    VLM-derived Intrinsic Material Token

    To validate the impact of VLM priors, we train a variant of MR estimation network without intrinsic material token guidance. As shown in Fig. 12 and Tab. 4, removing the VLM-derived tokens leads to clear material misclassification and increases both metallic and roughness errors. The ablated model relies heavily on low-level visual cues, such as color and specular highlights, and therefore mistakes strong reflections for metallic materials. This confirms that VLM guidance provides essential semantic and part-level material priors, enabling more physically grounded MR estimation that is robust to misleading appearance-based heuristics. In addition, removing the visual conditions also degrades MR quality, demonstrating their complementary role in providing dense spatial guidance for material generation.

    Decoding Probe of VLM Encoder

    To quantify the intrinsic material information encoded by the 1D material tokens, we conduct a decoding probe by replacing the VLM encoder with VAE and DINOv2 encoders under the same setting and directly decoding MR maps from the resulting tokens. As shown in Tab. 5, VLM features consistently outperform VAE and DINOv2 features, demonstrating that the resulting tokens carry richer material semantics and better disentangle intrinsic MR properties from observed appearance. This is because intrinsic material properties require semantic reasoning beyond observable appearance, which is better captured by the world knowledge encoded in VLM representations.

    VLM-token Attention Map Visualization

    To better understand the part-level spatial localization of the 1D material tokens, we visualize the attention from VLM tokens to noisy image tokens at the 4th layer of the Multi-Modal DiT. As shown in Fig. 13, the responses are strongly localized to material-relevant object parts, such as metallic ornaments, buckles, and other hardware regions. Notably, the VLM tokens themselves carry no explicit spatial coordinates; their spatial correspondence emerges through interaction with the image tokens inside the DiT. This indicates that the material tokens are not merely used as global semantic conditions, but establish part-level correspondence with regions exhibiting the associated material properties.

item.title: 重建场景只看「像不像」不够：LightHarness 让 VLM 显式推理光照，还维护一份「光源假设的修订史」 ｜ Beyond Appearance: Evidence-Guided Programmatic 3D Scene Reconstruction with Agentic Lighting Reasoning
item.description:
一句话：外观相似度无法区分「几何错了」「材质错了」还是「光照错了」。

要点：

  • 问题定位：image-to-code 式三维重建能产出可执行代码、生成可编辑内容并支持视觉仿真，但现有方法**主要依赖外观相似度**，因此无法区分几何、材质与光照上的错误
  • 为什么光照关键：光通过与几何、材质的交互塑造场景外观——着色、投影、反射都受它影响
  • LightHarness 是一个基于 VLM 的 **agentic** 框架，把显式光照推理放进迭代重建：用几何、本征与光照三类互补线索联合精修结构与外观，并用 **Lighting Reasoning Memory** 维护光源假设、支持证据与修订历史

为什么值得看：「重建出来的场景能不能换光照」是资产可用性的硬指标，而外观相似度根本测不出这件事。把光照当成需要显式假设、逐条验证并留修订史的对象，是 agentic 重建里最实际的一步——它直接对应灯光师的工作方式。

中文摘要：image-to-code 式的三维场景重建能产出可执行代码，生成可编辑的数字内容并支持视觉仿真；但现有方法主要依赖外观相似度，而这种相似度无法区分错误究竟出在几何、材质还是光照上。光通过与几何与材质的交互塑造场景外观，影响着色、投影与反射，因此作者把显式光照推理引入迭代重建，提出基于视觉语言模型的 agentic 框架 LightHarness：它利用几何、本征与光照三类互补线索联合精修场景结构与外观，并用「光照推理记忆」维护光源假设，记录支持证据与修订历史。对需要「换光照仍成立」的资产管线，这条把光照从隐变量变成了可审计的假设。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-19

本期推送：2026-11-20

Beyond Appearance: Evidence-Guided
Programmatic 3D Scene Reconstruction with Agentic Lighting Reasoning

Abstract

Image-to-code methods for 3D scene reconstruction produce executable code that generates editable digital content and supports visual simulation. However, existing methods primarily rely on appearance similarity, which provides limited guidance for distinguishing errors in geometry, materials, and illumination. Light shapes scene appearance through its interactions with geometry and materials, influencing shading, cast shadows, and reflections. We therefore present LightHarness, a VLM-based agentic framework that incorporates explicit lighting reasoning into iterative scene reconstruction. To be specific, we leverage complementary geometric, intrinsic, and illumination cues to jointly refine scene structure and appearance, and propose Lighting Reasoning Memory to maintain light-source hypotheses, which supports evidence, and revision history throughout iterations. Together, they support reasoning about partially visible and unseen sources, with evidence-guided verification directing subsequent revisions. Our framework reconstructs explicit scenes through coherent reasoning about geometry, materials, and illumination without additional training or differentiable rendering. Extensive experiments demonstrate superior image-to-code reconstruction accuracy under challenging shadows and complex illumination, further supporting downstream scene editing, object insertion, and versatile relighting.

1 Introduction

Reconstructing an executable, editable 3D scene from a single image connects visual understanding with digital scene creation. Image-to-code reconstruction offers a promising direction: a scene program (e.g., Blender, Three.js) explicitly represents geometry, spatial layout, materials, cameras, and light sources, enabling novel-view rendering and subsequent scene editing [35, 10, 29]. Except for spatial grounding that concerns object poses or location, lighting is also central to this process. Shading, cast shadows, highlights and reflections arise from the complex interactions between illumination, geometry, and materials. Accurate image-to-code reconstruction requires recovering object structure and layout together with the illumination that explains their observed appearance.

Recent advances in vision-language models (VLMs) [24, 9] have enabled scene construction through executable programs, connecting visual and semantic reasoning with explicit control over scene components. This capability supports a common iterative paradigm: an agent proposes or edits a scene program, inspects the rendered result, and revises its proposal based on visual feedback. SceneCraft [11] and BlenderAlchemy [12] demonstrate this paradigm to be effective in text-driven construction and appearance-guided editing, respectively. Extending it to reconstruction from visual input enjoys richer editing applications, and requires the VLMs to determine which scene configuration could explain the observed image. Recent systems formulate this problem through plan and observation management [35], staged refinement of scene attributes [10], or explicit geometric, material, and light modeling [26, 4] in synthetic game scenes.

Across these approaches, rendered-reference comparisons provide a central feedback signal for scene revision. However, such a discrepancy on appearance does not uniquely identify its underlying cause, because similar image differences can arise from geometry, reflectance, or illumination. For example, a dark region may arise from low surface reflectance, a surface facing away from light sources, or insufficient illumination from an unseen source. Simply brightening the material can reduce a local image discrepancy, but leave the underlying illumination error unresolved, leading to an incorrect material estimation. The challenge is therefore to connect observed lighting effects to their plausible geometric, material, and illumination explanations. This motivates our central question: How can we explicitly reason about scene geometry, materials, and light sources for more accurate image-to-code reconstruction beyond appearance?

To mitigate this, we propose LightHarness, a VLM-based agent framework that incorporates explicit lighting modeling into iterative scene generation and verification with complementary evidence and reasoning. We first associate light-source hypotheses with evidence of their interactions with scene geometry and materials. Specifically, we combine estimated HDR illumination [3], depth and surface orientation [27, 13], intrinsic albedo and shading [13]. These complementary sources of evidence relate appearance discrepancies to candidate revisions of the underlying scene factors, helping the generator agent determine which geometry, material, or light parameters to update during reconstruction, and finally output an executable Blender program. As for the verifier agent, we equip it with a rubric scorer and a VLM. The rubric scorer assesses rendered-reference agreement based on predefined criteria, while the VLM uses these assessments, reference-image history revisions, and decomposed rendering evidence to diagnose and propose refinement updates.

To preserve and refine illumination reasoning iteratively in the proposed agentic system, we design Lighting Reasoning Memory (LRM), shared by the generator and verifier agents. LRM associates each hypothesized light source with a group of stable parameters, including identity, visibility, location, color, etc., establishing a clear correspondence among observations, editable Blender elements and the revision history. Notably, we explicitly consider partially visible, occluded, and off-frame light sources as hypotheses, enabling a more complete model of scene illumination that accounts for both visible and inferred light sources. In each iteration, the generator uses this persistent lighting proxy to build scene programs and refine parameters, while the verifier examines it based on rendered evidence and recommends corrections. By incorporating source-specific observations, decisions, and their supporting evidence in a synergistic framework, LRM provides persistent illumination-centric context for LightHarness, enabling subsequent geometry, material, and lighting revisions to build coherently on historical judgments.

Extensive experiments demonstrate our competitive 3D image-to-code reconstruction accuracy. We further verify our effectiveness on hard cases under complex lights and shadows, and showcase that our method can generalize to rich downstream applications, including image relighting, material/texture editing, and harmonious object insertion. Our contributions can be summarized as follows:

  • •

    We propose a VLM-based 3D image-to-code reconstruction framework that incorporates explicit lighting modeling to guide the recovery of geometry, materials, and light sources in an executable scene program.

  • •

    We introduce Lighting Reasoning Memory to preserve source identities, supporting evidence, and revision history across generation and verification, combining geometric and intrinsic priors with light-transport evidence to guide iterative scene refinement.

  • •

    We demonstrate competitive 3D image-to-code reconstruction accuracy and further illustrate the utility of the reconstructed scenes through downstream applications, including image relighting, enhancement and complex light understanding.

    • 2 Related Work

    Lighting Estimation. Inverse rendering [14] aims to estimate scene geometry, reflectance, and illumination to explain observed image appearance and enable editing [15]. PhotoScene [33] optimizes materials and lighting on approximately aligned CAD geometry, while Materialist [28] combines intrinsic prediction with differentiable material and environment-light refinement. Multi-view methods further constrain material and illumination recovery through shared observations [32, 18]. LUMEN [3] instead predicts local HDR illumination, providing a lighting prior rather than a complete scene program. Generative relighting also incorporates physical guidance and local control through light-transport consistency [36], intrinsic conditioning and scribbles [6], or estimated illumination priors [34]. These methods provide complementary forms of lighting estimation and control, with different assumptions about available geometry and observations. Our focus is to use such evidence to guide geometry, material, and light revisions during executable scene reconstruction, with relighting as a downstream application.

    Executable Scene Representations and Agentic Reconstruction. SceneCraft [11] translates scene descriptions and spatial constraints into Blender programs, while BlenderAlchemy [12] searches scene edits through rendered feedback. For image-to-code reconstruction, VIGA [35] combines generation and verification with multimodal memory, and SEIG [10] refines geometry, materials, composition, and lighting in stages. HARMONY [26] and Lumera [4] incorporate geometric priors and explicit illumination, with Lumera retaining shared refinement history. VETR [21] additionally uses execution observations to distinguish proposed edits from their realized effects. Notably, Code Video Model [17] combines executable codes with frontier generative models, achieving versatile controllable video generation. Although these systems already incorporate multiple forms of scene evidence and iterative feedback, our focus is to maintain source-specific lighting hypotheses and connect memorable evolution to geometric, intrinsic, and decomposed rendering evidence throughout reconstruction.

    3 Method

    3.1 Motivation and Overview

    Image-to-code reconstruction represents geometry, materials, and lighting in an executable program, providing an interpretable proxy for rendering, scene manipulation, and downstream applications. Existing methods primarily exploit this problem through scene composition, spatial constraints, and interactive environments [11, 19, 8]. However, faithful reconstruction requires understanding how scene components interact with light to produce the observed appearance. Inferring lighting from incomplete observations is ill-posed because different scene configurations can produce similar images. A dark wall may indicate low reflectance, occlusion, or a surface facing away from illumination. Misinterpreting these effects can lead to incorrect materials or geometry, hampering reconstruction fidelity and subsequent editing. We therefore treat lighting reasoning as a crucial part of image-to-code reconstruction.

    As shown in Fig. 3, LightHarness formulates a T-round loop which follows Perceive → Generator → Execute & Render → Verifier and combines visual evidence E extracted from image I with Lighting Reasoning Memory (LRM) Mₜ. Perception forms the scene context, which guides the Generator in producing code Cₜ and light-source hypotheses. Following rendering, rubric scoring and VLM diagnosis assess the reconstruction and guide subsequent revisions. Generated scene states and verification findings update LRM, preserving evidence and reasoning across rounds. The best valid candidate is selected by its rubric score, yielding jointly refined geometry, materials, and lighting for a wide range of downstream applications.

    3.2 Enriched Evidence for Lighting Reasoning

    Lighting reasoning requires both the spatial structure governing light transport and evidence of its effects on surfaces. We extract complementary geometric, intrinsic, and lighting cues to support these judgments.

    Geometric evidence. SAM 3 [2] provides fine-grained semantic object masks, while VGGT [27] estimates relative depth and cameras to establish a common reconstruction coordinate system. For planar structures, we back-project reliable masked depth pixels and fit planes through robust estimation using least-squares refinement. Each plane provides a surface point and normal for reasoning about position, orientation, and illumination. Non-planar objects retain masks and depth cues without planar fitting.

    Intrinsic and lighting evidence. Marigold [13] estimates albedo and diffuse shading to help distinguish reflectance from light effects. LUMEN [3] offers an HDR image suggesting light-source directions and chromatic properties. Evidence is extracted once and remains fixed, while its interpretation and reasoning evolve with rendering feedback.

    3.3 Lighting Reasoning Memory

    Scene revisions can change a light source’s contribution even when its parameters remain unchanged. Lighting reasoning must therefore retain both current source states and the evidence underlying previous decisions. Therefore, we propose shared Lighting Reasoning Memory (LRM):

    Mₜ=(Sₜ,Hₜ),

    		(1)

    where Sₜ contains light-source states and Hₜ records diagnostic history. We connect the stable light-source identities with corresponding Blender elements, where each state describes light visibility, type, position, orientation, intensity and color. VLM visual reasoning [24, 9], guided by enriched evidence, also supports hypotheses of partially visible, occluded, and off-frame light sources.

    The history Hₜ associates sources with previous assessments, proposed revisions, implemented changes, and observed outcomes. It further relates multiple sources through semantic correspondence to support a coherent interpretation of scene illumination. Together, Sₜ and Hₜ guide subsequent geometry, material, and lighting reasoning. Their update is described as below.

    3.4 Evidence-Guided Verification

    The Verifier consists a deterministic rubric scorer and a VLM diagnosis to assess reconstruction quality and guide scene refinement. The scorer measures agreement with the reference image and enriched evidence, while the VLM interprets these measurements alongside rendered outputs and LRM to identify plausible causes of discrepancies.

    Rubric-based assessment. The rubric is six-fold as below. (1) Object-mask error measures projected-region disagreement. (2) Relative-depth error compares reliable overlapping regions after positive scale alignment and penalizes missing coverage. (3) Orientation error compares depth-derived plane normals while accounting for sign ambiguity. (4-5) Albedo and diffuse-shading errors are measured in trusted diffuse regions in linear color space. Shading uses one positive alignment scale shared across channels to preserve chromatic differences. (6) RGB error evaluates overall appearance. We aggregate these errors into scores qₜ:

    qₜ=(∑_k∈Kwₖe_t,k)/(∑_k∈Kwₖ),

    		(2)

    where K indexes mask, depth, orientation, albedo, shading, and RGB errors. Corresponding weights wₖ remain fixed across rounds at (2,1,0.5,0.5,1,1), with sensitivity examined through ablations provided in the Supp. Lower scores indicate better agreement and guide candidate selection without gradient-based optimization.

    Evidence-guided diagnosis. Beyond scalar assessment, the VLM combines component errors, rendered passes, source contributions, and LRM to recommend geometric, material, or lighting revisions. For an underlit wall, it examines orientation, occlusion, albedo, and relevant source contributions. Geometric discrepancies motivate structural revisions, whereas consistent geometry and albedo direct attention to lighting. Each recommendation specifies the discrepancy, proposed revision, and supporting evidence, providing guidance for the subsequent reconstruction round.

    3.5 Memory-assisted Scene Reconstruction Loop

    With enriched evidence, LRM, and the Verifier defined, we integrate them into a closed loop of perception, generation, execution/rendering, and verification. At round t, the perception module combines the input image I, fixed evidence E, and memory Mₜ into a scene context comprising structural cues, lighting hypotheses, and unresolved discrepancies. Conditioned on this context and preceding scene code, the Generator jointly reasons about structure and illumination to produce t-step code Cₜ and a light source state update ΔSₜ. After checking state consistency and source correspondence, we obtain

    (Cₜ,ΔSₜ)=VLM(I,E,Mₜ,Cₜ₋₁), S̃ₜ=Apply(Sₜ,ΔSₜ).

    		(3)

    The generated geometry and materials are combined with S̃ₜ under fixed camera and rendering settings. Blender ℝ then renders the candidate scene as

    Yₜ=ℝ(Cₜ,S̃ₜ),

    		(4)

    including RGB, masks, depth, surface information, albedo, diffuse shading, and individual light sources and world-illumination contributions. Masks and depth show scene layout and occlusion. Albedo and shading help separate material color from lighting, while light source attribution indicates which region it affects. The Verifier assesses these outputs against the reference evidence, producing the rubric score qₜ and evidence-guided recommendations.

    Following each valid round, we reorganize the light source state and append a record hₜ containing the diagnosis, implemented changes, scores, and references to archived outputs:

    Mₜ₊₁=(S̃ₜ, Hₜ\mathbin∥hₜ),

    		(5)

    where ∥ denotes history concatenation. The updated memory guides perception and generation in the next round, allowing subsequent reasoning to build on previous evidence and outcomes.

    Since revisions may improve some factors while degrading others, we select

    t^*=\arg\min_t∈T_validqₜ

    		(6)

    over completed valid rounds after T iterations. We return (C_t^*,S̃_t^*) together, preserving the correspondence between the selected executable scene and its lighting state. This closed loop connects evidence, diagnosis, and persistent memory to support coherent refinement of geometry, materials, and illumination.

    4 Experiments

    Our experiments compare reconstruction quality with recently blooming image-to-code methods, examine the roles of visual evidence and Lighting Reasoning Memory, and assess generalizable downstream application and hard cases.

    4.1 Implementation Details

    Framework development.

    We load external modules (i.e., SAM3, VGGT, Marigold, LUMEN) on two NVIDIA 4090-48G GPUs, and use GPT-6-Astra [24] as the Generator/Verifier VLM via API. All reconstructions are done with 10 rounds. We also examine our framework under different VLMs in the Supplementary materials.

    Data.

    We evaluate on 32 images drawn from diverse benchmarks from robotics, relighting and image enhancement, comprising 10 from Hypersim [25], 4 from LuxRemix [16], 10 from BAID [20], 7 from MIT-Adobe FiveK [1], and 1 from RoboDojo [5] with complex lighting conditions, diverse geometry and materials. The whole testing set contains 17 real photographs and 15 synthetic images, covering 22 indoor and 10 outdoor scenes.

    Metrics.

    We evaluate source-view consistency using PSNR [31], SSIM [30], LPIPS [37], and DreamSim [7]. Following SceneRig [19], we assess 3D reconstruction quality from the source view and nearby views at ±15^∘. By orbiting the camera around the world vertical axis through a pivot located four scene units along the original camera’s viewing direction, we use GPT-6-Astra as a judge to compute the mean-centered Bradley-Terry scores among these rendered pairs, with higher scores indicating stronger relative preference.

    Compared methods.

    We compare with recent SoTA image-to-code reconstruction methods, including VIGA [35], 3DCodeVerse [8], SceneRig [19]. All these methods use GPT-6-Astra as the backbone VLM with the same loop iterations and API. We additionally compare GPT-6-Sol with Codex [22] harness.

    4.2 Image-to-Code Reconstruction

    Qualitative results.

    Fig. 4 compares reconstructions across diverse geometry and lighting conditions. Our method better captures window–foreground contrast, localized illumination around bedside lamps, and combined window and ceiling lighting in the hall. It also preserves furniture arrangement and foreground animal composition, while competing methods exhibit layout distortions, simplified geometry, or mismatched illumination, supporting joint reasoning about scene structure, materials, and lighting. Notably, our method infers unseen light sources and structures through their illumination effects. In the fifth row, it reproduces striped shadows across the bedroom wall and bedding while preserving their spatial relationships, whereas competing methods miss these shadows or misinterpret the layout. The cast shadows in the last row further illustrate lighting reasoning beyond appearance, enabling more faithful image-to-code reconstruction. We present more visualized results under nearby views in the Supp.

    Hard case verification.

    Fig. 5 compares reconstructions of a scene with a prominent diagonal cast shadow. While competing methods distort or omit this shadow, LightHarness better reproduces its spatial extent while preserving the surrounding building structure. This result supports the value of enriched evidence and persistent lighting memory in relating shadow patterns to scene geometry and illumination, enabling more faithful image-to-code reconstruction under challenging lighting.

    Quantitative results.

    Table 1 shows that our method achieves the best PSNR, LPIPS, and DreamSim among the compared methods. Relative to the recent SoTA method, VIGA, LightHarness improves PSNR by 0.75 dB and reduces DreamSim by 10.7%, indicating our superiority in both pixel-level fidelity and perceptual similarity. The VLM-based evaluation and user preference further demonstrate our advantages at the scene level, ranking it first in all criteria covering completeness, layout, and appearance. These consistent preferences support the effectiveness of our framework in reconstructing scene composition and visual appearance.

    Inference cost.

    The latency mainly includes evidence extraction, GPT API and Blender rendering in the generation-verification loop. For a 768×576 image, these three parts cost 4.5 minutes, 118.8 minutes, and 1.1 minutes respectively. The latency is comparable with other baselines (VIGA [35] for 71.2 minutes and 3DCodeVerse [8] for 126.3 minutes). The critical bottleneck is API invocation, while other parts are relatively efficient with less than 6 minutes on two 4090-48 GB GPUs.

    User Study.

    We invite 29 participants to rank the reconstructed scenes according to (1) scene structure fidelity and (2) lighting appearance fidelity, using the reference images as guidance. We achieve the first-place preference rate on both criteria, indicating stronger human preference for its reconstruction of scene structure and illumination.

    4.3 Ablation Studies

    We conduct quantitative and qualitative ablation experiments to demonstrate the effectiveness of each design in our framework in Fig. 6 and Table 2.

    w/o enriched evidence.

    We disable the light and geometric evidence in Sec. 3.2, observing significant reconstruction error. As shown in Fig. 6 (c), the agent misjudges the wall light’s distance from the surface and misses background illumination.

    w/o geometric rubric.

    Discarding explicit constraints on geometry features leads to incomplete scene light reconstruction, as shown in Fig. 6 (d).

    w/o lighting rubric.

    Discarding lighting measurement produces wrong light source shapes and mismatched local illumination strength as shown in Fig. 6 (e).

    w/o lighting reasoning memory.

    We compare our full model with a variant that retains only current scene code and parameter values. Without memory, background illumination is missed as shown in Fig. 6 (f), highlighting the value of explicitly organizing light source hypotheses and diagnostic history across iterations.

    4.4 Generalizable Applications

    Building upon the precise executable scenes we reconstruct, our framework supports diverse downstream applications, including scene texture editing, harmonious object insertion, versatile relighting, and degraded illumination restoration. We also demonstrate that our rendered edits can combine with the frontier generative model, GPT-Image [23] to produce more physically realistic results. Note that simply applying generative models is hard to achieve precise physical modeling like lighting interaction with complex shadows and textures. Our integration with GPT-Image enables advanced editing ability.

    Material and Texture Editing.

    Our method can perform exact texture editing with multiple references in Fig. 7.

    Versatile relighting with flexible control.

    Our method achieves superior light control relative to simply applying GPT-Image, as shown in Fig. 8 and Fig. 9.

    Harmonious object insertion.

    Our framework enables physically realistic object insertion as shown in Fig. 10.

    5 Conclusion, Limitation and Future Work

    We propose LightHarness, a VLM-based agentic framework that integrates explicit lighting reasoning and persistent light-source memory into image-to-code 3D reconstruction. Complementary geometric, intrinsic, and illumination evidence guides reconstruction, while rubric-based assessment and VLM diagnosis support iterative refinement. Lighting reasoning memory preserves source identities, evidence, semantic relationships, and revision history, enabling coherent reasoning across rounds. Quantitative and qualitative results demonstrate our improved reconstruction fidelity under challenging shadows and complex illumination compared to recent SoTA methods. Based on the accurate programmatic scene reconstruction, our framework enables rich applications, including relighting, harmonious object insertion, material and texture editing with plausible physical modeling.

    Limitation.

    Our framework remains limited in inferring unseen scene objects from sparse and overlapping shadow cues. As shown in Fig. 11, it fails to reconstruct the off-frame people and sign suggested by their shadows, leaving the corresponding shadow patterns incomplete.

    Future work. We will incorporate complex scene examples through in-context learning and post-train open-source VLMs on challenging datasets to strengthen reasoning about unseen objects and their interactions with light. Reducing token budget is also meaningful. We argue that projecting visual representation back to executable codes is a highly promising direction in this field.

    LLM Usage Statement

    OpenAI Codex was used to assist with basic code generation, manuscript organization and language editing. Codex was not used to formulate research ideas, design the method or experiments, or draw scientific conclusions. All AI-assisted text was manually reviewed and revised by the authors. All AI-assisted code was inspected, executed, and verified for correctness, and the resulting visualizations and preprocessed data were checked against the source data and expected outputs. The authors take full responsibility for the final content, including all text, code, results, and claims.

    （参考文献见原文。）

Specifically, we combine estimated HDR illumination [3], depth and surface orientation [27, 13], intrinsic albedo and shading [13]. These complementary sources of evidence relate appearance discrepancies to candidate revisions of the underlying scene factors, helping the generator agent determine which geometry, material, or light parameters to update during reconstruction, and finally output an executable Blender program. As for the verifier agent, we equip it with a rubric scorer and a VLM. The rubric scorer assesses rendered-reference agreement based on predefined criteria, while the VLM uses these assessments, reference-image history revisions, and decomposed rendering evidence to diagnose and propose refinement updates.

To preserve and refine illumination reasoning iteratively in the proposed agentic system, we design Lighting Reasoning Memory (LRM), shared by the generator and verifier agents. LRM associates each hypothesized light source with a group of stable parameters, including identity, visibility, location, color, etc., establishing a clear correspondence among observations, editable Blender elements and the revision history. Notably, we explicitly consider partially visible, occluded, and off-frame light sources as hypotheses, enabling a more complete model of scene illumination that accounts for both visible and inferred light sources. In each iteration, the generator uses this persistent lighting proxy to build scene programs and refine parameters, while the verifier examines it based on rendered evidence and recommends corrections. By incorporating source-specific observations, decisions, and their supporting evidence in a synergistic framework, LRM provides persistent illumination-centric context for LightHarness, enabling subsequent geometry, material, and lighting revisions to build coherently on historical judgments.

Extensive experiments demonstrate our competitive 3D image-to-code reconstruction accuracy. We further verify our effectiveness on hard cases under complex lights and shadows, and showcase that our method can generalize to rich downstream applications, including image relighting, material/texture editing, and harmonious object insertion. Our contributions can be summarized as follows:

  • •

    We propose a VLM-based 3D image-to-code reconstruction framework that incorporates explicit lighting modeling to guide the recovery of geometry, materials, and light sources in an executable scene program.

  • •

    We introduce Lighting Reasoning Memory to preserve source identities, supporting evidence, and revision history across generation and verification, combining geometric and intrinsic priors with light-transport evidence to guide iterative scene refinement.

  • •

    We demonstrate competitive 3D image-to-code reconstruction accuracy and further illustrate the utility of the reconstructed scenes through downstream applications, including image relighting, enhancement and complex light understanding.

    • 2 Related Work

    Lighting Estimation. Inverse rendering [14] aims to estimate scene geometry, reflectance, and illumination to explain observed image appearance and enable editing [15]. PhotoScene [33] optimizes materials and lighting on approximately aligned CAD geometry, while Materialist [28] combines intrinsic prediction with differentiable material and environment-light refinement. Multi-view methods further constrain material and illumination recovery through shared observations [32, 18]. LUMEN [3] instead predicts local HDR illumination, providing a lighting prior rather than a complete scene program. Generative relighting also incorporates physical guidance and local control through light-transport consistency [36], intrinsic conditioning and scribbles [6], or estimated illumination priors [34]. These methods provide complementary forms of lighting estimation and control, with different assumptions about available geometry and observations. Our focus is to use such evidence to guide geometry, material, and light revisions during executable scene reconstruction, with relighting as a downstream application.

    Executable Scene Representations and Agentic Reconstruction. SceneCraft [11] translates scene descriptions and spatial constraints into Blender programs, while BlenderAlchemy [12] searches scene edits through rendered feedback. For image-to-code reconstruction, VIGA [35] combines generation and verification with multimodal memory, and SEIG [10] refines geometry, materials, composition, and lighting in stages. HARMONY [26] and Lumera [4] incorporate geometric priors and explicit illumination, with Lumera retaining shared refinement history. VETR [21] additionally uses execution observations to distinguish proposed edits from their realized effects. Notably, Code Video Model [17] combines executable codes with frontier generative models, achieving versatile controllable video generation. Although these systems already incorporate multiple forms of scene evidence and iterative feedback, our focus is to maintain source-specific lighting hypotheses and connect memorable evolution to geometric, intrinsic, and decomposed rendering evidence throughout reconstruction.

    3 Method

    3.1 Motivation and Overview

    Image-to-code reconstruction represents geometry, materials, and lighting in an executable program, providing an interpretable proxy for rendering, scene manipulation, and downstream applications. Existing methods primarily exploit this problem through scene composition, spatial constraints, and interactive environments [11, 19, 8]. However, faithful reconstruction requires understanding how scene components interact with light to produce the observed appearance. Inferring lighting from incomplete observations is ill-posed because different scene configurations can produce similar images. A dark wall may indicate low reflectance, occlusion, or a surface facing away from illumination. Misinterpreting these effects can lead to incorrect materials or geometry, hampering reconstruction fidelity and subsequent editing. We therefore treat lighting reasoning as a crucial part of image-to-code reconstruction.

    As shown in Fig. 3, LightHarness formulates a T-round loop which follows Perceive → Generator → Execute & Render → Verifier and combines visual evidence E extracted from image I with Lighting Reasoning Memory (LRM) Mₜ. Perception forms the scene context, which guides the Generator in producing code Cₜ and light-source hypotheses. Following rendering, rubric scoring and VLM diagnosis assess the reconstruction and guide subsequent revisions. Generated scene states and verification findings update LRM, preserving evidence and reasoning across rounds. The best valid candidate is selected by its rubric score, yielding jointly refined geometry, materials, and lighting for a wide range of downstream applications.

    3.2 Enriched Evidence for Lighting Reasoning

    Lighting reasoning requires both the spatial structure governing light transport and evidence of its effects on surfaces. We extract complementary geometric, intrinsic, and lighting cues to support these judgments.

    Geometric evidence. SAM 3 [2] provides fine-grained semantic object masks, while VGGT [27] estimates relative depth and cameras to establish a common reconstruction coordinate system. For planar structures, we back-project reliable masked depth pixels and fit planes through robust estimation using least-squares refinement. Each plane provides a surface point and normal for reasoning about position, orientation, and illumination. Non-planar objects retain masks and depth cues without planar fitting.

    Intrinsic and lighting evidence. Marigold [13] estimates albedo and diffuse shading to help distinguish reflectance from light effects. LUMEN [3] offers an HDR image suggesting light-source directions and chromatic properties. Evidence is extracted once and remains fixed, while its interpretation and reasoning evolve with rendering feedback.

    3.3 Lighting Reasoning Memory

    Scene revisions can change a light source’s contribution even when its parameters remain unchanged. Lighting reasoning must therefore retain both current source states and the evidence underlying previous decisions. Therefore, we propose shared Lighting Reasoning Memory (LRM):

    Mₜ=(Sₜ,Hₜ),

    		(1)

    where Sₜ contains light-source states and Hₜ records diagnostic history. We connect the stable light-source identities with corresponding Blender elements, where each state describes light visibility, type, position, orientation, intensity and color. VLM visual reasoning [24, 9], guided by enriched evidence, also supports hypotheses of partially visible, occluded, and off-frame light sources.

    The history Hₜ associates sources with previous assessments, proposed revisions, implemented changes, and observed outcomes. It further relates multiple sources through semantic correspondence to support a coherent interpretation of scene illumination. Together, Sₜ and Hₜ guide subsequent geometry, material, and lighting reasoning. Their update is described as below.

    3.4 Evidence-Guided Verification

    The Verifier consists a deterministic rubric scorer and a VLM diagnosis to assess reconstruction quality and guide scene refinement. The scorer measures agreement with the reference image and enriched evidence, while the VLM interprets these measurements alongside rendered outputs and LRM to identify plausible causes of discrepancies.

    Rubric-based assessment. The rubric is six-fold as below. (1) Object-mask error measures projected-region disagreement. (2) Relative-depth error compares reliable overlapping regions after positive scale alignment and penalizes missing coverage. (3) Orientation error compares depth-derived plane normals while accounting for sign ambiguity. (4-5) Albedo and diffuse-shading errors are measured in trusted diffuse regions in linear color space. Shading uses one positive alignment scale shared across channels to preserve chromatic differences. (6) RGB error evaluates overall appearance. We aggregate these errors into scores qₜ:
