    qₜ=(∑_k∈Kwₖe_t,k)/(∑_k∈Kwₖ),

    		(2)

    where K indexes mask, depth, orientation, albedo, shading, and RGB errors. Corresponding weights wₖ remain fixed across rounds at (2,1,0.5,0.5,1,1), with sensitivity examined through ablations provided in the Supp. Lower scores indicate better agreement and guide candidate selection without gradient-based optimization.

    Evidence-guided diagnosis. Beyond scalar assessment, the VLM combines component errors, rendered passes, source contributions, and LRM to recommend geometric, material, or lighting revisions. For an underlit wall, it examines orientation, occlusion, albedo, and relevant source contributions. Geometric discrepancies motivate structural revisions, whereas consistent geometry and albedo direct attention to lighting. Each recommendation specifies the discrepancy, proposed revision, and supporting evidence, providing guidance for the subsequent reconstruction round.

    3.5 Memory-assisted Scene Reconstruction Loop

    With enriched evidence, LRM, and the Verifier defined, we integrate them into a closed loop of perception, generation, execution/rendering, and verification. At round t, the perception module combines the input image I, fixed evidence E, and memory Mₜ into a scene context comprising structural cues, lighting hypotheses, and unresolved discrepancies. Conditioned on this context and preceding scene code, the Generator jointly reasons about structure and illumination to produce t-step code Cₜ and a light source state update ΔSₜ. After checking state consistency and source correspondence, we obtain

    (Cₜ,ΔSₜ)=VLM(I,E,Mₜ,Cₜ₋₁), S̃ₜ=Apply(Sₜ,ΔSₜ).

    		(3)

    The generated geometry and materials are combined with S̃ₜ under fixed camera and rendering settings. Blender ℝ then renders the candidate scene as

    Yₜ=ℝ(Cₜ,S̃ₜ),

    		(4)

    including RGB, masks, depth, surface information, albedo, diffuse shading, and individual light sources and world-illumination contributions. Masks and depth show scene layout and occlusion. Albedo and shading help separate material color from lighting, while light source attribution indicates which region it affects. The Verifier assesses these outputs against the reference evidence, producing the rubric score qₜ and evidence-guided recommendations.

    Following each valid round, we reorganize the light source state and append a record hₜ containing the diagnosis, implemented changes, scores, and references to archived outputs:

    Mₜ₊₁=(S̃ₜ, Hₜ\mathbin∥hₜ),

    		(5)

    where ∥ denotes history concatenation. The updated memory guides perception and generation in the next round, allowing subsequent reasoning to build on previous evidence and outcomes.

    Since revisions may improve some factors while degrading others, we select

    t^*=\arg\min_t∈T_validqₜ

    		(6)

    over completed valid rounds after T iterations. We return (C_t^*,S̃_t^*) together, preserving the correspondence between the selected executable scene and its lighting state. This closed loop connects evidence, diagnosis, and persistent memory to support coherent refinement of geometry, materials, and illumination.

    4 Experiments

    Our experiments compare reconstruction quality with recently blooming image-to-code methods, examine the roles of visual evidence and Lighting Reasoning Memory, and assess generalizable downstream application and hard cases.

    4.1 Implementation Details

    Framework development.

    We load external modules (i.e., SAM3, VGGT, Marigold, LUMEN) on two NVIDIA 4090-48G GPUs, and use GPT-6-Astra [24] as the Generator/Verifier VLM via API. All reconstructions are done with 10 rounds. We also examine our framework under different VLMs in the Supplementary materials.

    Data.

    We evaluate on 32 images drawn from diverse benchmarks from robotics, relighting and image enhancement, comprising 10 from Hypersim [25], 4 from LuxRemix [16], 10 from BAID [20], 7 from MIT-Adobe FiveK [1], and 1 from RoboDojo [5] with complex lighting conditions, diverse geometry and materials. The whole testing set contains 17 real photographs and 15 synthetic images, covering 22 indoor and 10 outdoor scenes.

    Metrics.

    We evaluate source-view consistency using PSNR [31], SSIM [30], LPIPS [37], and DreamSim [7]. Following SceneRig [19], we assess 3D reconstruction quality from the source view and nearby views at ±15^∘. By orbiting the camera around the world vertical axis through a pivot located four scene units along the original camera’s viewing direction, we use GPT-6-Astra as a judge to compute the mean-centered Bradley-Terry scores among these rendered pairs, with higher scores indicating stronger relative preference.

    Compared methods.

    We compare with recent SoTA image-to-code reconstruction methods, including VIGA [35], 3DCodeVerse [8], SceneRig [19]. All these methods use GPT-6-Astra as the backbone VLM with the same loop iterations and API. We additionally compare GPT-6-Sol with Codex [22] harness.

    4.2 Image-to-Code Reconstruction

    Qualitative results.

    Fig. 4 compares reconstructions across diverse geometry and lighting conditions. Our method better captures window–foreground contrast, localized illumination around bedside lamps, and combined window and ceiling lighting in the hall. It also preserves furniture arrangement and foreground animal composition, while competing methods exhibit layout distortions, simplified geometry, or mismatched illumination, supporting joint reasoning about scene structure, materials, and lighting. Notably, our method infers unseen light sources and structures through their illumination effects. In the fifth row, it reproduces striped shadows across the bedroom wall and bedding while preserving their spatial relationships, whereas competing methods miss these shadows or misinterpret the layout. The cast shadows in the last row further illustrate lighting reasoning beyond appearance, enabling more faithful image-to-code reconstruction. We present more visualized results under nearby views in the Supp.

    Hard case verification.

    Fig. 5 compares reconstructions of a scene with a prominent diagonal cast shadow. While competing methods distort or omit this shadow, LightHarness better reproduces its spatial extent while preserving the surrounding building structure. This result supports the value of enriched evidence and persistent lighting memory in relating shadow patterns to scene geometry and illumination, enabling more faithful image-to-code reconstruction under challenging lighting.

    Quantitative results.

    Table 1 shows that our method achieves the best PSNR, LPIPS, and DreamSim among the compared methods. Relative to the recent SoTA method, VIGA, LightHarness improves PSNR by 0.75 dB and reduces DreamSim by 10.7%, indicating our superiority in both pixel-level fidelity and perceptual similarity. The VLM-based evaluation and user preference further demonstrate our advantages at the scene level, ranking it first in all criteria covering completeness, layout, and appearance. These consistent preferences support the effectiveness of our framework in reconstructing scene composition and visual appearance.

    Inference cost.

    The latency mainly includes evidence extraction, GPT API and Blender rendering in the generation-verification loop. For a 768×576 image, these three parts cost 4.5 minutes, 118.8 minutes, and 1.1 minutes respectively. The latency is comparable with other baselines (VIGA [35] for 71.2 minutes and 3DCodeVerse [8] for 126.3 minutes). The critical bottleneck is API invocation, while other parts are relatively efficient with less than 6 minutes on two 4090-48 GB GPUs.

    User Study.

    We invite 29 participants to rank the reconstructed scenes according to (1) scene structure fidelity and (2) lighting appearance fidelity, using the reference images as guidance. We achieve the first-place preference rate on both criteria, indicating stronger human preference for its reconstruction of scene structure and illumination.

    4.3 Ablation Studies

    We conduct quantitative and qualitative ablation experiments to demonstrate the effectiveness of each design in our framework in Fig. 6 and Table 2.

    w/o enriched evidence.

    We disable the light and geometric evidence in Sec. 3.2, observing significant reconstruction error. As shown in Fig. 6 (c), the agent misjudges the wall light’s distance from the surface and misses background illumination.

    w/o geometric rubric.

    Discarding explicit constraints on geometry features leads to incomplete scene light reconstruction, as shown in Fig. 6 (d).

    w/o lighting rubric.

    Discarding lighting measurement produces wrong light source shapes and mismatched local illumination strength as shown in Fig. 6 (e).

    w/o lighting reasoning memory.

    We compare our full model with a variant that retains only current scene code and parameter values. Without memory, background illumination is missed as shown in Fig. 6 (f), highlighting the value of explicitly organizing light source hypotheses and diagnostic history across iterations.

    4.4 Generalizable Applications

    Building upon the precise executable scenes we reconstruct, our framework supports diverse downstream applications, including scene texture editing, harmonious object insertion, versatile relighting, and degraded illumination restoration. We also demonstrate that our rendered edits can combine with the frontier generative model, GPT-Image [23] to produce more physically realistic results. Note that simply applying generative models is hard to achieve precise physical modeling like lighting interaction with complex shadows and textures. Our integration with GPT-Image enables advanced editing ability.

    Material and Texture Editing.

    Our method can perform exact texture editing with multiple references in Fig. 7.

    Versatile relighting with flexible control.

    Our method achieves superior light control relative to simply applying GPT-Image, as shown in Fig. 8 and Fig. 9.

    Harmonious object insertion.

    Our framework enables physically realistic object insertion as shown in Fig. 10.

    5 Conclusion, Limitation and Future Work

    We propose LightHarness, a VLM-based agentic framework that integrates explicit lighting reasoning and persistent light-source memory into image-to-code 3D reconstruction. Complementary geometric, intrinsic, and illumination evidence guides reconstruction, while rubric-based assessment and VLM diagnosis support iterative refinement. Lighting reasoning memory preserves source identities, evidence, semantic relationships, and revision history, enabling coherent reasoning across rounds. Quantitative and qualitative results demonstrate our improved reconstruction fidelity under challenging shadows and complex illumination compared to recent SoTA methods. Based on the accurate programmatic scene reconstruction, our framework enables rich applications, including relighting, harmonious object insertion, material and texture editing with plausible physical modeling.

    Limitation.

    Our framework remains limited in inferring unseen scene objects from sparse and overlapping shadow cues. As shown in Fig. 11, it fails to reconstruct the off-frame people and sign suggested by their shadows, leaving the corresponding shadow patterns incomplete.

    Future work. We will incorporate complex scene examples through in-context learning and post-train open-source VLMs on challenging datasets to strengthen reasoning about unseen objects and their interactions with light. Reducing token budget is also meaningful. We argue that projecting visual representation back to executable codes is a highly promising direction in this field.

    LLM Usage Statement

    OpenAI Codex was used to assist with basic code generation, manuscript organization and language editing. Codex was not used to formulate research ideas, design the method or experiments, or draw scientific conclusions. All AI-assisted text was manually reviewed and revised by the authors. All AI-assisted code was inspected, executed, and verified for correctness, and the resulting visualizations and preprocessed data were checked against the source data and expected outputs. The authors take full responsibility for the final content, including all text, code, results, and claims.

    （参考文献见原文。）

item.title: 「模型知道的比它画出来的多」可能是个统计假象：这篇指出读出难易与「有没有隐藏知识」是两件事 ｜ Probing Physics in Motion Diffusion Models Against Their Own Estimate
item.description:
一句话：从激活里解码物理比从输入输出解码更容易，但这只说明「读出有多容易」。

要点：

  • 要挑战的结论：近期研究称视频扩散模型「知道的比展示出来的多」——物理属性从它们的**激活**里解码，比从输入或输出里解码更准
  • 反驳很干净：扩散模型本来就用这些同样的激活来计算干净样本估计，因此这种比较实际测的是「**读出有多容易**」，而不是「模型是否藏了什么」
  • 作者因此在运动学纹理等设定下，用模型**自己的估计**作为对照，去检验是否真的存在被隐藏的物理知识

为什么值得看：这条治的是整个「世界模型懂物理吗」讨论里最常见的方法论漏洞：拿更容易的探针当证据。做工程判断时，它能帮你分辨论文里哪些结论站得住、哪些只是读出效应。

中文摘要：近期研究声称视频扩散模型「知道的比它展示出来的多」：物理属性从模型的激活中解码，比从输入或输出中解码更准确。这篇对此提出一个干净的质疑：扩散模型本来就是用同一批激活来计算干净样本估计的，因此这种比较实际测量的是「读出（readout）有多容易」，而不是「模型是否藏了额外信息」——模型是否隐藏了知识，是另一个问题。作者因此以模型自身的估计作为对照，在运动学纹理等设定下检验是否真的存在被隐藏的物理知识。对每天读「世界模型懂不懂物理」类论文的人，这是一把有用的方法学尺子。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-11-19

本期推送：2026-11-20

Probing Physics in Motion Diffusion Models
Against Their Own Estimate

Abstract

Recent studies report that video diffusion models “know more than they show”: physical properties decode better from their activations than from their inputs or outputs. But a diffusion model computes its clean-sample estimate from those same activations, so such a comparison measures how easily a readout extracts the information. Whether the model hides anything is a separate question. We set out to find hidden physical knowledge in kinematic text-to-motion diffusion models, where the physics of every intermediate estimate can be computed exactly, and recorded every layer along the sampling trajectories of MDM (two checkpoints) and MotionDiffuse. Against the usual baselines the layers do look ahead of the model’s own estimate on balance and flight. With every readout tuned the same way, the estimate closes the gap: for balance and flight, adding a layer gains at most 0.01, a size that a positive control shows we would detect. The fall rate of jumps is the one clear exception. Early in denoising, MDM’s layers add about 0.08 in R² (up to 0.11 in a refit) that the estimate does not yet show, and the gain fades as sampling proceeds; on MotionDiffuse it is small and not robust. The estimate also flags floating samples without training, but aborting them saves under a tenth of the compute. In a video model, plausibility that linear probes miss in Wan 2.1’s clean latent becomes readable after one fixed nonlinearity.

1 Introduction

Text-to-motion models turn a sentence into seconds of fluent human movement [(Guo et al., 2022; Tevet et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2023; Guo et al., 2024; Rempe et al., 2026)]. Most are kinematic. They output joint positions and rotations directly, with no simulator, so whatever physics they produce is learned from motion capture and never enforced. Physics-based generators instead move a simulated character, so gravity and contact hold by construction [(Peng et al., 2018; Tessler et al., 2024)]. Kinematic models’ most visible failures are therefore physical: bodies hover above the ground, feet slide while planted, and jumps do not fall as they should. Most remedies act from outside the generator. They project samples through a physics simulator [(Yuan et al., 2023)], condition on physical parameters [(Watanabe et al., 2025)], model contact and body forces explicitly [(Xing et al., 2026)], or optimize the sampling noise [(Stölzle et al., 2026)]. Whether the generator itself represents the physics it gets wrong is a separate and useful question: if the physics is present inside the model but lost on the way out, the internal signal could flag failing samples before compute is spent finishing them.

For video diffusion models, recent work answers yes. Physical quantities are linearly decodable from transformer activations and are reported to be built inside the model rather than inherited from its input [(Kneifl et al., 2026)]. Plausibility is decodable from the internal states of models whose outputs violate physics, a finding its authors summarize as models that “know more than they show” [(Esmati et al., 2026)]. Probes on denoising features are used to prune implausible samples early [(Tang et al., 2026)].

These conclusions rest on a comparison between a probe on internal activations and a readout of what the model takes in or puts out. In a diffusion model, the estimate of the clean sample at each step is computed from the activations at that step together with the noisy input (and, in MotionDiffuse, the text), so it cannot carry information about the outcome that they lack (Section 3.3). A probe that beats a readout of the estimate shows only that the information is easier for that probe to use in the activations [(Xu et al., 2020)]. The output may still contain all of it. How much such a gap means depends on three things: whether the two readouts are equally flexible and equally well tuned; whether the gap holds within a prompt, or only reflects which prompt was given; and whether there was enough training data for the comparison to be stable.

We set out to show that a motion diffusion model, too, knows more than it shows, and to use that knowledge to stop failing samples early. Text-to-motion diffusion suits the test, because all three conditions can be checked: the physics of a motion follows exactly from its joint positions, the models we study expose a clean-motion estimate at every step (MDM predicts it, [Tevet et al., 2023]; MotionDiffuse computes it from its noise prediction, [Zhang et al., 2022]), and sampling is cheap enough to record thousands of complete trajectories. We record every transformer layer along each model’s own sampling path, for 6,000 motions from 250 prompts with two MDM checkpoints and 3,000 with MotionDiffuse, and compute dynamic balance (the extrapolated center of mass relative to the area of foot support; [Hof et al., 2005]), flight, gravity during flight, and floating from the final motions. Two choices were made along the way. We added a set of jump-heavy prompts once it was clear that the main prompts contain too few falling bodies to test gravity, and we redefined “airborne” after finding that the first definition counted hovering and crawling as flight (Appendix C). The result is not the one we set out to show.

Contributions.

  • •

    Physics is readable early. A fifth of the way through denoising, linear probes on the layers already recover the final motion’s dynamic balance and flight (R²=0.84 and AUC 0.97 on the 50-step model), stably across seeds and on held-out prompts (Section 4.2).

  • •

    The apparent hidden knowledge is a readout effect. Standard baselines make the layers look better informed than the estimate. Read with equal care, the estimate matches them. For balance and flight, on all three models, adding a layer gains at most 0.01, and a positive control shows that the protocol would detect a gain of that size. Floating behaves the same on the jump prompts; only in the smaller main data sets does the layer help (Section 4.3). With too little training data the comparison can flip, which explains a pilot study that pointed the other way (Section 4.4).

  • •

    One exception, and it fades. Only for the fall rate of jumps do the layers know more. A fifth of the way through denoising, MDM’s layers add about 0.08 in R² (up to 0.11 in a refit) to the best readout of the estimate, and on the 50-step model the gain survives every control we applied. It fades as sampling proceeds and the estimate catches up. On MotionDiffuse the same gain is small and not robust (Section 4.3).

  • •

    The output is enough for early warning. Decoded partway through sampling, MDM’s own estimate flags samples that will float, without training and about as well as a trained probe on the layers. Aborting them saves under a tenth of the compute, because floating affects only 9 to 18% of samples and concentrates in a few prompts (Section 4.5).

  • •

    A related issue in video. A linear probe at chance is the main evidence that plausibility is absent from the clean VAE latent of a video diffusion model [(Esmati et al., 2026)]. One fixed, training-free nonlinearity, the size of local frame-to-frame change, makes it readable from the same latent: a linear readout of it reaches 78% pairwise accuracy on IntPhys, and 80% together with the grid features (Section 4.6).

  • •

    What actually fails. Once bodies that hover without falling are separated out, MDM’s jumps fall at close to the right rate in the median. The common failure is floating, and on test captions the original 1000-step checkpoint floats about twice as often as the 50-step one (Section 4.1).

    • Section 5 turns these findings into five checks for probing studies that claim a generator knows more than it shows.

    2 Related Work

    Text-to-motion generation.

    HumanML3D [(Guo et al., 2022)] established the standard benchmark and a redundant pose representation with root velocities, joint positions, velocities and rotations, and binary foot-contact labels. MotionDiffuse [(Zhang et al., 2022)] was among the first diffusion models for text-to-motion generation, predicting the noise at every step, and MDM [(Tevet et al., 2023)] applies a transformer diffusion model directly to this representation and predicts the clean motion. Tokenized approaches quantize motion and model the token sequence, autoregressively [(Zhang et al., 2023)] or with masked modeling over residual codebooks [(Guo et al., 2024)], and MLD [(Chen et al., 2023a)] runs diffusion in the latent space of a motion autoencoder. Kimodo [(Rempe et al., 2026)] is a recent large kinematic motion diffusion model trained on studio motion capture and designed to reduce floating and foot skating. We study MDM and MotionDiffuse because both work directly in pose space, so their clean-motion estimate at every step can be scored with the same physics as the final output.

    Kinematic and physics-based motion generation.

    The models above are kinematic: they generate poses directly, and floating, foot sliding and ground penetration are widely reported for them. Character animation has long repaired the most common of these artifacts after generation, from predicted foot contacts: PFNN edits each generated pose with a simple two-joint inverse kinematics along the contact labels to remove foot sliding [(Holden et al., 2017)], earlier work constrains heel and toe velocity to zero during contact by optimizing in an autoencoder’s hidden space [(Holden et al., 2016)], and the Neural State Machine predicts contact labels for feet, hands and hips for use in inverse-kinematics post-processing [(Starke et al., 2019)]. Such fixes keep planted feet in place, but they cannot make an airborne body fall at the right rate or tell a floating body from a jump. Physics-based controllers instead generate motion inside a simulator, where gravity and contact hold by construction, at the cost of learning a control policy [(Peng et al., 2018; Tessler et al., 2024)]. Hybrids keep a kinematic generator and make its output physical with a simulator: PhysDiff [(Yuan et al., 2023)] projects intermediate samples through a simulated motion-imitation policy during diffusion, and CLoSD [(Tevet et al., 2024)] pairs a kinematic diffusion planner with a simulated tracking controller; related systems drive humanoid robots [(Wang et al., 2026)]. Other methods make a kinematic model’s output more physical without simulating it. SimDiff [(Watanabe et al., 2025)] conditions a frozen MDM on environment parameters learned from simulator-augmented data. PhysibleMDM [(Stölzle et al., 2026)] optimizes the diffusion noise of a frozen model at inference time against kinematic and inverse-dynamics feasibility measures, and InterPhys [(Xing et al., 2026)] models human-object, human-scene and internal body forces with soft force- and torque-balance constraints. Guidance steers the sampling of motion diffusion models toward spatial constraints [(Karunratanakul et al., 2023; Xie et al., 2024)], and noise optimization adjusts the diffusion noise of a frozen model against any loss defined on the generated motion [(Karunratanakul et al., 2024)]. All of these act on a model’s inputs, outputs, sampling or environment. We ask what a kinematic generator represents internally about the physics it does not enforce, a question that does not arise for physics-based generators, where our labels hold by construction; our early-warning experiment measures how much an internal or decoded signal can save.

    Physics inside generative models.

    Linear probes reveal scene geometry such as depth in latent image diffusion models [(Chen et al., 2023b)]. In video encoders, speed and acceleration become linearly accessible at intermediate depth, with control tasks and attentive probes as comparisons [(Joseph et al., 2026)]. Layerwise probing has since been compared across video foundation models with different pretraining [(Punzo et al., 2026)] and extended to camera motion, intuitive physics and anomalies [(Musa et al., 2026)], and the probe direction at such layers has been used to steer an encoder’s physical expectations [(Alam, 2026)]. For video diffusion transformers, [Kneifl et al. (2026)] fit ridge probes to activations of forward-noised simulated videos and report that speed, momentum and gravity are decodable well beyond what ridge probes recover from the noisy input latent; for gravity the margin persists as the input becomes clean, while for rolling speed the clean latent eventually carries the information. [Esmati et al. (2026)] invert real videos through the model and find plausibility linearly decodable from mean-pooled transformer states, while a linear probe on the clean VAE latent is at chance. [Tang et al. (2026)] use probes on denoising features to prune implausible video candidates early, comparing against random selection, best-of-N selection, preference tuning and a likelihood-based scorer. In image diffusion, CNN probes on early denoising signals predict the quality of the final image [(Cui et al., 2026)]. Similar probes outperform an off-the-shelf evaluator applied to the decoded clean estimate [(Guo et al., 2026)], and in diffusion driving planners, first-step state probes select better trajectories than a privileged score of the clean preview’s true quality in three of four settings [(Zhang et al., 2026)]. Without probes, video models that predict masked content in a learned representation space show violation-of-expectation effects on intuitive-physics benchmarks including IntPhys, while pixel-space video prediction stays closer to chance [(Garrido et al., 2025)]. [Guo et al. (2026)] and [Zhang et al. (2026)] do compare probes with the clean estimate, but they read it with an off-the-shelf evaluator or score it by its true quality. None compares the internal probe with an equally flexible, equally tuned readout of the model’s own clean-sample estimate, measures what the layer adds to that estimate, or reports how that comparison depends on training-set size. These are the comparisons we add, together with within-prompt scoring for generated samples; [Esmati et al. (2026)] do score pairs within a scene, which we adopt for our video test. Unlike [Kneifl et al. (2026)] and [Esmati et al. (2026)], we also record along the model’s own sampling trajectory rather than from noised simulated videos or inverted real ones.

    Probing methodology.

    Linear probes [(Alain & Bengio, 2016)] measure what a fixed readout can decode, not what a model uses or contains [(Belinkov, 2022)]. Control tasks separate a representation’s content from what a probe can memorize [(Hewitt & Liang, 2019)]. An information-theoretic view argues that the best-performing probe should be used, shows with the data-processing inequality that a contextual representation carries no more information about a property than the sentence it was computed from, and therefore measures the gain over a control representation, noting that ease of extraction still lacks a formal definition [(Pimentel et al., 2020b)]; minimum-description-length probing makes the dependence on probe complexity and data size explicit [(Voita & Titov, 2020)], and Pareto probing reports accuracy against probe complexity rather than at one capacity [(Pimentel et al., 2020a)]. Usable (V-) information [(Xu et al., 2020)] resolves the tension between these views: Shannon information cannot grow under processing, but the information a given family of readouts can extract can. Conditional probing [(Hewitt et al., 2021)] applies this to ask what a representation adds beyond a baseline representation, by comparing a readout of the baseline with a readout of both. Amnesic probing asks a different question, whether a model uses a property, by removing it and measuring the change in behavior [(Elazar et al., 2021)]; we do not test use. Our comparison is a conditional probe whose baseline is the model’s own clean-sample estimate, which is a known deterministic function of the probed activations and the noisy input (and, in MotionDiffuse, the text). That fixes the direction of the Shannon comparison and leaves usable information under a stated readout family as the quantity to measure (Section 3.3).

    3 Setup

    3.1 Model, sampling and recording

    We study MDM [(Tevet et al., 2023)], a kinematic diffusion model: a transformer encoder (8 layers, width 512) with a CLIP text encoder, using two official HumanML3D checkpoints: the 50-step model and the original 1000-step model. Both generate 120 frames (6 s at 20 fps) in the HumanML3D representation [(Guo et al., 2022)], with classifier-free guidance at scale 2.5. At six denoising steps, evenly spaced from the first to the last, we record the output of every transformer layer at every fourth frame (dropping the condition token), the noisy input xₜ, and the model’s clean-motion estimate x̂₀ with its decoded joints. Guidance runs a conditional and an unconditional pass; we record the activations of the conditional pass and the guided estimate that the sampler uses. “20% of denoising” denotes the second recorded step (step 10 of 50, or 200 of 1000). Figure 2 summarizes what we record and compare.

    A second model.

    To test whether the results depend on MDM’s design, we repeat the main analyses on MotionDiffuse [(Zhang et al., 2022)], also kinematic but different where it matters. It predicts the noise rather than the clean motion, so its estimate x̂₀=(xₜ-√1-ᾱₜ ε̂)/√ᾱₜ is computed from its prediction and the noisy input; it uses no guidance; and its 8 transformer layers (width 512, linear attention, one token per frame) receive the text in every layer, through cross-attention and stylization blocks, rather than as a token. We use its official HumanML3D checkpoint and sampler (1000 DDPM steps), the same prompts, seeds, frames and recorded steps as for MDM (20% of denoising is step 200), and choose its layers by the same rule as MDM’s (Section 3.3; layer 3 for balance, layer 6 for flight and gravity). Its noise schedule is linear where MDM’s is cosine, so a given fraction of denoising is noisier for MotionDiffuse (Table 9). Since the text reaches every layer, its estimate is a function of its activations, the noisy input and the text, (a_ℓ,xₜ,u) in the notation of Section 3.3, so for this model the bound of Section 3.3 includes the text, which is one reason we also test the text directly.

    Prompts and runs.

    The prompt set combines 64 curated prompts (everyday locomotion, jumps and hops, balance-challenging actions, upper-body actions) with 186 captions sampled from the HumanML3D test split, 250 in total, and each prompt is sampled 4 times: 1,000 motions per run. We run each model with three seeds: 6,000 motions from the two MDM checkpoints and 3,000 from MotionDiffuse. Because few of these motions contain flight, we also run every model on a jump-heavy prompt set with three seeds: the 14 curated jump, hop, leap and skip prompts plus one caption from every HumanML3D test motion whose caption names one of these actions, 245 distinct prompts sampled 4 times each (2,940 motions per model). A pilot used only the curated prompts (256 motions), every second frame, and a single held-out set of 12 prompts.

    3.2 Physical labels

    All labels are computed from joint positions, with y the vertical axis, both for the final motion and for the clean-motion estimate at each recorded step.

    Center of mass, contact and support.

    The center of mass is cₜ=∑ₛmₛ\tfrac12(p_a(s),t+p_b(s),t), with standard segment mass fractions mₛ placed at segment midpoints, where a(s) and b(s) are the joints at the two ends of segment s[(Winter, 2009)]. An ankle (toe) joint is in contact when it is lower than 12 cm (6 cm) and moves less per frame than HumanML3D’s contact threshold. The support region Sₜ is the convex hull of the contacting foot joints on the ground plane, padded by 4 cm.

    Balance.

    Dynamic balance uses the extrapolated center of mass [(Hof et al., 2005)],

    x^XCoMₜ=cˣᶻₜ+ċˣᶻₜ/ω₀, ω₀=√g/h, g=9.81 m/s²,

    		(1)

    where h is the motion’s median center-of-mass height. The dynamic balance margin is the signed distance from x^XCoMₜ to the boundary of Sₜ, positive inside; the static balance margin uses cˣᶻₜ instead. Both are undefined without foot contact. The extrapolated center of mass routinely leaves the support region during normal stepping, so we treat the margins as continuous quantities rather than failure labels (Figure 3a,b). They are kinematic quantities; a test of physical feasibility would need the center of pressure or inverse dynamics.

    Floating, flight and gravity.

    The lowest-foot height is the height of the lowest foot joint, and a frame is in flight when no foot is in contact. A frame is airborne when every foot joint is above its contact height and no knee, wrist or the pelvis is within 15 cm of the floor, so that crawling and cartwheels do not count as airborne (Appendix C). Over each airborne stretch of at least 0.2 s we fit c_y(t)=a₀+a₁t+a₂t² to the center-of-mass height. Ballistic flight requires the flight gravityĝ=-2a₂ to equal g=9.81 m/s², a test that needs no calibration (Figure 3c,d). Every frame of the stretch carries its ĝ. Because in the main data most airborne frames lie in stretches that barely fall (Section 4.3), this flight gravity mixes two questions, and for probing we also split it at the floating cut-off below: whether an airborne frame belongs to a floating or a falling stretch (floats or falls, scored by AUC), and the fitted gravity of falling stretches alone (the fall rate).

    Per-sample failures.

    An airborne stretch with ĝ<2 m/s² is floating: the body is off the ground and unsupported, but barely falls. For each sample, the floating rate is the share of frames in floating stretches, and the raised-contact rate is the share of contact frames whose lowest foot is higher than 5 cm. Two further per-sample rates serve only as inputs to the early-warning readouts (Section 3.4): the mean |ĝ-g| over stretches that do fall, and the share of support frames with a negative dynamic balance margin.

    3.3 What the model shows, and a fair comparison

    In our data, a linear probe on MDM’s last layer predicts the final motion’s dynamic balance better than the balance computed from the model’s own estimate at the same step (Table 2). It is tempting to conclude that the model knows how balanced the motion will be and fails to show it. But the estimate is computed from that layer, so everything it contains about balance has passed through the layer. The probe’s advantage can mean only that the layer holds the information in a form a linear readout finds easy, while the estimate holds it in a form that needs a nonlinear readout or a computed quantity. To call the knowledge hidden, a readout of the layer has to beat an equally flexible readout of the estimate, or add to it. The rest of this section makes the argument precise.

    At each step the model shows its clean-motion estimate x̂₀⁽ᵏ⁾: 263 features per frame, from which joints and every label above follow exactly. We number MDM’s encoder layers 0 to 7. Each layer’s output is a deterministic function of the previous layer’s, and the output of layer 7, the last, is mapped to the conditional estimate by a fixed linear projection at every frame. Guidance combines this conditional estimate with an unconditional one, which depends only on xₜ and the step. Write a_ℓ⁽ᵏ⁾ for the full conditional output of layer ℓ at step k (every token, including the condition token), xₜ for that step’s noisy input, and u for the text condition. The guided estimate is then a function of (a_ℓ⁽ᵏ⁾,xₜ) for every ℓ, and the activations are a function of (xₜ,u). For any label y of the final motion, the data-processing inequality therefore gives

    I(y; x̂₀⁽ᵏ⁾) ≤ I(y; a_ℓ⁽ᵏ⁾,xₜ) ≤ I(y; xₜ,u).

    		(2)

    The estimate cannot carry information about the outcome that the activations and the noisy input lack. The same argument bounds the video studies of Section 2 from the other side: under forward noising the activations are functions of the clean latent, the text prompt and noise drawn independently of both and of the label, and under deterministic inversion they are functions of the clean latent and the prompt alone, so no layer can carry more information about the label than the clean latent together with the prompt.

    Shannon information therefore cannot separate these representations. What differs is how much of the information a given readout can use. For a family V of readouts, the V-information I_V(X→y) is the reduction in the best expected loss on y that a readout in V achieves by seeing X[(Xu et al., 2020)]. Unlike Shannon information, it can grow under processing, which is how a probe on the layer can beat a readout of the estimate. The question that bears on hidden knowledge is what the layer adds to the estimate [(Hewitt et al., 2021)],

    I_V(a_ℓ⁽ᵏ⁾→y|x̂₀⁽ᵏ⁾) = H_V(y|x̂₀⁽ᵏ⁾)-H_V(y|x̂₀⁽ᵏ⁾,a_ℓ⁽ᵏ⁾),

    		(3)

    which we measure as the gain in R² (or AUC) from adding the layer to a readout of the estimate. For squared-error readouts, once the baseline R² is fixed, the two determine each other:

    Proposition 1.

    Let V predict Gaussians ℕ(f(·),σ²), with f from a regression class and σ>0 free, and let the class on (x̂₀⁽ᵏ⁾,a_ℓ⁽ᵏ⁾) contain every function in the class on x̂₀⁽ᵏ⁾. Writing R²_X for the best R² the class reaches from X,

    I_V(a_ℓ⁽ᵏ⁾→y|x̂₀⁽ᵏ⁾) = \tfrac12\log(1-R²_x̂₀⁽ᵏ⁾)/(1-R²_x̂₀⁽ᵏ⁾,a_ℓ⁽ᵏ⁾) ≥ 0.

    		(4)

    For a fixed baseline, the gain in R² is therefore a monotone transform of the conditional usable information (proof in Appendix G), and in population it cannot be negative: a negative measured gain only reflects fitting the larger readout on finite data. Its value depends on the family, so we report it for linear readouts, a fixed MLP and readouts tuned on held-out prompts, test whether it survives within a prompt, and vary the amount of training data. Our per-frame probes see only the conditional pass, without the condition token, and one recorded frame at a time, so strictly they could see less than the estimate. On the 50-step model, adding the condition token gains at most 0.004 for balance, flight and floating (Appendix A).

    Readouts.

    For each label and recorded step we compare six readouts, each predicting the final motion’s per-frame label:

  • •

    Explicit: the same label computed from the estimate’s joints, with a linear calibration fit on the training folds (for the flight AUC, the raw value);

  • •

    Estimate, linear: a ridge probe on the estimate’s 263 features, the usual baseline in probing studies;

  • •

    Estimate, MLP: a small MLP on everything the estimate shows, that is its 263 features plus the labels computed from it (Section 3.2, with foot contacts and foot sliding speed) and indicators for undefined values;

  • •

    Layer, linear and Layer, MLP: ridge and the same MLP on one layer’s 512 activations at the frame (its slice of a_ℓ);

  • •

    Estimate + layer, MLP: the same MLP on both, which asks whether the layer adds anything to what the estimate shows.

    • We also report a ridge probe on the noisy input xₜ. Ridge probes standardize their inputs and choose the penalty from {1,10,…,10⁴} by efficient leave-one-out cross-validation on the training frames. The MLP has two hidden layers of 256 units with ReLU and dropout 0.1, and is trained with AdamW (learning rate 10⁻³, weight decay 10⁻⁴) with early stopping on 15% of the training prompts. The layer is fixed per label as the one with the best mean linear score at 20% of denoising: layer 7 for both balance measures, 6 for flight, and 5 for gravity and its two parts, on both MDM checkpoints. This choice favors the layer in a standalone comparison; for what the layer adds to the estimate, we also test every layer and all layers together (Section 4.3).

    Tuned readouts on pooled seeds.

    The fixed MLP and the leave-one-out penalty (which validates on frames of motions seen in training) could each favor one side. We therefore repeat the comparison with every run of a checkpoint pooled, three seeds and 3,000 motions, under five folds grouped by prompt across seeds, and with every readout tuned on a validation split of 15% of the training prompts. The families are ridge, with the penalty chosen from 10⁻¹ to 10⁶; an MLP family that adds a linear map to an MLP, so that it contains the linear readout, with five configurations (64 to 1024 hidden units, one or two hidden layers, dropout 0.1 or 0.3, weight decay 10⁻⁴ to 10⁻²); and, as the tuned readout, whichever of the two has the lower validation error. The same procedure reads the estimate’s 263 raw features alone, everything the estimate shows, the layer, and estimate and layer together. The conditional gain uses a readout of estimate and layer that may fall back to the estimate alone: among the candidates for both inputs and for the estimate alone, it keeps the one with the lowest validation error, so that the larger input cannot lower the score merely by being harder to fit. Confidence intervals resample prompts with replacement (1,000 replicates, the same draw for every readout). They do not include training variance, which we measure by refitting with two further validation splits and initializations. We report many intervals (targets, models, layers and steps) without correcting for multiplicity, read them as descriptive, and draw conclusions only from patterns that hold across models, layers and scores. The analysis was not preregistered: the tuned readouts, the jump-heavy runs, the split of flight gravity and the second model were added after the first results (Appendix B).

    Evaluation.

    All readouts share five folds grouped by prompt, so no test prompt is seen in training. We report R² for continuous labels and ROC-AUC for flight and for floats or falls, pooled over all test frames. Since physics differs greatly between prompts, a readout could score well by recognizing the prompt alone. The within-prompt score removes that possibility: we subtract each prompt’s mean from both target and prediction and report the Pearson correlation of the residuals, which only sample-specific information can raise. A prompt also says when things tend to happen (a jump in the middle of the clip, say), which a per-frame readout could exploit within a prompt. With seeds pooled, the within-prompt-and-frame score removes this as well, by subtracting the mean over the 12 samples of the same prompt at the same frame. The within-prompt score cannot be raised by information that enters a prediction additively through the prompt, and the within-prompt-and-frame score by information that enters additively through the prompt and the frame:

    Proposition 2.

    If a prediction has the form ŷ=f(X)+h(c), with X the readout’s input, where h depends only on the cell c (the prompt, or the prompt and the frame), then its within-cell score equals that of f(X).

    A gain within prompt and frame is therefore information beyond anything the text and the timing of a prompt could add on their own (proof in Appendix G); interactions between the text and the estimate are tested separately, by giving the readout the text itself (Section 4.3). To see how the comparison depends on data, we also retrain the linear layer probe and the explicit calibration on random subsets of 13 to all (≈200) training prompts per fold, and the tuned readouts with seeds pooled on subsets of 25, 50 and 100, and evaluate on the same test folds.

    3.4 Early warning

    Can a sample that will float be caught partway through sampling and replaced? A sample fails if its final motion has any floating. We compare four strategies and count cost in denoising steps per delivered motion (1 = one full sample): generating once; finish, then filter, which checks the final motion and regenerates if it floats; early abort, which scores the sample at 20% or 40% of denoising and restarts it if the score is high; and early abort followed by the final check. Retries stop after a budget of attempts, and the last attempt is always delivered. The early score is (i) a training-free rule, abort if the decoded estimate already shows floating; (ii) a ridge readout, trained out of fold and set to abort the same share of samples, of everything the estimate shows (its features averaged over frames and its per-sample failure rates), of the frame-averaged activations of one layer (layer 3 of the 50-step model and layer 6 of the 1000-step model, each chosen on the first seed), or of both; (iii) random aborts at the same rate; or (iv) a perfect detector, as a ceiling. All strategies are simulated with the same random draws, on the 6,000 recorded MDM samples. Each already contains its estimate at every recorded step and its final motion, so every decision uses what an online run would see; a retry draws another recorded sample of the same prompt (200 simulated requests per prompt). Strategies that end with the final check are compared at equal delivered failure by varying the budget from 1 to 20 attempts.

    4 Results

    4.1 What goes wrong physically

    When MDM’s bodies leave the ground and fall, they fall at close to the right rate (Table 1): the median fitted gravity on the curated jump prompts is 9.54 to 9.75 m/s2 for the 50-step model and 9.13 to 9.22 m/s2 for the 1000-step model, somewhat slower than real jumps in the processed form of its training data (median 10.33 m/s2, Appendix E). Individual stretches spread widely around these medians (standard deviation 2.24 m/s2 on the jump-heavy runs, against 0.7 to 1.0 m/s2 for real jumps). The common failure is floating. On HumanML3D test captions, 3.8 to 4.7% of the 50-step model’s frames lie in floating stretches, against 8.6 to 9.7% for the 1000-step model. On the curated jump prompts the figures are 0.6 to 0.8% and 4.8 to 9.3%. The raised-contact rate, a foot in contact but more than 5 cm up, follows the same pattern. Part of the floating is implied by the prompt: a person “walking on a balance beam” is generated without a beam and floats in nearly every sample. On test captions the original 1000-step checkpoint floats about twice as often as the 50-step one, in all three seeds and under every threshold setting we tried (Appendix D). On real motion capture the same labels flag floating in 0.09% of frames (Appendix E).

    A typical floating stretch is an ordinary walking pose with the whole body several centimeters off the floor for about half a second, in a motion that touches the floor elsewhere (Figure 1, Appendix C). Our first definition of airborne looked only at the feet, so it fitted such stretches, and stretches supported by the hands or knees, as flight. That made the 1000-step model’s jumps appear to fall far too slowly (medians of 3.75 and 7.55 m/s2 in the two seeds labelled that way), an effect that disappears once floating is separated out.

    4.2 Physics is readable early in denoising

    Linear probes recover the final motion’s physics from the activations well before sampling ends (Figure 4, Table 2). At 20% of denoising, the best layer of the 50-step model reaches R²=0.838±0.001 for dynamic balance, 0.868 for the lowest-foot height and 0.820 for flight gravity, and an AUC of 0.973 for flight. In these data the flight-gravity score mostly reflects whether an airborne body floats or falls (Section 4.3). Layer 7 is the best layer for dynamic balance in all six runs. The result transfers across prompt types: for dynamic balance at 20%, the best layer scores 0.835 on curated prompts and 0.839 on test captions. The 1000-step model is less readable at the same fraction of denoising (0.697 for dynamic balance).

    Taken at face value, the standard comparison suggests hidden knowledge. For dynamic balance, flight and, on the 50-step model, gravity, the best layer beats both the explicit label and the linear probe on the estimate at the same step. For dynamic balance the gap over the explicit label is +0.045 to +0.065 in the three 50-step seeds and +0.018 to +0.060 in the three 1000-step seeds. Only the lowest-foot height, which the estimate shows directly, and static balance on the 50-step model (0.769 against 0.759) favor the explicit label, and flight gravity on the 1000-step model is a tie (0.692 against 0.691).

    4.3 The advantage disappears under a fair readout

    Table 3 and Figure 5 compare the readouts with the three seeds of each model pooled and every readout tuned on held-out prompts (Section 3.3). A first version with one fixed MLP per seed gives the same ordering (Appendix B). For balance and flight the estimate is read as well as the layer: for both balance measures its tuned readout beats the tuned layer, by 0.015 to 0.029 in R² on both MDM checkpoints and by 0.12 and 0.18 on MotionDiffuse, and for flight the estimate ties or leads. Adding the layer to the estimate gains nothing. With the readout that may fall back to the estimate, every interval covers zero or lies below it, across prompts and within prompt and frame, and so does every interval in two refits with other validation splits and initializations, run for dynamic balance on the 50-step model. The layer sweep shows the same for every layer: none adds more than 0.007, and only one interval, for flight at layer 7 of the 1000-step model, barely excludes zero (Figure 6). On MDM, whose conditional estimate is a fixed linear map of layer 7, a gain from that layer could come only from directions the output head discards.

    This null result is not produced by the estimator. Without the fallback, the larger readout scores within 0.003 of the estimate or below it for balance and flight, so the fallback hides no gain there. It keeps the estimate alone in one to five of the five folds (Table 8). On the scale of Proposition 1, the largest balance gain is 0.001 nats, against 0.063 for the fall rate below.

    A positive control shows what the protocol can detect (Table 10). We take the estimate readout’s out-of-fold residual, add noise so that its best linear use would raise R² by 0.005, 0.01 or 0.02 on the squared-error scale, add it to the layer’s activations along a random direction, and rerun the protocol unchanged on the 50-step model. For dynamic balance even the smallest signal is found: the gain is +0.013 [0.009, 0.017], more than the linear amount because the tuned readouts extract more, against +0.000 [-0.001, 0.001] for the real layer. For flight and floating the pooled AUC, near 0.97, barely moves even at 0.02, partly because the readouts are selected by squared error. The within-prompt-and-frame score does find the signal, from 0.005 for flight and from 0.01 for floating on the jump prompts, and on that score the real layer adds nothing (-0.008 and 0.000). For these two targets the evidence for no gain is therefore that score, and a gain below 0.01 for floating could go undetected.

    Two details show where the estimate’s advantage comes from. First, the readout family matters: restricted to linear readouts, the layer does add a little (up to 0.02 on MDM, 0.05 to 0.07 on MotionDiffuse), so part of what the estimate shows needs a nonlinear readout. Second, on MDM the input matters more than the family: from its 263 raw features alone the tuned estimate only ties the tuned layer, and the physics labels computed from it add about 0.02 for dynamic balance (Table 7). On MotionDiffuse the raw features alone already beat the tuned layer, by 0.12 and 0.18 (Table 3), and the labels add nothing. A temporal readout that sees all 30 recorded frames gives the same ordering in all six runs (Appendix A). In the terms of Section 3.3, the usable information the layer adds about balance and flight depends on the readout family, and for the most flexible readouts we tried it is indistinguishable from zero.

    Flight gravity: floating and falling.

    The fitted flight gravity mixes two questions. In the main data most of its labelled frames (76% and 83%) lie in floating stretches, so its score mostly measures whether an airborne body floats or falls, and only 57 and 78 prompts contain falling frames, too few for reliable tuned readouts. We therefore split the target (Section 3.2) and use the jump-heavy runs, in which most labelled frames fall (11,640 and 13,444 frames from 233 and 240 prompts).

    Whether an airborne body floats or falls is visible in the estimate on the jump prompts, where 236 prompts have airborne stretches on the 50-step model. Its tuned readout reaches an AUC of 0.97 on both MDM checkpoints, and no single layer, nor all eight together, adds more than 0.007 in pooled AUC (Figure 6). Across the three fits the layer adds at most 0.004 in pooled AUC, and 0.019 [0.008, 0.030] within prompt in one of them. The layer adds more only in the smaller main data, where just 106 prompts have airborne stretches. There, on the 50-step model, it adds +0.008 [0.001, 0.015] in pooled AUC and +0.054 [0.013, 0.089] in the within-prompt correlation, and in two refits up to 0.014 pooled and 0.08 to 0.11 within prompt and frame.

    The fall rate of the stretches that do fall is the one case in which the layers know more. On the jump prompts of the 50-step model, adding the layer raises R² from 0.35 to 0.43, a gain of +0.077 [0.051, 0.107], or 0.063 nats (Tables 3 and 8, Figure 7), with similar gains within prompt and frame and in two refits. With more training prompts the gain first shrinks and then levels off from 100 prompts on (0.085, then 0.077; Figure 9b). It replicates on the 1000-step model (+0.076 [0.053, 0.096]), though there it is smaller within prompt and frame (+0.021) and with fewer training prompts (Figure 9c), and the layer alone is no longer clearly ahead of the estimate (0.309 against 0.287, an interval that covers zero), so the two carry partly different information. On both MDM checkpoints every layer from 3 to 7 adds 0.06 to 0.08 (Figure 6). The standard comparison overstates even this genuine case: the layer’s ridge probe beats the explicit label by three times the conditional gain on the 50-step model and 1.5 times on the 1000-step model, because the fall rate fitted to a 20% estimate predicts the final one poorly.

    Four checks leave the gain in place. It is not only the layer knowing where a jump is: in 92% of the 11,640 falling frames, from 7,125 falling stretches, the 20% estimate is airborne too, and there the layer still adds +0.069. It is not a weak readout of the estimate’s timing: the estimate’s readout already includes its own fitted fall rate, and a temporal readout over all 30 recorded frames still leaves the layer ahead in every seed (Appendix A). It is not the text: giving the readout the prompt’s CLIP embedding, the model’s own text input, does not help on held-out prompts, and the layer’s gain beyond estimate and text is unchanged. And label noise is not the ceiling: on real motion capture the gravity label’s spread would allow an R² of 0.81 to 0.91 (Appendix E).

    The gain is, however, transient (Figure 8). At 40% of denoising layer 5 still adds 0.043 on both MDM checkpoints (Figure 8d). By 60% no layer adds more than 0.02, and at 80% the interval for layer 5 covers zero, because the estimate’s readout improves faster than the layer’s. A separate layer sweep gives up to about 0.06 at 40%, and the same readout differs by up to 0.016 between that sweep and the step run. At a fifth of the denoising steps, then, MDM’s middle and late layers carry information about how fast a jump will fall that its estimate does not yet show in any form we could read: a step-wise case of a model knowing more than it shows, of the kind the video studies report. Such a gain must vanish by the end of sampling, when the final motion is a function of the estimate, so what the measurement adds is its size and duration: about 0.08 in R², for about two fifths of the trajectory.

    A second model.

    MotionDiffuse (Section 3.1) predicts the noise, receives the text in every layer and uses no guidance, and it gives the same picture for balance and flight. On its main data the tuned estimate beats the tuned layer by 0.12 in R² for dynamic balance and 0.18 for static balance, more than on MDM. Adding any one of its eight layers gains at most 0.001 for dynamic balance, and its chosen layers add nothing for static balance or flight. Floating follows MDM’s pattern: on the main data, where only 50 prompts have airborne stretches, its layers add 0.016 to 0.034 in AUC and the layer alone beats the estimate (0.988 against 0.940), while on its jump prompts (2,940 motions, 235 prompts with such stretches) they add nothing, and the same holds for flight and for the unsplit flight gravity (at most +0.002).

    The fall rate again shows a gain, but a smaller and less stable one. At 20% of denoising (step 200 of 1000), adding layer 6 raises R² from 0.365 to 0.390, +0.025 [0.003, 0.047] (Table 3, Figures 5 and 6). It holds within prompt (+0.022 [0.007, 0.038]), but within prompt and frame its interval covers zero (+0.017 [-0.001, 0.036]), and in two refits with other validation splits and initializations it is +0.022 [0.007, 0.041] and 0, the fallback keeping the estimate in every fold of the second. It again comes from the later layers (layers 5 to 7 add 0.018 to 0.025 and all eight together 0.047, layers 0 to 3 nothing), the text does not explain it (estimate, text and layer together gain the same +0.025 over the estimate as without the text), and it fades with denoising: +0.012 [0.003, 0.022] at 40% and +0.007 [-0.002, 0.016] at 60%.

    At matched noise the gap to MDM is larger still, because the same fraction of denoising is not the same noise level on the two models. At 20% MotionDiffuse’s signal-to-noise ratio is 0.002, against MDM’s 0.10, and it reaches MDM’s range only between 40 and 60% (Table 9). At 60%, with a ratio of 0.24, between MDM’s at 20% (0.10) and 40% (0.52), MotionDiffuse’s gain is +0.007, against MDM’s +0.077 and +0.043 at those steps.

    Across targets and on all three models, then, a readout of what the model shows, tuned as carefully as the probe on its activations, accounts for what the activations predict about the final motion’s balance and flight, and about floating on the jump prompts. In the smaller main data sets adding a layer does help with floating (the chosen layer gains up to 0.026 in AUC, removing up to 43% of the misranked pairs, and single MotionDiffuse layers up to 0.034; Table 8). The apparent knowledge in Table 2 came from comparing a trained probe on the activations with an untrained or linear readout of the estimate. The fall rate of jumps is the exception, and it is found by the same controls that remove the other advantages.

    4.4 Small training sets can reverse the comparison
item.content:encoded:
一句话：从激活里解码物理比从输入输出解码更容易，但这只说明「读出有多容易」。

要点：

  • 要挑战的结论：近期研究称视频扩散模型「知道的比展示出来的多」——物理属性从它们的**激活**里解码，比从输入或输出里解码更准
  • 反驳很干净：扩散模型本来就用这些同样的激活来计算干净样本估计，因此这种比较实际测的是「**读出有多容易**」，而不是「模型是否藏了什么」
  • 作者因此在运动学纹理等设定下，用模型**自己的估计**作为对照，去检验是否真的存在被隐藏的物理知识

为什么值得看：这条治的是整个「世界模型懂物理吗」讨论里最常见的方法论漏洞：拿更容易的探针当证据。做工程判断时，它能帮你分辨论文里哪些结论站得住、哪些只是读出效应。

中文摘要：近期研究声称视频扩散模型「知道的比它展示出来的多」：物理属性从模型的激活中解码，比从输入或输出中解码更准确。这篇对此提出一个干净的质疑：扩散模型本来就是用同一批激活来计算干净样本估计的，因此这种比较实际测量的是「读出（readout）有多容易」，而不是「模型是否藏了额外信息」——模型是否隐藏了知识，是另一个问题。作者因此以模型自身的估计作为对照，在运动学纹理等设定下检验是否真的存在被隐藏的物理知识。对每天读「世界模型懂不懂物理」类论文的人，这是一把有用的方法学尺子。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-11-19

本期推送：2026-11-20

Probing Physics in Motion Diffusion Models
Against Their Own Estimate

Abstract

Recent studies report that video diffusion models “know more than they show”: physical properties decode better from their activations than from their inputs or outputs. But a diffusion model computes its clean-sample estimate from those same activations, so such a comparison measures how easily a readout extracts the information. Whether the model hides anything is a separate question. We set out to find hidden physical knowledge in kinematic text-to-motion diffusion models, where the physics of every intermediate estimate can be computed exactly, and recorded every layer along the sampling trajectories of MDM (two checkpoints) and MotionDiffuse. Against the usual baselines the layers do look ahead of the model’s own estimate on balance and flight. With every readout tuned the same way, the estimate closes the gap: for balance and flight, adding a layer gains at most 0.01, a size that a positive control shows we would detect. The fall rate of jumps is the one clear exception. Early in denoising, MDM’s layers add about 0.08 in R² (up to 0.11 in a refit) that the estimate does not yet show, and the gain fades as sampling proceeds; on MotionDiffuse it is small and not robust. The estimate also flags floating samples without training, but aborting them saves under a tenth of the compute. In a video model, plausibility that linear probes miss in Wan 2.1’s clean latent becomes readable after one fixed nonlinearity.

1 Introduction

Text-to-motion models turn a sentence into seconds of fluent human movement [(Guo et al., 2022; Tevet et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2023; Guo et al., 2024; Rempe et al., 2026)]. Most are kinematic. They output joint positions and rotations directly, with no simulator, so whatever physics they produce is learned from motion capture and never enforced. Physics-based generators instead move a simulated character, so gravity and contact hold by construction [(Peng et al., 2018; Tessler et al., 2024)]. Kinematic models’ most visible failures are therefore physical: bodies hover above the ground, feet slide while planted, and jumps do not fall as they should. Most remedies act from outside the generator. They project samples through a physics simulator [(Yuan et al., 2023)], condition on physical parameters [(Watanabe et al., 2025)], model contact and body forces explicitly [(Xing et al., 2026)], or optimize the sampling noise [(Stölzle et al., 2026)]. Whether the generator itself represents the physics it gets wrong is a separate and useful question: if the physics is present inside the model but lost on the way out, the internal signal could flag failing samples before compute is spent finishing them.

For video diffusion models, recent work answers yes. Physical quantities are linearly decodable from transformer activations and are reported to be built inside the model rather than inherited from its input [(Kneifl et al., 2026)]. Plausibility is decodable from the internal states of models whose outputs violate physics, a finding its authors summarize as models that “know more than they show” [(Esmati et al., 2026)]. Probes on denoising features are used to prune implausible samples early [(Tang et al., 2026)].

These conclusions rest on a comparison between a probe on internal activations and a readout of what the model takes in or puts out. In a diffusion model, the estimate of the clean sample at each step is computed from the activations at that step together with the noisy input (and, in MotionDiffuse, the text), so it cannot carry information about the outcome that they lack (Section 3.3). A probe that beats a readout of the estimate shows only that the information is easier for that probe to use in the activations [(Xu et al., 2020)]. The output may still contain all of it. How much such a gap means depends on three things: whether the two readouts are equally flexible and equally well tuned; whether the gap holds within a prompt, or only reflects which prompt was given; and whether there was enough training data for the comparison to be stable.

We set out to show that a motion diffusion model, too, knows more than it shows, and to use that knowledge to stop failing samples early. Text-to-motion diffusion suits the test, because all three conditions can be checked: the physics of a motion follows exactly from its joint positions, the models we study expose a clean-motion estimate at every step (MDM predicts it, [Tevet et al., 2023]; MotionDiffuse computes it from its noise prediction, [Zhang et al., 2022]), and sampling is cheap enough to record thousands of complete trajectories. We record every transformer layer along each model’s own sampling path, for 6,000 motions from 250 prompts with two MDM checkpoints and 3,000 with MotionDiffuse, and compute dynamic balance (the extrapolated center of mass relative to the area of foot support; [Hof et al., 2005]), flight, gravity during flight, and floating from the final motions. Two choices were made along the way. We added a set of jump-heavy prompts once it was clear that the main prompts contain too few falling bodies to test gravity, and we redefined “airborne” after finding that the first definition counted hovering and crawling as flight (Appendix C). The result is not the one we set out to show.

Contributions.

  • •

    Physics is readable early. A fifth of the way through denoising, linear probes on the layers already recover the final motion’s dynamic balance and flight (R²=0.84 and AUC 0.97 on the 50-step model), stably across seeds and on held-out prompts (Section 4.2).

  • •

    The apparent hidden knowledge is a readout effect. Standard baselines make the layers look better informed than the estimate. Read with equal care, the estimate matches them. For balance and flight, on all three models, adding a layer gains at most 0.01, and a positive control shows that the protocol would detect a gain of that size. Floating behaves the same on the jump prompts; only in the smaller main data sets does the layer help (Section 4.3). With too little training data the comparison can flip, which explains a pilot study that pointed the other way (Section 4.4).

  • •

    One exception, and it fades. Only for the fall rate of jumps do the layers know more. A fifth of the way through denoising, MDM’s layers add about 0.08 in R² (up to 0.11 in a refit) to the best readout of the estimate, and on the 50-step model the gain survives every control we applied. It fades as sampling proceeds and the estimate catches up. On MotionDiffuse the same gain is small and not robust (Section 4.3).

  • •

    The output is enough for early warning. Decoded partway through sampling, MDM’s own estimate flags samples that will float, without training and about as well as a trained probe on the layers. Aborting them saves under a tenth of the compute, because floating affects only 9 to 18% of samples and concentrates in a few prompts (Section 4.5).

  • •

    A related issue in video. A linear probe at chance is the main evidence that plausibility is absent from the clean VAE latent of a video diffusion model [(Esmati et al., 2026)]. One fixed, training-free nonlinearity, the size of local frame-to-frame change, makes it readable from the same latent: a linear readout of it reaches 78% pairwise accuracy on IntPhys, and 80% together with the grid features (Section 4.6).

  • •

    What actually fails. Once bodies that hover without falling are separated out, MDM’s jumps fall at close to the right rate in the median. The common failure is floating, and on test captions the original 1000-step checkpoint floats about twice as often as the 50-step one (Section 4.1).

    • Section 5 turns these findings into five checks for probing studies that claim a generator knows more than it shows.

    2 Related Work

    Text-to-motion generation.

    HumanML3D [(Guo et al., 2022)] established the standard benchmark and a redundant pose representation with root velocities, joint positions, velocities and rotations, and binary foot-contact labels. MotionDiffuse [(Zhang et al., 2022)] was among the first diffusion models for text-to-motion generation, predicting the noise at every step, and MDM [(Tevet et al., 2023)] applies a transformer diffusion model directly to this representation and predicts the clean motion. Tokenized approaches quantize motion and model the token sequence, autoregressively [(Zhang et al., 2023)] or with masked modeling over residual codebooks [(Guo et al., 2024)], and MLD [(Chen et al., 2023a)] runs diffusion in the latent space of a motion autoencoder. Kimodo [(Rempe et al., 2026)] is a recent large kinematic motion diffusion model trained on studio motion capture and designed to reduce floating and foot skating. We study MDM and MotionDiffuse because both work directly in pose space, so their clean-motion estimate at every step can be scored with the same physics as the final output.

    Kinematic and physics-based motion generation.

    The models above are kinematic: they generate poses directly, and floating, foot sliding and ground penetration are widely reported for them. Character animation has long repaired the most common of these artifacts after generation, from predicted foot contacts: PFNN edits each generated pose with a simple two-joint inverse kinematics along the contact labels to remove foot sliding [(Holden et al., 2017)], earlier work constrains heel and toe velocity to zero during contact by optimizing in an autoencoder’s hidden space [(Holden et al., 2016)], and the Neural State Machine predicts contact labels for feet, hands and hips for use in inverse-kinematics post-processing [(Starke et al., 2019)]. Such fixes keep planted feet in place, but they cannot make an airborne body fall at the right rate or tell a floating body from a jump. Physics-based controllers instead generate motion inside a simulator, where gravity and contact hold by construction, at the cost of learning a control policy [(Peng et al., 2018; Tessler et al., 2024)]. Hybrids keep a kinematic generator and make its output physical with a simulator: PhysDiff [(Yuan et al., 2023)] projects intermediate samples through a simulated motion-imitation policy during diffusion, and CLoSD [(Tevet et al., 2024)] pairs a kinematic diffusion planner with a simulated tracking controller; related systems drive humanoid robots [(Wang et al., 2026)]. Other methods make a kinematic model’s output more physical without simulating it. SimDiff [(Watanabe et al., 2025)] conditions a frozen MDM on environment parameters learned from simulator-augmented data. PhysibleMDM [(Stölzle et al., 2026)] optimizes the diffusion noise of a frozen model at inference time against kinematic and inverse-dynamics feasibility measures, and InterPhys [(Xing et al., 2026)] models human-object, human-scene and internal body forces with soft force- and torque-balance constraints. Guidance steers the sampling of motion diffusion models toward spatial constraints [(Karunratanakul et al., 2023; Xie et al., 2024)], and noise optimization adjusts the diffusion noise of a frozen model against any loss defined on the generated motion [(Karunratanakul et al., 2024)]. All of these act on a model’s inputs, outputs, sampling or environment. We ask what a kinematic generator represents internally about the physics it does not enforce, a question that does not arise for physics-based generators, where our labels hold by construction; our early-warning experiment measures how much an internal or decoded signal can save.

    Physics inside generative models.

    Linear probes reveal scene geometry such as depth in latent image diffusion models [(Chen et al., 2023b)]. In video encoders, speed and acceleration become linearly accessible at intermediate depth, with control tasks and attentive probes as comparisons [(Joseph et al., 2026)]. Layerwise probing has since been compared across video foundation models with different pretraining [(Punzo et al., 2026)] and extended to camera motion, intuitive physics and anomalies [(Musa et al., 2026)], and the probe direction at such layers has been used to steer an encoder’s physical expectations [(Alam, 2026)]. For video diffusion transformers, [Kneifl et al. (2026)] fit ridge probes to activations of forward-noised simulated videos and report that speed, momentum and gravity are decodable well beyond what ridge probes recover from the noisy input latent; for gravity the margin persists as the input becomes clean, while for rolling speed the clean latent eventually carries the information. [Esmati et al. (2026)] invert real videos through the model and find plausibility linearly decodable from mean-pooled transformer states, while a linear probe on the clean VAE latent is at chance. [Tang et al. (2026)] use probes on denoising features to prune implausible video candidates early, comparing against random selection, best-of-N selection, preference tuning and a likelihood-based scorer. In image diffusion, CNN probes on early denoising signals predict the quality of the final image [(Cui et al., 2026)]. Similar probes outperform an off-the-shelf evaluator applied to the decoded clean estimate [(Guo et al., 2026)], and in diffusion driving planners, first-step state probes select better trajectories than a privileged score of the clean preview’s true quality in three of four settings [(Zhang et al., 2026)]. Without probes, video models that predict masked content in a learned representation space show violation-of-expectation effects on intuitive-physics benchmarks including IntPhys, while pixel-space video prediction stays closer to chance [(Garrido et al., 2025)]. [Guo et al. (2026)] and [Zhang et al. (2026)] do compare probes with the clean estimate, but they read it with an off-the-shelf evaluator or score it by its true quality. None compares the internal probe with an equally flexible, equally tuned readout of the model’s own clean-sample estimate, measures what the layer adds to that estimate, or reports how that comparison depends on training-set size. These are the comparisons we add, together with within-prompt scoring for generated samples; [Esmati et al. (2026)] do score pairs within a scene, which we adopt for our video test. Unlike [Kneifl et al. (2026)] and [Esmati et al. (2026)], we also record along the model’s own sampling trajectory rather than from noised simulated videos or inverted real ones.

    Probing methodology.

    Linear probes [(Alain & Bengio, 2016)] measure what a fixed readout can decode, not what a model uses or contains [(Belinkov, 2022)]. Control tasks separate a representation’s content from what a probe can memorize [(Hewitt & Liang, 2019)]. An information-theoretic view argues that the best-performing probe should be used, shows with the data-processing inequality that a contextual representation carries no more information about a property than the sentence it was computed from, and therefore measures the gain over a control representation, noting that ease of extraction still lacks a formal definition [(Pimentel et al., 2020b)]; minimum-description-length probing makes the dependence on probe complexity and data size explicit [(Voita & Titov, 2020)], and Pareto probing reports accuracy against probe complexity rather than at one capacity [(Pimentel et al., 2020a)]. Usable (V-) information [(Xu et al., 2020)] resolves the tension between these views: Shannon information cannot grow under processing, but the information a given family of readouts can extract can. Conditional probing [(Hewitt et al., 2021)] applies this to ask what a representation adds beyond a baseline representation, by comparing a readout of the baseline with a readout of both. Amnesic probing asks a different question, whether a model uses a property, by removing it and measuring the change in behavior [(Elazar et al., 2021)]; we do not test use. Our comparison is a conditional probe whose baseline is the model’s own clean-sample estimate, which is a known deterministic function of the probed activations and the noisy input (and, in MotionDiffuse, the text). That fixes the direction of the Shannon comparison and leaves usable information under a stated readout family as the quantity to measure (Section 3.3).

    3 Setup

    3.1 Model, sampling and recording

    We study MDM [(Tevet et al., 2023)], a kinematic diffusion model: a transformer encoder (8 layers, width 512) with a CLIP text encoder, using two official HumanML3D checkpoints: the 50-step model and the original 1000-step model. Both generate 120 frames (6 s at 20 fps) in the HumanML3D representation [(Guo et al., 2022)], with classifier-free guidance at scale 2.5. At six denoising steps, evenly spaced from the first to the last, we record the output of every transformer layer at every fourth frame (dropping the condition token), the noisy input xₜ, and the model’s clean-motion estimate x̂₀ with its decoded joints. Guidance runs a conditional and an unconditional pass; we record the activations of the conditional pass and the guided estimate that the sampler uses. “20% of denoising” denotes the second recorded step (step 10 of 50, or 200 of 1000). Figure 2 summarizes what we record and compare.

    A second model.

    To test whether the results depend on MDM’s design, we repeat the main analyses on MotionDiffuse [(Zhang et al., 2022)], also kinematic but different where it matters. It predicts the noise rather than the clean motion, so its estimate x̂₀=(xₜ-√1-ᾱₜ ε̂)/√ᾱₜ is computed from its prediction and the noisy input; it uses no guidance; and its 8 transformer layers (width 512, linear attention, one token per frame) receive the text in every layer, through cross-attention and stylization blocks, rather than as a token. We use its official HumanML3D checkpoint and sampler (1000 DDPM steps), the same prompts, seeds, frames and recorded steps as for MDM (20% of denoising is step 200), and choose its layers by the same rule as MDM’s (Section 3.3; layer 3 for balance, layer 6 for flight and gravity). Its noise schedule is linear where MDM’s is cosine, so a given fraction of denoising is noisier for MotionDiffuse (Table 9). Since the text reaches every layer, its estimate is a function of its activations, the noisy input and the text, (a_ℓ,xₜ,u) in the notation of Section 3.3, so for this model the bound of Section 3.3 includes the text, which is one reason we also test the text directly.

    Prompts and runs.

    The prompt set combines 64 curated prompts (everyday locomotion, jumps and hops, balance-challenging actions, upper-body actions) with 186 captions sampled from the HumanML3D test split, 250 in total, and each prompt is sampled 4 times: 1,000 motions per run. We run each model with three seeds: 6,000 motions from the two MDM checkpoints and 3,000 from MotionDiffuse.
