Because few of these motions contain flight, we also run every model on a jump-heavy prompt set with three seeds: the 14 curated jump, hop, leap and skip prompts plus one caption from every HumanML3D test motion whose caption names one of these actions, 245 distinct prompts sampled 4 times each (2,940 motions per model). A pilot used only the curated prompts (256 motions), every second frame, and a single held-out set of 12 prompts.

    3.2 Physical labels

    All labels are computed from joint positions, with y the vertical axis, both for the final motion and for the clean-motion estimate at each recorded step.

    Center of mass, contact and support.

    The center of mass is cₜ=∑ₛmₛ\tfrac12(p_a(s),t+p_b(s),t), with standard segment mass fractions mₛ placed at segment midpoints, where a(s) and b(s) are the joints at the two ends of segment s[(Winter, 2009)]. An ankle (toe) joint is in contact when it is lower than 12 cm (6 cm) and moves less per frame than HumanML3D’s contact threshold. The support region Sₜ is the convex hull of the contacting foot joints on the ground plane, padded by 4 cm.

    Balance.

    Dynamic balance uses the extrapolated center of mass [(Hof et al., 2005)],

    x^XCoMₜ=cˣᶻₜ+ċˣᶻₜ/ω₀, ω₀=√g/h, g=9.81 m/s²,

    		(1)

    where h is the motion’s median center-of-mass height. The dynamic balance margin is the signed distance from x^XCoMₜ to the boundary of Sₜ, positive inside; the static balance margin uses cˣᶻₜ instead. Both are undefined without foot contact. The extrapolated center of mass routinely leaves the support region during normal stepping, so we treat the margins as continuous quantities rather than failure labels (Figure 3a,b). They are kinematic quantities; a test of physical feasibility would need the center of pressure or inverse dynamics.

    Floating, flight and gravity.

    The lowest-foot height is the height of the lowest foot joint, and a frame is in flight when no foot is in contact. A frame is airborne when every foot joint is above its contact height and no knee, wrist or the pelvis is within 15 cm of the floor, so that crawling and cartwheels do not count as airborne (Appendix C). Over each airborne stretch of at least 0.2 s we fit c_y(t)=a₀+a₁t+a₂t² to the center-of-mass height. Ballistic flight requires the flight gravityĝ=-2a₂ to equal g=9.81 m/s², a test that needs no calibration (Figure 3c,d). Every frame of the stretch carries its ĝ. Because in the main data most airborne frames lie in stretches that barely fall (Section 4.3), this flight gravity mixes two questions, and for probing we also split it at the floating cut-off below: whether an airborne frame belongs to a floating or a falling stretch (floats or falls, scored by AUC), and the fitted gravity of falling stretches alone (the fall rate).

    Per-sample failures.

    An airborne stretch with ĝ<2 m/s² is floating: the body is off the ground and unsupported, but barely falls. For each sample, the floating rate is the share of frames in floating stretches, and the raised-contact rate is the share of contact frames whose lowest foot is higher than 5 cm. Two further per-sample rates serve only as inputs to the early-warning readouts (Section 3.4): the mean |ĝ-g| over stretches that do fall, and the share of support frames with a negative dynamic balance margin.

    3.3 What the model shows, and a fair comparison

    In our data, a linear probe on MDM’s last layer predicts the final motion’s dynamic balance better than the balance computed from the model’s own estimate at the same step (Table 2). It is tempting to conclude that the model knows how balanced the motion will be and fails to show it. But the estimate is computed from that layer, so everything it contains about balance has passed through the layer. The probe’s advantage can mean only that the layer holds the information in a form a linear readout finds easy, while the estimate holds it in a form that needs a nonlinear readout or a computed quantity. To call the knowledge hidden, a readout of the layer has to beat an equally flexible readout of the estimate, or add to it. The rest of this section makes the argument precise.

    At each step the model shows its clean-motion estimate x̂₀⁽ᵏ⁾: 263 features per frame, from which joints and every label above follow exactly. We number MDM’s encoder layers 0 to 7. Each layer’s output is a deterministic function of the previous layer’s, and the output of layer 7, the last, is mapped to the conditional estimate by a fixed linear projection at every frame. Guidance combines this conditional estimate with an unconditional one, which depends only on xₜ and the step. Write a_ℓ⁽ᵏ⁾ for the full conditional output of layer ℓ at step k (every token, including the condition token), xₜ for that step’s noisy input, and u for the text condition. The guided estimate is then a function of (a_ℓ⁽ᵏ⁾,xₜ) for every ℓ, and the activations are a function of (xₜ,u). For any label y of the final motion, the data-processing inequality therefore gives

    I(y; x̂₀⁽ᵏ⁾) ≤ I(y; a_ℓ⁽ᵏ⁾,xₜ) ≤ I(y; xₜ,u).

    		(2)

    The estimate cannot carry information about the outcome that the activations and the noisy input lack. The same argument bounds the video studies of Section 2 from the other side: under forward noising the activations are functions of the clean latent, the text prompt and noise drawn independently of both and of the label, and under deterministic inversion they are functions of the clean latent and the prompt alone, so no layer can carry more information about the label than the clean latent together with the prompt.

    Shannon information therefore cannot separate these representations. What differs is how much of the information a given readout can use. For a family V of readouts, the V-information I_V(X→y) is the reduction in the best expected loss on y that a readout in V achieves by seeing X[(Xu et al., 2020)]. Unlike Shannon information, it can grow under processing, which is how a probe on the layer can beat a readout of the estimate. The question that bears on hidden knowledge is what the layer adds to the estimate [(Hewitt et al., 2021)],

    I_V(a_ℓ⁽ᵏ⁾→y|x̂₀⁽ᵏ⁾) = H_V(y|x̂₀⁽ᵏ⁾)-H_V(y|x̂₀⁽ᵏ⁾,a_ℓ⁽ᵏ⁾),

    		(3)

    which we measure as the gain in R² (or AUC) from adding the layer to a readout of the estimate. For squared-error readouts, once the baseline R² is fixed, the two determine each other:

    Proposition 1.

    Let V predict Gaussians ℕ(f(·),σ²), with f from a regression class and σ>0 free, and let the class on (x̂₀⁽ᵏ⁾,a_ℓ⁽ᵏ⁾) contain every function in the class on x̂₀⁽ᵏ⁾. Writing R²_X for the best R² the class reaches from X,

    I_V(a_ℓ⁽ᵏ⁾→y|x̂₀⁽ᵏ⁾) = \tfrac12\log(1-R²_x̂₀⁽ᵏ⁾)/(1-R²_x̂₀⁽ᵏ⁾,a_ℓ⁽ᵏ⁾) ≥ 0.

    		(4)

    For a fixed baseline, the gain in R² is therefore a monotone transform of the conditional usable information (proof in Appendix G), and in population it cannot be negative: a negative measured gain only reflects fitting the larger readout on finite data. Its value depends on the family, so we report it for linear readouts, a fixed MLP and readouts tuned on held-out prompts, test whether it survives within a prompt, and vary the amount of training data. Our per-frame probes see only the conditional pass, without the condition token, and one recorded frame at a time, so strictly they could see less than the estimate. On the 50-step model, adding the condition token gains at most 0.004 for balance, flight and floating (Appendix A).

    Readouts.

    For each label and recorded step we compare six readouts, each predicting the final motion’s per-frame label:

  • •

    Explicit: the same label computed from the estimate’s joints, with a linear calibration fit on the training folds (for the flight AUC, the raw value);

  • •

    Estimate, linear: a ridge probe on the estimate’s 263 features, the usual baseline in probing studies;

  • •

    Estimate, MLP: a small MLP on everything the estimate shows, that is its 263 features plus the labels computed from it (Section 3.2, with foot contacts and foot sliding speed) and indicators for undefined values;

  • •

    Layer, linear and Layer, MLP: ridge and the same MLP on one layer’s 512 activations at the frame (its slice of a_ℓ);

  • •

    Estimate + layer, MLP: the same MLP on both, which asks whether the layer adds anything to what the estimate shows.

    • We also report a ridge probe on the noisy input xₜ. Ridge probes standardize their inputs and choose the penalty from {1,10,…,10⁴} by efficient leave-one-out cross-validation on the training frames. The MLP has two hidden layers of 256 units with ReLU and dropout 0.1, and is trained with AdamW (learning rate 10⁻³, weight decay 10⁻⁴) with early stopping on 15% of the training prompts. The layer is fixed per label as the one with the best mean linear score at 20% of denoising: layer 7 for both balance measures, 6 for flight, and 5 for gravity and its two parts, on both MDM checkpoints. This choice favors the layer in a standalone comparison; for what the layer adds to the estimate, we also test every layer and all layers together (Section 4.3).

    Tuned readouts on pooled seeds.

    The fixed MLP and the leave-one-out penalty (which validates on frames of motions seen in training) could each favor one side. We therefore repeat the comparison with every run of a checkpoint pooled, three seeds and 3,000 motions, under five folds grouped by prompt across seeds, and with every readout tuned on a validation split of 15% of the training prompts. The families are ridge, with the penalty chosen from 10⁻¹ to 10⁶; an MLP family that adds a linear map to an MLP, so that it contains the linear readout, with five configurations (64 to 1024 hidden units, one or two hidden layers, dropout 0.1 or 0.3, weight decay 10⁻⁴ to 10⁻²); and, as the tuned readout, whichever of the two has the lower validation error. The same procedure reads the estimate’s 263 raw features alone, everything the estimate shows, the layer, and estimate and layer together. The conditional gain uses a readout of estimate and layer that may fall back to the estimate alone: among the candidates for both inputs and for the estimate alone, it keeps the one with the lowest validation error, so that the larger input cannot lower the score merely by being harder to fit. Confidence intervals resample prompts with replacement (1,000 replicates, the same draw for every readout). They do not include training variance, which we measure by refitting with two further validation splits and initializations. We report many intervals (targets, models, layers and steps) without correcting for multiplicity, read them as descriptive, and draw conclusions only from patterns that hold across models, layers and scores. The analysis was not preregistered: the tuned readouts, the jump-heavy runs, the split of flight gravity and the second model were added after the first results (Appendix B).

    Evaluation.

    All readouts share five folds grouped by prompt, so no test prompt is seen in training. We report R² for continuous labels and ROC-AUC for flight and for floats or falls, pooled over all test frames. Since physics differs greatly between prompts, a readout could score well by recognizing the prompt alone. The within-prompt score removes that possibility: we subtract each prompt’s mean from both target and prediction and report the Pearson correlation of the residuals, which only sample-specific information can raise. A prompt also says when things tend to happen (a jump in the middle of the clip, say), which a per-frame readout could exploit within a prompt. With seeds pooled, the within-prompt-and-frame score removes this as well, by subtracting the mean over the 12 samples of the same prompt at the same frame. The within-prompt score cannot be raised by information that enters a prediction additively through the prompt, and the within-prompt-and-frame score by information that enters additively through the prompt and the frame:

    Proposition 2.

    If a prediction has the form ŷ=f(X)+h(c), with X the readout’s input, where h depends only on the cell c (the prompt, or the prompt and the frame), then its within-cell score equals that of f(X).

    A gain within prompt and frame is therefore information beyond anything the text and the timing of a prompt could add on their own (proof in Appendix G); interactions between the text and the estimate are tested separately, by giving the readout the text itself (Section 4.3). To see how the comparison depends on data, we also retrain the linear layer probe and the explicit calibration on random subsets of 13 to all (≈200) training prompts per fold, and the tuned readouts with seeds pooled on subsets of 25, 50 and 100, and evaluate on the same test folds.

    3.4 Early warning

    Can a sample that will float be caught partway through sampling and replaced? A sample fails if its final motion has any floating. We compare four strategies and count cost in denoising steps per delivered motion (1 = one full sample): generating once; finish, then filter, which checks the final motion and regenerates if it floats; early abort, which scores the sample at 20% or 40% of denoising and restarts it if the score is high; and early abort followed by the final check. Retries stop after a budget of attempts, and the last attempt is always delivered. The early score is (i) a training-free rule, abort if the decoded estimate already shows floating; (ii) a ridge readout, trained out of fold and set to abort the same share of samples, of everything the estimate shows (its features averaged over frames and its per-sample failure rates), of the frame-averaged activations of one layer (layer 3 of the 50-step model and layer 6 of the 1000-step model, each chosen on the first seed), or of both; (iii) random aborts at the same rate; or (iv) a perfect detector, as a ceiling. All strategies are simulated with the same random draws, on the 6,000 recorded MDM samples. Each already contains its estimate at every recorded step and its final motion, so every decision uses what an online run would see; a retry draws another recorded sample of the same prompt (200 simulated requests per prompt). Strategies that end with the final check are compared at equal delivered failure by varying the budget from 1 to 20 attempts.

    4 Results

    4.1 What goes wrong physically

    When MDM’s bodies leave the ground and fall, they fall at close to the right rate (Table 1): the median fitted gravity on the curated jump prompts is 9.54 to 9.75 m/s2 for the 50-step model and 9.13 to 9.22 m/s2 for the 1000-step model, somewhat slower than real jumps in the processed form of its training data (median 10.33 m/s2, Appendix E). Individual stretches spread widely around these medians (standard deviation 2.24 m/s2 on the jump-heavy runs, against 0.7 to 1.0 m/s2 for real jumps). The common failure is floating. On HumanML3D test captions, 3.8 to 4.7% of the 50-step model’s frames lie in floating stretches, against 8.6 to 9.7% for the 1000-step model. On the curated jump prompts the figures are 0.6 to 0.8% and 4.8 to 9.3%. The raised-contact rate, a foot in contact but more than 5 cm up, follows the same pattern. Part of the floating is implied by the prompt: a person “walking on a balance beam” is generated without a beam and floats in nearly every sample. On test captions the original 1000-step checkpoint floats about twice as often as the 50-step one, in all three seeds and under every threshold setting we tried (Appendix D). On real motion capture the same labels flag floating in 0.09% of frames (Appendix E).

    A typical floating stretch is an ordinary walking pose with the whole body several centimeters off the floor for about half a second, in a motion that touches the floor elsewhere (Figure 1, Appendix C). Our first definition of airborne looked only at the feet, so it fitted such stretches, and stretches supported by the hands or knees, as flight. That made the 1000-step model’s jumps appear to fall far too slowly (medians of 3.75 and 7.55 m/s2 in the two seeds labelled that way), an effect that disappears once floating is separated out.

    4.2 Physics is readable early in denoising

    Linear probes recover the final motion’s physics from the activations well before sampling ends (Figure 4, Table 2). At 20% of denoising, the best layer of the 50-step model reaches R²=0.838±0.001 for dynamic balance, 0.868 for the lowest-foot height and 0.820 for flight gravity, and an AUC of 0.973 for flight. In these data the flight-gravity score mostly reflects whether an airborne body floats or falls (Section 4.3). Layer 7 is the best layer for dynamic balance in all six runs. The result transfers across prompt types: for dynamic balance at 20%, the best layer scores 0.835 on curated prompts and 0.839 on test captions. The 1000-step model is less readable at the same fraction of denoising (0.697 for dynamic balance).

    Taken at face value, the standard comparison suggests hidden knowledge. For dynamic balance, flight and, on the 50-step model, gravity, the best layer beats both the explicit label and the linear probe on the estimate at the same step. For dynamic balance the gap over the explicit label is +0.045 to +0.065 in the three 50-step seeds and +0.018 to +0.060 in the three 1000-step seeds. Only the lowest-foot height, which the estimate shows directly, and static balance on the 50-step model (0.769 against 0.759) favor the explicit label, and flight gravity on the 1000-step model is a tie (0.692 against 0.691).

    4.3 The advantage disappears under a fair readout

    Table 3 and Figure 5 compare the readouts with the three seeds of each model pooled and every readout tuned on held-out prompts (Section 3.3). A first version with one fixed MLP per seed gives the same ordering (Appendix B). For balance and flight the estimate is read as well as the layer: for both balance measures its tuned readout beats the tuned layer, by 0.015 to 0.029 in R² on both MDM checkpoints and by 0.12 and 0.18 on MotionDiffuse, and for flight the estimate ties or leads. Adding the layer to the estimate gains nothing. With the readout that may fall back to the estimate, every interval covers zero or lies below it, across prompts and within prompt and frame, and so does every interval in two refits with other validation splits and initializations, run for dynamic balance on the 50-step model. The layer sweep shows the same for every layer: none adds more than 0.007, and only one interval, for flight at layer 7 of the 1000-step model, barely excludes zero (Figure 6). On MDM, whose conditional estimate is a fixed linear map of layer 7, a gain from that layer could come only from directions the output head discards.

    This null result is not produced by the estimator. Without the fallback, the larger readout scores within 0.003 of the estimate or below it for balance and flight, so the fallback hides no gain there. It keeps the estimate alone in one to five of the five folds (Table 8). On the scale of Proposition 1, the largest balance gain is 0.001 nats, against 0.063 for the fall rate below.

    A positive control shows what the protocol can detect (Table 10). We take the estimate readout’s out-of-fold residual, add noise so that its best linear use would raise R² by 0.005, 0.01 or 0.02 on the squared-error scale, add it to the layer’s activations along a random direction, and rerun the protocol unchanged on the 50-step model. For dynamic balance even the smallest signal is found: the gain is +0.013 [0.009, 0.017], more than the linear amount because the tuned readouts extract more, against +0.000 [-0.001, 0.001] for the real layer. For flight and floating the pooled AUC, near 0.97, barely moves even at 0.02, partly because the readouts are selected by squared error. The within-prompt-and-frame score does find the signal, from 0.005 for flight and from 0.01 for floating on the jump prompts, and on that score the real layer adds nothing (-0.008 and 0.000). For these two targets the evidence for no gain is therefore that score, and a gain below 0.01 for floating could go undetected.

    Two details show where the estimate’s advantage comes from. First, the readout family matters: restricted to linear readouts, the layer does add a little (up to 0.02 on MDM, 0.05 to 0.07 on MotionDiffuse), so part of what the estimate shows needs a nonlinear readout. Second, on MDM the input matters more than the family: from its 263 raw features alone the tuned estimate only ties the tuned layer, and the physics labels computed from it add about 0.02 for dynamic balance (Table 7). On MotionDiffuse the raw features alone already beat the tuned layer, by 0.12 and 0.18 (Table 3), and the labels add nothing. A temporal readout that sees all 30 recorded frames gives the same ordering in all six runs (Appendix A). In the terms of Section 3.3, the usable information the layer adds about balance and flight depends on the readout family, and for the most flexible readouts we tried it is indistinguishable from zero.

    Flight gravity: floating and falling.

    The fitted flight gravity mixes two questions. In the main data most of its labelled frames (76% and 83%) lie in floating stretches, so its score mostly measures whether an airborne body floats or falls, and only 57 and 78 prompts contain falling frames, too few for reliable tuned readouts. We therefore split the target (Section 3.2) and use the jump-heavy runs, in which most labelled frames fall (11,640 and 13,444 frames from 233 and 240 prompts).

    Whether an airborne body floats or falls is visible in the estimate on the jump prompts, where 236 prompts have airborne stretches on the 50-step model. Its tuned readout reaches an AUC of 0.97 on both MDM checkpoints, and no single layer, nor all eight together, adds more than 0.007 in pooled AUC (Figure 6). Across the three fits the layer adds at most 0.004 in pooled AUC, and 0.019 [0.008, 0.030] within prompt in one of them. The layer adds more only in the smaller main data, where just 106 prompts have airborne stretches. There, on the 50-step model, it adds +0.008 [0.001, 0.015] in pooled AUC and +0.054 [0.013, 0.089] in the within-prompt correlation, and in two refits up to 0.014 pooled and 0.08 to 0.11 within prompt and frame.

    The fall rate of the stretches that do fall is the one case in which the layers know more. On the jump prompts of the 50-step model, adding the layer raises R² from 0.35 to 0.43, a gain of +0.077 [0.051, 0.107], or 0.063 nats (Tables 3 and 8, Figure 7), with similar gains within prompt and frame and in two refits. With more training prompts the gain first shrinks and then levels off from 100 prompts on (0.085, then 0.077; Figure 9b). It replicates on the 1000-step model (+0.076 [0.053, 0.096]), though there it is smaller within prompt and frame (+0.021) and with fewer training prompts (Figure 9c), and the layer alone is no longer clearly ahead of the estimate (0.309 against 0.287, an interval that covers zero), so the two carry partly different information. On both MDM checkpoints every layer from 3 to 7 adds 0.06 to 0.08 (Figure 6). The standard comparison overstates even this genuine case: the layer’s ridge probe beats the explicit label by three times the conditional gain on the 50-step model and 1.5 times on the 1000-step model, because the fall rate fitted to a 20% estimate predicts the final one poorly.

    Four checks leave the gain in place. It is not only the layer knowing where a jump is: in 92% of the 11,640 falling frames, from 7,125 falling stretches, the 20% estimate is airborne too, and there the layer still adds +0.069. It is not a weak readout of the estimate’s timing: the estimate’s readout already includes its own fitted fall rate, and a temporal readout over all 30 recorded frames still leaves the layer ahead in every seed (Appendix A). It is not the text: giving the readout the prompt’s CLIP embedding, the model’s own text input, does not help on held-out prompts, and the layer’s gain beyond estimate and text is unchanged. And label noise is not the ceiling: on real motion capture the gravity label’s spread would allow an R² of 0.81 to 0.91 (Appendix E).

    The gain is, however, transient (Figure 8). At 40% of denoising layer 5 still adds 0.043 on both MDM checkpoints (Figure 8d). By 60% no layer adds more than 0.02, and at 80% the interval for layer 5 covers zero, because the estimate’s readout improves faster than the layer’s. A separate layer sweep gives up to about 0.06 at 40%, and the same readout differs by up to 0.016 between that sweep and the step run. At a fifth of the denoising steps, then, MDM’s middle and late layers carry information about how fast a jump will fall that its estimate does not yet show in any form we could read: a step-wise case of a model knowing more than it shows, of the kind the video studies report. Such a gain must vanish by the end of sampling, when the final motion is a function of the estimate, so what the measurement adds is its size and duration: about 0.08 in R², for about two fifths of the trajectory.

    A second model.

    MotionDiffuse (Section 3.1) predicts the noise, receives the text in every layer and uses no guidance, and it gives the same picture for balance and flight. On its main data the tuned estimate beats the tuned layer by 0.12 in R² for dynamic balance and 0.18 for static balance, more than on MDM. Adding any one of its eight layers gains at most 0.001 for dynamic balance, and its chosen layers add nothing for static balance or flight. Floating follows MDM’s pattern: on the main data, where only 50 prompts have airborne stretches, its layers add 0.016 to 0.034 in AUC and the layer alone beats the estimate (0.988 against 0.940), while on its jump prompts (2,940 motions, 235 prompts with such stretches) they add nothing, and the same holds for flight and for the unsplit flight gravity (at most +0.002).

    The fall rate again shows a gain, but a smaller and less stable one. At 20% of denoising (step 200 of 1000), adding layer 6 raises R² from 0.365 to 0.390, +0.025 [0.003, 0.047] (Table 3, Figures 5 and 6). It holds within prompt (+0.022 [0.007, 0.038]), but within prompt and frame its interval covers zero (+0.017 [-0.001, 0.036]), and in two refits with other validation splits and initializations it is +0.022 [0.007, 0.041] and 0, the fallback keeping the estimate in every fold of the second. It again comes from the later layers (layers 5 to 7 add 0.018 to 0.025 and all eight together 0.047, layers 0 to 3 nothing), the text does not explain it (estimate, text and layer together gain the same +0.025 over the estimate as without the text), and it fades with denoising: +0.012 [0.003, 0.022] at 40% and +0.007 [-0.002, 0.016] at 60%.

    At matched noise the gap to MDM is larger still, because the same fraction of denoising is not the same noise level on the two models. At 20% MotionDiffuse’s signal-to-noise ratio is 0.002, against MDM’s 0.10, and it reaches MDM’s range only between 40 and 60% (Table 9). At 60%, with a ratio of 0.24, between MDM’s at 20% (0.10) and 40% (0.52), MotionDiffuse’s gain is +0.007, against MDM’s +0.077 and +0.043 at those steps.

    Across targets and on all three models, then, a readout of what the model shows, tuned as carefully as the probe on its activations, accounts for what the activations predict about the final motion’s balance and flight, and about floating on the jump prompts. In the smaller main data sets adding a layer does help with floating (the chosen layer gains up to 0.026 in AUC, removing up to 43% of the misranked pairs, and single MotionDiffuse layers up to 0.034; Table 8). The apparent knowledge in Table 2 came from comparing a trained probe on the activations with an untrained or linear readout of the estimate. The fall rate of jumps is the exception, and it is found by the same controls that remove the other advantages.

    4.4 Small training sets can reverse the comparison

item.title: 纹理合成既要真实又要可解释：GramStatTexNet 把「分析-合成」的统计量换成学出来的，还保留金字塔结构 ｜ GramStatTexNet: Efficient, Interpretable, and Neuro-Inspired Texture Analysis-by-Synthesis
item.description:
一句话：深度网络真实但不可解释；神经科学启发的金字塔可解释，却依赖少量手工统计量、难以泛化。

要点：

  • 两条路各有短板：深度网络合成真实感强，但表示**不透明、过参数化**，与生物视觉几乎没有直接联系；神经科学启发的金字塔模型可解释、紧凑，却依赖**少量人工挑选的统计量**，难以泛化与扩展
  • GramStatTexNet 走混合路线：把多尺度金字塔结构与可学的统计表示结合，做「分析-合成」式纹理建模
  • 定位是同时拿到效率、可解释性与合成质量，而不是在两者之间二选一

为什么值得看：纹理是材质管线的地基，而「可解释 + 可扩展」意味着能定向编辑而不是随机重采样。对需要可控纹理生成（而不是抽卡式生成）的团队，这类分析-合成框架更接近工具。

中文摘要：深度网络在纹理合成上的真实感很强，但常依赖不透明、过参数化的表示，与生物视觉几乎没有直接联系；反过来，受神经科学启发的金字塔模型可解释且紧凑，却依赖少量人工挑选的统计量，难以泛化或扩展。GramStatTexNet 因此提出一个混合式的「分析-合成」框架，把多尺度金字塔结构与可学习的统计表示结合起来，在保留可解释性的同时提升效率与合成质量。对材质管线而言，可解释意味着可以定向编辑纹理的某个统计层面，而不是只能重新采样。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-11-19

本期推送：2026-11-20

GramStatTexNet: Efficient, Interpretable, and Neuro-Inspired Texture Analysis-by-Synthesis

Abstract

Deep networks achieve high realism in texture synthesis but often rely on opaque, over-parameterized representations that have limited direct connection to biological vision. Neuroscience-informed pyramid models are interpretable, compact, and biologically inspired, but rely on small, hand-curated statistics sets that are difficult to generalize or extend. We introduce GramStatTexNet, a hybrid analysis-by-synthesis framework that combines the multi-scale Gabor filter structure of classical models with the flexibility of Gramian-based correlations, organized into structured filter families. This structured representation enables analyses that are challenging for deep-feature methods: each statistic carries a named filter-family identity, allowing us to decompose synthesis fidelity into per-family contributions and to learn an interpretable, low-dimensional embedding that preserves perceptual texture content. We compare our framework to classical and deep texture-synthesis baselines across diverse texture categories, and on multiple perceptual metrics, highlighting the compactness and interpretability advantages of this hybrid representation, alongside competitive synthesis quality. This same framework extends naturally to peripheral textures via spatial pooling, and to dynamic textures using a spatiotemporal filter bank. GramStatTexNet provides a unified, interpretable framework for analyzing and modeling visual information with natural extensions across space, time, and eccentricity. Project page: https://vdutell.github.io/gstn

1 Introduction

The human visual system demonstrates impressive performance and efficiency at processing and interpreting the dynamic visual world. In particular, human vision has the ability to recognize complex textures that are essential for identifying objects, surfaces, and materials. Humans achieve this both for static scenes and in the context of motion, enabling us to navigate and interact seamlessly with our environment. Understanding how to model these capabilities is crucial for advancing applications in computer vision and machine learning. These goals are also closely related to interpretability, where biological-vision can serve as a natural source of inspiration for learning effective and more transparent visual representations.

Neuroscience-informed approaches to texture synthesis (and closely related peripheral vision) often model visual areas using non-parametric multi-scale pyramids, decomposing images into filter responses, and aggregating features into statistics sets [43]. These statistics sets are predictive of neural responses to natural scenes [65], produce perceptually plausible textures, and serve as models of peripheral vision when applied over spatial pooling regions [47, 17]. Despite the success of such models for texture images, they rely on hand-curated statistics sets, which are challenging to design and to extend. One example of this is the spatiotemporal domain, where spatial statistics often lack clear analogues in time.

Deep-learning based approaches to texture and peripheral synthesis offer strong results in terms of quality and speed, and eliminate the need for hand-curated features, but their reliance on over-parameterized latent spaces comes at the cost of interpretability and biological feasibility. Gram-matrix-based approaches synthesize textures by matching correlations between filter responses, using either deep multi-layer networks [22] or single-layer random filters [56]. This approach has also been successful for generating peripheral syntheses [57, 13]. However, these models rely on pretrained layers from networks like VGG [53], and thus offer no representational compression compared to the highly efficient texture models from visual neuroscience.

In this work, we introduce GramStatTexNet (GSTN), an analysis-by-synthesis approach that bridges interpretability, biological plausibility, and synthesis quality in texture modeling. Our model generates texture syntheses comparable in quality to deep network-based models while remaining interpretable and efficient in representation size. We organize statistical representations into structured families and use contrastive learning to identify the most critical statistics for texture differentiation, reducing representation size while minimizing synthesis quality reduction and exposing which spatial-frequency, orientation, and color correlations carry texture identity, yielding testable hypotheses about which correlations visual cortex may encode. We further demonstrate that the same framework is compatible with classical peripheral-vision synthesis pipelines via spatial pooling, and extends naturally to dynamic video textures. Together, GramStatTexNet provides a unified, interpretable framework for modeling visual information that operates across space, time, and eccentricity.

2 Previous Work

Early approaches to texture synthesis were deeply rooted in efforts to model human vision both in neuroscience and computer vision. Julesz’ [28] early work utilized N-th order statistics in pixel space. Texture representation in Fourier space [34], and later in pyramid space [6, 19] improved texture models significantly [24]. Along with considerable improvement in synthesis quality, came a strong link to the neuroscience of human visual processing, with the oriented multi-scale filters of the steerable pyramid [51] mirroring both the receptive fields of neurons found in area V1 [55, 33], as well as their response properties [39]. The Portilla & Simoncelli (P&S) model [43] further improved synthesis quality by including pixel, autocorrelation, and magnitude statistics on pyramid responses.

For video, early methods resampled frames of the input [49], reproducing a clip without generating new spatiotemporal structure, or modeled temporal evolution with linear dynamical systems over a low-dimensional appearance model [15]. In vision science, motion has long been modeled with spatiotemporally oriented filters [1, 52], and oriented spacetime energies have been used to represent and recognize dynamic textures [11, 12]. Yet the compact pyramid-plus-correlation tradition of [Portilla and Simoncelli [43]] has not, to our knowledge, been extended to temporal synthesis, despite extensive characterization of human spatiotemporal sensitivity [29, 31].

Summary statistics texture models have been extended as peripheral vision models, with the incorporation of spatial pooling [47, 17]. This method involves synthesizing texture locally in many small overlapping regions, which when optimized jointly, lead to full-field image syntheses. By progressively increasing the size of these regions with increased distance from central vision, these models reflect loss of information in peripheral vision beyond the simple blurring of photoreceptor density loss. As analysis-by-synthesis models, they enable the synthesis of ‘metamers’ or ‘mongrels’. These image syntheses appear lossy when viewed foveally (with central vision), but appear normal when viewed peripherally (metamers), and have been shown to capture the information available to human peripheral vision, therefore predicting human performance on a wide range of visual tasks (mongrels). These models have been since extended to incorporate color [57], GPU acceleration [5], expanded field of view [4], and have been combined with deep learning to explore higher-level similarities and divergences in human and machine vision [23].

In addition to neural-inspired approaches, pure computer vision and deep learning approaches have had success in realistic synthesis of both static and dynamic textures. In the spatial domain, state-of-the-art texture synthesis often uses diffusion models to generate photorealistic results [7, 61], with the advantage of controllability through text prompting. In addition, neural cellular automata enable ultra-compact spatial [36] and real-time controllable spatiotemporal [41] synthesis. Deep features have also been used to evaluate texture properties directly, such as tileability [46]. For dynamic textures, long-range spatial and temporal dependencies have been shown to improve syntheses [62].

Closest to our approach, a line of work in deep learning generalizes these classical summary statistics to learned features [22, 54]. Style transfer [21] is the extension of a spatial texture method [22] which synthesizes textures by matching summary statistics defined as correlations between layers of pre-trained image networks such as VGG-Net [53], with even a single layer of random filters sufficing [56]. Like the classical models, this approach has been extended to peripheral vision [13, 57] and, with two-stream architectures, to video [54]. On one hand, these methods demonstrate strong results in terms of synthesis quality while eliminating the need for hand-curated statistics sets. However, compared to pyramid-based models they have three major disadvantages: 1) They are highly-overparametrized, with orders of magnitude more statistics. 2) They replace human visual neuroscience-informed filters with less biologically-feasible convolutional layers. 3) Their summary statistics of deep network hidden layer correlations are difficult to interpret.

3 GramStatTexNet

We present a simple but powerful model (Figure 1) that combines the interpretable and biologically-inspired pyramid filters of [43] with the Gramian matrix representation of [22]. GramStatTexNet (GSTN) leverages the GPU-accelerated multi-scale pyramids from [5], convolving input images with pyramid filters at individual combinations of orientation, phase, scale, and color, the output of which we call ‘pyramid images’. We treat each pyramid image as a channel, and calculate the pair-wise correlations between each pyramid image pair, collapsing over space as a Gram matrix. We use the upper triangle and diagonal of this matrix as the full statistics set for downstream analysis, where each statistic corresponds to a pairwise correlation between filter responses. This can be used not only to analyze the properties of a given texture, but also to synthesize new texture images.

3.1 Texture Synthesis

We first apply our model in an analysis-by-synthesis framework to generate novel texture images, matching the statistics set of an input image, and synthesizing new textures by optimizing noise images to match the statistics set. We demonstrate good synthesis quality over a variety of texture types and regularities, sampling textures from a variety of categories from the Describable Texture Dataset (DTD) [9] (Figure 2). Comparing GSTN to other related texture synthesis models, we see quality improvement over the P&S [43] multi-scale-pyramid synthesis method, and competitive quality to the much larger, deep-network and convolution-based synthesis methods [22, 56], despite over an order of magnitude fewer statistics. Evaluating these results quantitatively, and including MS-SSIM [59] (Figure 3), we find that GSTN outperforms P&S on the majority of categories across all nine evaluation metrics tested (30–46 of 47 categories per metric; Appendix Figure 10). Gatys  [22] is superior on deep-feature metrics (DISTS, LPIPS, DreamSim  [14, 64, 20]), which share VGG features or are trained on object-centric similarity judgments, while GSTN is better performing on classical perceptual and structural metrics (FSIM, SSIM, VIF, GMSD, HaarPSI  [63, 58, 50, 60, 44], PSD-L2) in 32–46 of 47 categories (Appendix Figure 11). Overall, this indicates quality parity of GSTN with Gatys at a 30× smaller representation. In addition, Ustyuzhaninov’s random-filter model [56] has slightly higher quality but uses 18× more statistics, while μNCA [36] is far more compact but must be trained per texture and has severe loss of detail.

4 Interpretable Representation of Texture

4.1 Correlation Families

An advantage of our method is that the Gramian representation for a given input texture is comprised of correlations between known pyramid filters, and is thus transparent and interpretable such that the properties of any given texture can be analyzed and understood from first-principles. In addition, through ablation, the quality of syntheses can be attributed to different statistical families. To make sense of these Gramian correlation statistics, we organize them into families falling into two main groups. First, statistics appending or correlating one or more non-sub-band (non-pyramid level) filter images, which we call ‘Non-sub-band’, and includes marginal statistics. The second group we call ‘Sub-band’ and computes correlations exclusively between sub-band images (Table 1). We further organize the Sub-band group into sub-groups, based on which properties are shared and differ between the pyramid images correlated. The hand-curated statistics sets from [43] rely heavily on correlation statistics analogous to the first 3 non-sub-band and first 6 sub-band families, which we call ‘structured’ statistics. These share all properties except for one (e.g. Cross-scale at neighboring levels). Family codes mark the varying attribute with X (e.g., sub_Xori: sub-band pairs differing only in orientation; sub_Xmulti: pairs differing in several attributes), and each channel is indexed as _L_O_C.

To analyze how statistical families differ across texture types, we group images by category [9] and evaluate the per-category mean and within-category standard deviation of each family’s z-scored correlations (Figure 4). Unsupervised hierarchical clustering on the mean fingerprints recovers an interpretable global organization, with regular/structured textures (chequered, striped, polka-dotted, grid) on the left, balanced soft/irregular textures (frilly, veined, lacelike, bubbly) on the right, and stochastic mid-frequency textures (flecked, marbled, cracked, fibrous) in the middle.

Several categories show distinctive single-family signatures that map onto recognizable image properties: chequered has the strongest marginal deviation, likely reflecting that its pixels are mostly either fully dark or fully light; lined and banded show elevated Magnitude multi-attr. (sub_magn_Xmulti), capturing the repetition of a single dominant orientation across spatial scales; frilly and veined show strong lowpass elevation, reflecting their smooth, gradual variation rather than sharp edges; and crosshatched shows elevated highpass, reflecting the fine-scale edges produced by its overlapping line patterns. Three families (Cross-phase re × im (sub_Xri_eq), Cross-phase re × mag (sub_Xrm_eq), and Imaginary multi-attr. (sub_imag_Xmulti)) are nearly flat, indicating that they may carry little information; we test their causal relevance via family ablation.

The heterogeneity heatmap (Figure 4, bottom) shows that texture types banded, lined, and zigzagged are diverse in statistics across exemplars (corresponding to a broad range of stripe widths, orientations, and contrasts), while soft/irregular categories on the right (frilly, cobwebbed, freckled) are statistically tight despite visual diversity, suggesting the family-level summary captures a stable statistical regime even when individual exemplars of a texture type look quite different.

4.2 Family-Based Ablation

To understand how synthesis quality is related to different family groups, we perform paired ablation experiments, synthesizing textures with each family removed (DROP) and with each family alone (KEEP ONLY) (Figure 5). DROP demonstrates which families are necessary, and KEEP ONLY shows which are sufficient. We find that no single family is sufficient on its own. Even the largest individual family (Mixed-phase multi-attr., n=15,336) produces visibly degraded textures, and the union of structured families related to classical pyramid statistics (n=1,758) preserves only coarse texture identity. The bulk of synthesis-relevant information is carried by the large unstructured families whose correlations span multiple filter attributes simultaneously (Non-oriented × band (pass_multi), Mixed-phase multi-attr. (sub_Xmulti)). Interestingly, synths from the families with near-zero values in Figure 4 (Cross-phase re × im (sub_Xri_eq), Cross-phase re × mag (sub_Xrm_eq), Imaginary multi-attr.(sub_imag_Xmulti)) show some of the worst quality, consistent with these carrying little information. Conversely, dropping individual families produces only minor visual degradation in most cases, with even the Mixed-phase multi-attr. drop of 15,336 statistics causing little visible loss, and reflecting substantial redundancy in the statistical representation. One notable exception is that dropping Non-oriented × band visibly disrupts synthesis. Together, these results suggest that the classical structured-statistics approach captures only a fraction of synthesis-relevant content; the bulk of texture identity is encoded in cross-attribute correlations (Non-oriented × band, Mixed-phase multi-attr.) that are absent from classical pyramid models, and may explain their characteristic synthesis limitations. The structured families approximate a subset of the P&S statistics, whose correlations drive V2 responses in macaque and human [18] and predict V4 selectivity and human texture discrimination  [38]. This grounding is at the level of families, not GSTN itself; the cross-attribute families are untested, making their importance a testable hypothesis about what higher visual areas encode beyond the classical set.

5 Feature Importance Ordering

To further investigate the contribution of individual texture statistics and families to synthesis quality, we use contrastive learning to reduce the correlation statistics to a compressed feature vector that can group textures (Figure 1, right). We train a single fully connected layer (28,929x100) on the output of GSTN using InfoNCE [40] to group texture crops from the same parent texture in the compressed space. We find that the trained single layer is sufficient to group same texture crops in embedding space (Appendix Figure 15). We solve the contrastive learning problem using gradient-based optimization. However, in this case with a single-layer encoder, it can also be solved analytically; we derive this solution in Appendix A.11.

To evaluate the importance of different statistics to the contrastive learning task, we order statistics from most to least important based on both the absolute value of their weightings (Appendix Figure 16), as well as by their Shapley values [48] (not shown, similar results). We find correlations between sub-band filter outputs with few or no shared attributes (Mixed-phase multi-attr.) are most important to the contrastive learning task. By contrast, correlations between lowpass filter outputs are least important for grouping textures. We visualize the relative contributions of individual families to the total statistics set when ordered by importance (Appendix Figure 17), and find that Mixed-phase multi-attr., highpass, Magnitude multi-attr., and Non-oriented × band families make an out-sized contribution to the most important statistics.

To evaluate the transfer of importance in the contrastive task to synthesis quality, we perform a set of additional synthesis ablation experiments, matching only statistics of the highest weighting in the contrastive learning task (Figure 6). We find that importance in contrastive learning broadly transfers to synthesis quality: by selecting the top-ranked statistics, we achieve acceptable syntheses with only 5,000 of the total 28,929 statistics, an 83% reduction. Statistics from bottom of the ranking, by contrast, produce extremely poor syntheses, confirming that the ranking carries real information about which statistics are needed for texture reproduction.

When we compare top-ranked statistics to randomly-selected control sets of the same size, we find that randomly chosen statistics in fact out-perform the top-ranked ones for synthesis (Figure 3), even achieving acceptable synthesis with only 1000 statistics in some cases (Figure 6). We believe this reflects a property of the contrastive task, which selects statistics that discriminate between texture categories, and for which a few specific families (Mixed-phase multi-attr., highpass) maximally separate categories in the compressed embedding space. Synthesis, on the other hand, requires statistics that broadly constrain perceptual appearance across many aspects of a texture. A random subset of statistics samples broadly across the full feature space, including individually low-discriminability statistics that nonetheless contribute to constraining the synthesis to produce a coherent texture. The top-N subset may be more compact and more interpretable, but provides a narrower basis for reconstruction. This finding aligns with the classical distinction between discriminative and generative objectives in machine learning [37]: representations optimized to discriminate between categories are not necessarily optimal for modeling the joint statistical structure within them. This result also echoes [56], where correlations on random convolutional filters prove sufficient for texture synthesis.

6 Beyond Static Foveal Synthesis

Having established an interpretable statistical representation for static textures, we now demonstrate that the same framework extends naturally beyond the static and uniform texture image setting. We present two extensions: applying the model over spatial pooling regions to produce foveated syntheses compatible with peripheral-vision pipelines, and replacing the spatial filter bank with a spatiotemporal one to synthesize dynamic textures. Neither extension requires changes to the underlying analysis-by-synthesis pipeline, only to the spatial aggregation of the model, or a temporal dimension to the filter bank; these illustrate the generality and interoperability of our pyramid plus correlation-statistics approach.

Peripheral Synthesis: Demonstrating compatibility with peripheral-vision synthesis, we combine our method with spatial pooling following [17, 47] and motivated by evidence that pooled summary statistics predict crowding [3], generating foveated synthesis on full-size images which have non-uniform texture (Figure 7). The resulting syntheses preserve high fidelity at gaze center and progressively introduce spatial distortions toward the periphery, matching the smooth, spatially-varying degradation pattern produced by prior peripheral synthesis pipelines [17, 5]. Utilizing the reduced representation learned via contrastive learning, we reduce the size of our peripheral syntheses significantly, while retaining high quality. Our resolution study (Appendix Table 5, Figure 14) quantifies the tradeoff for a fixed statistic budget with quality falling as region size grows, though regions are evaluated in isolation rather than jointly optimized. While we do not run psychophysical validation here, we show GSTN remains compatible with spatially-pooled synthesis pipelines.

Dynamic Textures: Extending human vision inspired models such as the Portilla–Simoncelli image model [43] to the spatiotemporal domain is non-trivial, as its hand-selected cross-scale and cross-orientation statistics lack clear analogues in the time domain. Instead of hand picking important statistics, our method, leveraging all combinations of filter correlation statistics with the Gram matrix, can be naturally extended to video textures. We extend the spatial pyramid into the time domain by designing a bank of 3D Gabor filters arranged in stacked concentric rings in spatiotemporal frequency space, similar to oriented spacetime-energy representations  [11, 12] with each filter paired with its quadrature complement. The filter bank is parameterized to span the spatiotemporal frequency range of human visual sensitivity [29]; details and visualizations in Appendix.

We apply the same Gram matrix model to calculate correlations between our spatiotemporal filters, synthesizing texture videos by matching the set of filter correlation statistics. While contrastive learning in the spatiotemporal case is not computationally feasible given resource constraints, we are able to reduce our model size somewhat based on our findings from the spatial-only case, removing lowpass filters. Our model synthesizes videos that visually match well to the target textures (Figure 8), and results span a set of texture videos chosen to maximize variety in structure and motion properties, while maintaining computational tractability (Table 7). Quantitatively, cellular automaton model DyNCA  [41] better matches spatial features, while GSTN better matches motion; videos are at https://vdutell.github.io/gstn. We do not claim improvement over prior dynamic-texture synthesis methods including [54, 41], but instead show that the same pyramid + correlation framework that succeeds on static textures extends naturally to video.

7 Discussion

GramStatTexNet merges the interpretability of biologically inspired multi-scale pyramid filters with the flexibility of Gramian-based correlations. By organizing statistics into structured filter families, we identify a compressed subset of correlations that retain synthesis quality while substantially reducing representation size, and expose which spatial-frequency, orientation, and color correlations carry texture identity. The same framework extends naturally to peripheral and dynamic textures via spatial pooling and a spatiotemporal filter bank, providing a unified, interpretable framework for modeling visual information across space, time, and eccentricity.

Limitations Our depletion analysis uses GSTN-wrap for computational efficiency; replication on GSTN-zpad is left to future work, though we expect qualitatively similar findings, with improvement gains mirroring the full statistics set. We provide no new neural or psychophysical validation of this representation, for static, peripheral, or dynamic textures; validation against human observers remains future work. Finally, contrastive compression is currently tractable only for the spatial model.

Future work Psychophysical evaluation of peripheral and dynamic-texture syntheses would test whether the compressed representation preserves perceptually relevant information. Scaling contrastive compression to spatiotemporal statistics would reveal which spatiotemporal correlations carry the most information for dynamic texture identity. Finally, the GSTN statistics could be matched via gradient-guidance with diffusion-based generative models, which we leave to future work.

Broader Impacts This is foundational research on interpretable, biologically-inspired visual representations, with no direct path to negative societal applications. Our syntheses are visibly lower-fidelity than current diffusion-based methods, so we do not meaningfully advance generative misuse with deepfakes. Potential positive impacts include: (i) interpretable, family-decomposed representations that link learned features to well-characterized properties of biological vision: our pyramid filters approximate V1 response properties, and the family taxonomy offers a hypothesis space, not validated here, for how V2 might combine V1 outputs, complementing macaque single-unit [65] and macaque/human [18] evidence of V2 selectivity for the structured-family statistics; (ii) compressed representations that reduce storage and compute for downstream pipelines; and (iii) compatibility with foveated rendering, with potential applications in low-bandwidth AR/VR and accessibility tools.

8 Acknowledgments and Disclosures

We thank the many individuals whose feedback and helpful discussions improved this paper, including Bruno Olshausen, Ayush Tewari, Prafull Sharma, Eric Li, Shaden Alshammari, as well as the anonymous reviewers and AC. This work was funded by the CSAIL MEnTorEd Opportunities in Research (METEOR) Fellowship, US National Science Foundation under grant number 1955219, as well as National Science Foundation Grant BCS-1826757 to PI Rosenholtz. The authors acknowledge the MIT SuperCloud [45] and Lincoln Laboratory Supercomputing Center for providing HPC resources that have contributed to the research results reported within this paper.

（参考文献见原文。）

Appendix A Appendix

A.1 Image and Video Synthesis

We synthesized visualized textures following the synthesis procedure in [Koevesdi et al. [30]], using the filter portion of the codebase from [5], with the pyramid settings at 4 orientations, 6 edge levels, edge start at level 1, with marginal statistics included. For image synthesis batched over the DTD dataset, we used Prodigy optimizer [35]. For image synthesis on individual textures, foveated synthesis, and spatiotemporal generation, we used the L-BFGS solver [32] as demonstrated for textures in [22]. See Appendix section A.2 for details on optimizers.

Synthesis Baselines

Syntheses for random filters [56] were created by a custom Pytorch port from the official Theano repo (https://github.com/ivust/random-texture-synthesis) with 20k iterations and the Prodigy solver [35]. Synths for Gatys et al [22] were created from an unofficial Pytorch repo for [22] (https://github.com/trsvchn/deep-textures). Synths for Portilla & Simoncelli [43] were created using the official color extension package in Matlab (https://www.cns.nyu.edu/pub/eero/colorTextureSynth.tgz). Syntheses for µNCA [36] used the canonical JAX notebook from the official repository (https://github.com/google-research/self-organising-systems), trained per texture at 256×256 (one seed; the polka-dotted failure was confirmed over three seeds). Table 3 reports this run; Figure 2 shows the 128×128 native-resolution run. DyNCA [41] syntheses used the authors’ official implementation (https://github.com/IVRL/DyNCA), fitting both motion and appearance to the target video at 64×64 for 5,000 iterations, matched to the GSTN video resolution.

GSTN-wrap vs. GSTN-zpad.

GSTN-wrap and GSTN-zpad differ in the boundary condition of the steerable-pyramid convolutions. GSTN-wrap assumes the texture is stationary and tile-able and is faster, but does not retain edge boundaries. GSTN-zpad instead pads the image with a border of zeros before the Fourier transform, so opposite edges no longer interact and the boundary behaves as a non-repeating edge with no tiling assumption, at the cost of compute time.

Peripheral Synthesis

Spatial pooling of our model for peripheral syntheses was incorporated by tiling the image with overlapping pooling regions of 16x16 pixels tiled across the image, then synthesizing our texture model at each region in parallel. We utilize the pooling method from [5], warping the image, synthesizing over uniformly-tiled regions in the warped image space, and un-warping after synthesis, with parameters matched as closely as possible to [17].

Video Synthesis

To synthesize novel videos matching the statistics of input videos, we follow the same procedure as for images, calculating the spatiotemporal statistics vector from a target video. Then, starting with a white-noise video, we use L-BFGS to adjust pixel values in the synthetic video, using backpropagation of the mean squared error in statistics space between the synthetic and target video. This results in a synthetic video that matches the statistics of the original target video, but with scrambling of absolute spatial and temporal localization. Given this loss of spatial and temporal information, we use texture videos from the DynTex Database [42], which we spatially center-crop and downsample to 64x64 to minimize artifacts and ensure uniformity using 20 frames at 15 fps (DynTex IDs 54pb110, 54pi110, 55fc210, 6440110, 6441210).

A.2 Optimizers: L-BFGS, Madgrad, Prodigy Comparison

L-BFGS [32] is often the optimizer of choice for statistical texture synthesis given its speed and efficiency at jointly optimizing the pixel space to find the target image, due to it being a second order method. However, the calculation of the Hessian makes batching image syntheses problematic, and non-batched synthesis on dataset scale intractably slow. To address this, we explored the use of MADGRAD [10] and Prodigy [35] as alternative optimizers that are batch-compatible, and produce synthesis comparable to L-BFGS, the de-facto gold standard for pixel-backpropagation based synthesis (Figure 9). L-BFGS uses 100 outer iterations of Strong-Wolfe-line-searched LBFGS (lr=0.5, max_iter=100, history=20, tolerance_grad=1e-7); MADGRAD uses 20k iterations at lr=0.07, momentum=0.99; Prodigy uses 20k iterations with auto-tuned step size (lr=0.04, d0=1e-2, betas=(0.99, 0.999), safeguard_warmup=True). All optimizers minimize MSE between target and synthesis Gram-statistic vectors with wrap or zero-padded mode, and the best-loss iterate is reported.

The choice of optimizer was determined by individual experiment requirements. For single-image qualitative comparisons, foveated peripheral synthesis, and video synthesis, we use L-BFGS, which converges efficiently on individual targets due to its second-order Hessian approximation. However, as discussed above, the Hessian computation does not separate cleanly across batched images, making L-BFGS intractable for large-scale evaluation. For experiments requiring batched synthesis across the validation set including texture variety, depletion experiments, and all quantitative results, we use Prodigy.

A.3 Computational Resources

For the image synthesis experiments, synthesizing a single condition for the DTD-141 (141 subset) used two NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 GPUs, taking approximately 3-4 hours for the GSTN-wrap, and 6-8 hours for the GSTN-zpad condition with the Prodigy solver. Total estimated runtime for the image experiments is 1-2 weeks GPU time. For the video syntheses, synthesis ran on a single NVIDIA A-100 and took 1-2 hours for a single video. Foveated syntheses ran on a single NVIDIA A-100 and took 2-4 hours. Storage was <100GB for all datasets and experiments. Many additional preliminary and failed experiments, testing different optimizers, hyperparameters, resolutions, and pyramid settings were conducted than were reported in the paper, and while none individually used significant resources, altogether the use was not negligible.

A.4 Datasets

For the spatial texture model, we utilized the Describable Textures Database (DTD) [9], keeping the largest centered square and resizing the image to 256x256 for synthesis, and 5-crops for the contrastive learning. For training the contrastive learning module, we used the entire training subset of split 1, which samples all 47 texture types. For the evaluations of our syntheses and depletions, for computational tractability, we sampled 3 randomly chosen images from each category of the validation subset of validation split 1, for a total of 141 images (DTD-141). For computational reasons, we also evaluate [43], [22], and [56] on this DTD-141 subset. Because [36] takes many hours for a single synthesis, it was evaluated only on the 11-texture subset of Figure 2.

For the video texture model, we utilized the Dynamic Texture Database (DynTex) [42]. For computational tractability, we synthesized a small subset of videos selected to vary in frequency, shape, and motion type, but do not evaluate on the entire dataset.

A.5 Full Statistics Image Synthesis

We compare quantitative performance of GSTN per texture category over DTD-141 on a variety of metrics. A set of bias-neutral metrics (VIF, GMSD, HaarPSI, PSD-L2) was added to address the concern that local-moment metrics (SSIM, FSIM) are structurally aligned with GSTN’s Gram-of-pyramid-bands representation while deep-feature metrics (DISTS [14], LPIPS [64], DreamSim [20]) are aligned with Gatys’ deep-VGG training objective. VIF  [50] is grounded in natural-scene statistics and Gaussian scale-mixture wavelet models; GMSD [60] compares the spatial deviation of local gradient-magnitude similarity; HaarPSI [44] uses Haar-wavelet feature similarity; PSD-L2 is the L2 distance between log power-spectral densities. None of these share architecture or training objective with GSTN or Gatys, but all four consistently favor GSTN-zpad in per-category comparisons (Figures 10, 11), supporting that GSTN-zpad’s advantage over P&S is not a metric-bias artifact; against Gatys, results split by metric family (Figure 11).

A.6 Seed Sensitivity

We tested the sensitivity of our method to multiple seeds to evaluate the stability of synthesis quality (Table 2, Figure 12). We find that both qualitatively and quantitatively, texture identity accounts for far more of the variation than seed, and this trend is consistent across all metrics tested.

A.7 Quantitative Comparisons on 11-Texture Subset

Table 3 reports quantitative performance on the 11 textures of Figure 2, including μNCA. GSTN is comparable to Gatys and Ustyuzhaninov on many metrics at a much smaller size, while μNCA, the smallest model, is worst on 7 of 9 metrics.

A.8 Efficiency Comparisons

We performed an efficiency evaluation across models, size, inference, and synthesis time (Table  4). Overall, GSTN shows balanced efficiency compared to other methods, with the lowest GPU memory load, and with Prodigy optimizer can be highly parallelized on a single GPU to decrease effective per-image synthesis time. While Gatys dominates in speed, its representation size (number of statistics) is very large in comparison. And while μNCA is by far the smallest model in terms of number of statistics, as a cellular automaton it unrolls over many steps at full resolution, leading to a huge effective memory footprint, and its synthesis time is by far the worst (though the synthesis time may perform better and be parallelizable natively on a TPU).
item.content:encoded:
一句话：深度网络真实但不可解释；神经科学启发的金字塔可解释，却依赖少量手工统计量、难以泛化。

要点：

  • 两条路各有短板：深度网络合成真实感强，但表示**不透明、过参数化**，与生物视觉几乎没有直接联系；神经科学启发的金字塔模型可解释、紧凑，却依赖**少量人工挑选的统计量**，难以泛化与扩展
  • GramStatTexNet 走混合路线：把多尺度金字塔结构与可学的统计表示结合，做「分析-合成」式纹理建模
  • 定位是同时拿到效率、可解释性与合成质量，而不是在两者之间二选一

为什么值得看：纹理是材质管线的地基，而「可解释 + 可扩展」意味着能定向编辑而不是随机重采样。对需要可控纹理生成（而不是抽卡式生成）的团队，这类分析-合成框架更接近工具。

中文摘要：深度网络在纹理合成上的真实感很强，但常依赖不透明、过参数化的表示，与生物视觉几乎没有直接联系；反过来，受神经科学启发的金字塔模型可解释且紧凑，却依赖少量人工挑选的统计量，难以泛化或扩展。GramStatTexNet 因此提出一个混合式的「分析-合成」框架，把多尺度金字塔结构与可学习的统计表示结合起来，在保留可解释性的同时提升效率与合成质量。对材质管线而言，可解释意味着可以定向编辑纹理的某个统计层面，而不是只能重新采样。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-11-19

本期推送：2026-11-20

GramStatTexNet: Efficient, Interpretable, and Neuro-Inspired Texture Analysis-by-Synthesis

Abstract

Deep networks achieve high realism in texture synthesis but often rely on opaque, over-parameterized representations that have limited direct connection to biological vision. Neuroscience-informed pyramid models are interpretable, compact, and biologically inspired, but rely on small, hand-curated statistics sets that are difficult to generalize or extend. We introduce GramStatTexNet, a hybrid analysis-by-synthesis framework that combines the multi-scale Gabor filter structure of classical models with the flexibility of Gramian-based correlations, organized into structured filter families. This structured representation enables analyses that are challenging for deep-feature methods: each statistic carries a named filter-family identity, allowing us to decompose synthesis fidelity into per-family contributions and to learn an interpretable, low-dimensional embedding that preserves perceptual texture content. We compare our framework to classical and deep texture-synthesis baselines across diverse texture categories, and on multiple perceptual metrics, highlighting the compactness and interpretability advantages of this hybrid representation, alongside competitive synthesis quality. This same framework extends naturally to peripheral textures via spatial pooling, and to dynamic textures using a spatiotemporal filter bank. GramStatTexNet provides a unified, interpretable framework for analyzing and modeling visual information with natural extensions across space, time, and eccentricity. Project page: https://vdutell.github.io/gstn

1 Introduction

The human visual system demonstrates impressive performance and efficiency at processing and interpreting the dynamic visual world. In particular, human vision has the ability to recognize complex textures that are essential for identifying objects, surfaces, and materials. Humans achieve this both for static scenes and in the context of motion, enabling us to navigate and interact seamlessly with our environment. Understanding how to model these capabilities is crucial for advancing applications in computer vision and machine learning. These goals are also closely related to interpretability, where biological-vision can serve as a natural source of inspiration for learning effective and more transparent visual representations.

Neuroscience-informed approaches to texture synthesis (and closely related peripheral vision) often model visual areas using non-parametric multi-scale pyramids, decomposing images into filter responses, and aggregating features into statistics sets [43]. These statistics sets are predictive of neural responses to natural scenes [65], produce perceptually plausible textures, and serve as models of peripheral vision when applied over spatial pooling regions [47, 17]. Despite the success of such models for texture images, they rely on hand-curated statistics sets, which are challenging to design and to extend. One example of this is the spatiotemporal domain, where spatial statistics often lack clear analogues in time.

Deep-learning based approaches to texture and peripheral synthesis offer strong results in terms of quality and speed, and eliminate the need for hand-curated features, but their reliance on over-parameterized latent spaces comes at the cost of interpretability and biological feasibility. Gram-matrix-based approaches synthesize textures by matching correlations between filter responses, using either deep multi-layer networks [22] or single-layer random filters [56]. This approach has also been successful for generating peripheral syntheses [57, 13]. However, these models rely on pretrained layers from networks like VGG [53], and thus offer no representational compression compared to the highly efficient texture models from visual neuroscience.

In this work, we introduce GramStatTexNet (GSTN), an analysis-by-synthesis approach that bridges interpretability, biological plausibility, and synthesis quality in texture modeling. Our model generates texture syntheses comparable in quality to deep network-based models while remaining interpretable and efficient in representation size. We organize statistical representations into structured families and use contrastive learning to identify the most critical statistics for texture differentiation, reducing representation size while minimizing synthesis quality reduction and exposing which spatial-frequency, orientation, and color correlations carry texture identity, yielding testable hypotheses about which correlations visual cortex may encode. We further demonstrate that the same framework is compatible with classical peripheral-vision synthesis pipelines via spatial pooling, and extends naturally to dynamic video textures. Together, GramStatTexNet provides a unified, interpretable framework for modeling visual information that operates across space, time, and eccentricity.

2 Previous Work

Early approaches to texture synthesis were deeply rooted in efforts to model human vision both in neuroscience and computer vision. Julesz’ [28] early work utilized N-th order statistics in pixel space. Texture representation in Fourier space [34], and later in pyramid space [6, 19] improved texture models significantly [24]. Along with considerable improvement in synthesis quality, came a strong link to the neuroscience of human visual processing, with the oriented multi-scale filters of the steerable pyramid [51] mirroring both the receptive fields of neurons found in area V1 [55, 33], as well as their response properties [39]. The Portilla & Simoncelli (P&S) model [43] further improved synthesis quality by including pixel, autocorrelation, and magnitude statistics on pyramid responses.

For video, early methods resampled frames of the input [49], reproducing a clip without generating new spatiotemporal structure, or modeled temporal evolution with linear dynamical systems over a low-dimensional appearance model [15]. In vision science, motion has long been modeled with spatiotemporally oriented filters [1, 52], and oriented spacetime energies have been used to represent and recognize dynamic textures [11, 12]. Yet the compact pyramid-plus-correlation tradition of [Portilla and Simoncelli [43]] has not, to our knowledge, been extended to temporal synthesis, despite extensive characterization of human spatiotemporal sensitivity [29, 31].

Summary statistics texture models have been extended as peripheral vision models, with the incorporation of spatial pooling [47, 17]. This method involves synthesizing texture locally in many small overlapping regions, which when optimized jointly, lead to full-field image syntheses. By progressively increasing the size of these regions with increased distance from central vision, these models reflect loss of information in peripheral vision beyond the simple blurring of photoreceptor density loss. As analysis-by-synthesis models, they enable the synthesis of ‘metamers’ or ‘mongrels’. These image syntheses appear lossy when viewed foveally (with central vision), but appear normal when viewed peripherally (metamers), and have been shown to capture the information available to human peripheral vision, therefore predicting human performance on a wide range of visual tasks (mongrels). These models have been since extended to incorporate color [57], GPU acceleration [5], expanded field of view [4], and have been combined with deep learning to explore higher-level similarities and divergences in human and machine vision [23].

In addition to neural-inspired approaches, pure computer vision and deep learning approaches have had success in realistic synthesis of both static and dynamic textures. In the spatial domain, state-of-the-art texture synthesis often uses diffusion models to generate photorealistic results [7, 61], with the advantage of controllability through text prompting. In addition, neural cellular automata enable ultra-compact spatial [36] and real-time controllable spatiotemporal [41] synthesis. Deep features have also been used to evaluate texture properties directly, such as tileability [46]. For dynamic textures, long-range spatial and temporal dependencies have been shown to improve syntheses [62].

Closest to our approach, a line of work in deep learning generalizes these classical summary statistics to learned features [22, 54]. Style transfer [21] is the extension of a spatial texture method [22] which synthesizes textures by matching summary statistics defined as correlations between layers of pre-trained image networks such as VGG-Net [53], with even a single layer of random filters sufficing [56]. Like the classical models, this approach has been extended to peripheral vision [13, 57] and, with two-stream architectures, to video [54]. On one hand, these methods demonstrate strong results in terms of synthesis quality while eliminating the need for hand-curated statistics sets. However, compared to pyramid-based models they have three major disadvantages: 1) They are highly-overparametrized, with orders of magnitude more statistics. 2) They replace human visual neuroscience-informed filters with less biologically-feasible convolutional layers. 3) Their summary statistics of deep network hidden layer correlations are difficult to interpret.

3 GramStatTexNet

We present a simple but powerful model (Figure 1) that combines the interpretable and biologically-inspired pyramid filters of [43] with the Gramian matrix representation of [22]. GramStatTexNet (GSTN) leverages the GPU-accelerated multi-scale pyramids from [5], convolving input images with pyramid filters at individual combinations of orientation, phase, scale, and color, the output of which we call ‘pyramid images’. We treat each pyramid image as a channel, and calculate the pair-wise correlations between each pyramid image pair, collapsing over space as a Gram matrix. We use the upper triangle and diagonal of this matrix as the full statistics set for downstream analysis, where each statistic corresponds to a pairwise correlation between filter responses. This can be used not only to analyze the properties of a given texture, but also to synthesize new texture images.

3.1 Texture Synthesis

We first apply our model in an analysis-by-synthesis framework to generate novel texture images, matching the statistics set of an input image, and synthesizing new textures by optimizing noise images to match the statistics set. We demonstrate good synthesis quality over a variety of texture types and regularities, sampling textures from a variety of categories from the Describable Texture Dataset (DTD) [9] (Figure 2). Comparing GSTN to other related texture synthesis models, we see quality improvement over the P&S [43] multi-scale-pyramid synthesis method, and competitive quality to the much larger, deep-network and convolution-based synthesis methods [22, 56], despite over an order of magnitude fewer statistics. Evaluating these results quantitatively, and including MS-SSIM [59] (Figure 3), we find that GSTN outperforms P&S on the majority of categories across all nine evaluation metrics tested (30–46 of 47 categories per metric; Appendix Figure 10). Gatys  [22] is superior on deep-feature metrics (DISTS, LPIPS, DreamSim  [14, 64, 20]), which share VGG features or are trained on object-centric similarity judgments, while GSTN is better performing on classical perceptual and structural metrics (FSIM, SSIM, VIF, GMSD, HaarPSI  [63, 58, 50, 60, 44], PSD-L2) in 32–46 of 47 categories (Appendix Figure 11). Overall, this indicates quality parity of GSTN with Gatys at a 30× smaller representation. In addition, Ustyuzhaninov’s random-filter model [56] has slightly higher quality but uses 18× more statistics, while μNCA [36] is far more compact but must be trained per texture and has severe loss of detail.

4 Interpretable Representation of Texture

4.1 Correlation Families

An advantage of our method is that the Gramian representation for a given input texture is comprised of correlations between known pyramid filters, and is thus transparent and interpretable such that the properties of any given texture can be analyzed and understood from first-principles. In addition, through ablation, the quality of syntheses can be attributed to different statistical families.
